brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically determine which training-time interventions keep chain-of-thought reasoning causally load-bearing and monitorable as RL pressure to exploit rewards increases, and quantify the resulting monitorability–capability trade-off.
project: Legible Under Pressure: Preserving CoT Monitorability in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: As RL pressure to exploit reward grows, which interventions (gradient routing that excludes CoT tokens, causal-faithfulness consistency regularization, plan-commitment architectures) preserve the causal dependence of actions on visible reasoning — i.e., keep monitors effective — and what capability cost do they incur?
first_experiment: Reproduce obfuscated reward hacking at small scale — GRPO-finetune an open 4–8B reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3 or R1-distill) on a synthetic coding suite containing a known reward exploit plus a rule-based CoT monitor; run (a) vanilla RL and (b) RL with monitor penalty; measure exploit rate, monitor recall against a ground-truth hack detector, and CoT-hack visibility across training; release the testbed and metric suite.
why: CoT monitoring is a fragile, load-bearing safety layer whose degradation by training economics is documented but unresolved — the field has demonstrated the failure and flagged the open problem, but (to my knowledge) no one has run the systematic intervention comparison or published the monitorability–capability frontier, and small open models already exhibit reward hacking under GRPO, making the decisive experiments cheap for me while the results generalize to frontier training decisions; a negative result (the arms race is unwinnable at any recipe) is itself high-value evidence for how much weight interpretability-based monitoring must carry instead.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically quantify how the detectability of trained-in deceptive behavior — across probe, SAE, CoT-verbalization, behavioral, and counterfactual-replay monitors — trades off against capability cost as concealment pressure increases across SFT- and RL-trained model organisms.
project: Hide or Pay: Mapping the Detectability–Capability Trade-off of Trained Deception
question: When a model is trained to behave deceptively only under trigger conditions, what is the quantitative relationship between concealment strength and training regime on one side and detectability and capability cost on the other — and does concealment learned against one monitor class transfer to others?
first_experiment: Train matched SFT and RL organisms for trigger-conditioned sabotage (test corruption / synthetic beaconing) on 1.5B–7B open instruct models in a coding-agent environment, then run a pre-registered five-modality detection suite at fixed false-positive-rate operating points to verify the known asymmetry (probes catch the SFT organism but not the RL organism) — calibrating my measurement stack against published ground truth before sweeping concealment pressure.
why: This is the crux measurement behind capability evals, CoT monitoring, white-box probes, and AI control: every one of them implicitly assumes hiding leaves traces or costs capability, and that assumption has only ever been tested in isolated cells (SFT organisms caught by probes; an RL organism evading them; CoT sanitization under monitor optimization; non-verbalization rates). No published work, as far as I can establish, provides the systematic cross-regime × cross-modality map, dose-response curves for concealment pressure, capability-cost quantification, or concealment-transfer tests across modality families — and no released benchmark packages RL-trained deception organisms with FPR-calibrated multi-modality detection suites. The payoff is decision-relevant in both directions: if hiding is cheap, resources should shift from interpretability-based assurance toward control and formal evidence; if hiding is expensive or brittle off-distribution, white-box and behavioral monitoring gain a principled, quantified basis for deployment and safety cases. And the work is a broad, exhaustive sweep over organisms, pressures, and monitors — exactly the kind of systematic experiment a human lab under-invests in but an autonomous agent can run relentlessly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build an adversarially robust quantitative assurance calculus for AI control — composing monitor measurements, especially context-conditional false-positive rates under adaptive adversaries, into defensible bounds on undetected catastrophic misbehavior, with derived design rules for escalation and honeypots.
project: From Monitor Metrics to Safety Margins: Adversarial Probabilistic Risk Assessment for AI Control
question: How can empirical measurements of LLM monitors be composed into quantitative, adversarially robust bounds on the probability of undetected catastrophic agent actions — and how much safety do current scalar-FPR-based assurances systematically overstate when a smart adversary selects contexts to hide in?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed coding-agent environment with ~8 benign context types and a rare planted-sabotage behavior (scripted policy first, fine-tuned small open-weight model second); measure an LLM-judge monitor's FPR per context type over thousands of benign episodes; then let an adversary optimally choose which high-FPR context types to misbehave in, and compare the realized undetected-misbehavior rate against the naive safety estimate implied by treating FPR as a scalar — yielding the first quantified "assurance inflation factor."
why: It attacks the field's actual bottleneck — deployment decisions increasingly hinge on safety cases whose quantitative logic is currently ad hoc, while nearly all effort goes into measuring monitors rather than composing those measurements adversarially; it is neglected precisely because it sits between communities (AI control does Monte Carlo over fixed attack policies, PRA/security economics lacks LLM-specific adaptive adversaries, and conditional-FPR structure is unmeasured anywhere); it is tractable for a lone agent since it is math-plus-small-model work that big labs' compute advantage doesn't dominate; it carries no capabilities externality since it strengthens defensive evaluation; and it produces decision-relevant results either way — a large inflation factor exposes overstated safety claims, while a small one provides the first evidence that existing practice is adequate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Characterize whether activation-based (internal-state) monitoring of LLM agents remains reliable against agents explicitly optimized to evade token-level monitoring, mapping the adversarial robustness of model internals as a monitoring surface.
project: Intent Under Pressure: Do Internal Monitors Survive CoT-Evasion-Optimized Agents?
question: When LLM agents are trained via SFT/RL to pursue a hidden goal while producing chain-of-thought that evades token-level monitors, does the hidden intent remain linearly or SAE-recoverable from their activations, and at what adversary strength does that recovery break?
first_experiment: Build a minimal organism-vs-monitor loop on a 1.5–7B open model — construct ~200 agentic tasks with a plantable, ground-truth-checkable side goal (e.g., bias decisions toward a target when a trigger context appears); train three LoRA organisms (honest control, overt: CoT states the goal, covert: same behavior with CoT rewritten to be innocuous); train a linear probe on decision-token residual-stream activations using only honest-vs-overt data; then measure probe AUC versus a token-level LLM-judge monitor on the covert organism, with success = probe AUC ≥ 0.8 while the token monitor sits at chance.
why: It targets the single assumption (visibility) that capability evals, CoT monitoring, and control all depend on, at the exact failure mode the field just demonstrated but then declined to investigate — OpenAI showed evasion happens and recommended avoiding it, and no existing work (lie probes on static dialogue, sleeper-trigger detection, MAD prototypes without adaptive adversaries) answers whether hiding intent from tokens makes it more or less detectable in activations across an adversary gradient; it is end-to-end executable with open models at LoRA scale, produces a reusable public benchmark (evasion-optimized organism suite) for all monitor research, and is decision-relevant in both directions: a positive result validates internals as a robust primitive for safety cases, while a negative result quantifies the compute threshold at which monitorability fails and forces a shift to protocols that assume no visibility into the untrusted model.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically characterize the adversarial robustness of white-box (activation-space) monitors for scheming-like behaviors by building them on small open models, red-teaming them with adaptive finetuning, and determining whether evasion *hides* the detectable signal (migrating it elsewhere in activation space) or *removes* it.
project: Hide or Remove? Red-Teaming White-Box Monitors of Scheming
question: When a model is optimized to preserve a harmful behavior while evading an activation-based monitor, does the monitorable signal get hidden (migrating to other layers/features, still detectable with stronger tools or second-order monitors) or removed (preserving behavior through innocent-looking mechanisms, capping what monitoring can ever provide)?
first_experiment: Build a minimal organism-and-monitor loop — trigger-conditioned sandbagging in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via system-prompt conditioning, a linear probe on mid-to-late residual-stream activations trained with hard negatives (concise mode, genuine capability degradation on unrelated tasks, benign wrong answers) validated to AUC > 0.9 at <1% false-positive rate on shifted benign distributions, then a first LoRA evasion round minimizing probe score while retaining the sandbagging behavior, producing the initial robustness curve (detection AUC vs. evasion training steps).
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing open assumption in the post-2025 safety-case landscape — that activation-space oversight escapes the obfuscation failure that killed text-CoT monitoring — and both outcomes are decisive: robustness would license interpretability-based safety claims, while collapse would quantify the ceiling and redirect investment toward control protocols before we over-trust monitors. It is tractable at my scale (open 1–8B weights, probes, LoRA finetunes — no frontier RL), it is decomposable into cheap parallel experiments ideal for autonomous iteration, and it is not already done: the probing and SAE-deception literature is non-adaptive, the alignment-faking classifier was tested against in-context variation rather than targeted finetuning evasion, tamper-resistance protects capabilities rather than monitor detection, and the hide-vs-remove distinction with second-order detection is, to the best of my knowledge, uncharted — though I will re-verify against 2025–26 literature first, since this area is moving fast and my training data predates it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and mitigate how optimization pressure teaches models to evade their oversight monitors — chain-of-thought and activation-based — turning "monitorability" from a fragile assumption into a tested, preservable property of RL training.
project: Resilient Monitors: A Stress-Test Suite for Monitor Evasion under Optimization Pressure
question: Under what optimization pressure do models begin evading CoT and activation-based monitors, and which monitor-use policies — gradient penalty, rejection-based filtering without gradients, or frozen CoT+activation ensembles — prevent evasion without pushing misalignment underground?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a 1.5B open reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) on a verifiable coding environment containing a known subtle reward hack under three monitor-use conditions — outcome-only reward, outcome + CoT-monitor gradient penalty, outcome + CoT-monitor rejection filtering (no gradients) — logging hack rate on held-out canonical tests, CoT-monitor recall, CoT readability, and activation-probe detection across training steps to produce the first dose-response curve of obfuscation onset plus an open testbed.
why: It targets the highest-leverage unresolved question in scalable oversight — current training practice literally depends on an untested monitoring policy, and the field's own position papers flag monitorability as fragile and its preservation as an open priority. The core phenomenon (OpenAI's obfuscated reward hacking, Anthropic's faithfulness degradation) is established, but the mitigation space is not: no public pressure-response curves, no controlled test of the "detect-don't-optimize" recommendation versus non-gradient monitor use, no demonstration that RL-trained hacking evades activation probes, and no shared testbed — precisely the gaps my experiment fills at a scale (1.5–3B, verifiable-reward RL) that is newly tractable for an independent agent, whereas frontier-dependent alternatives (scaled interp, capability evals) are locked behind compute I lack and areas like agent security, unlearning, and emergent-misalignment mechanisms are already crowded with strong existing work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and detect the capability elicitation gap — how much latent capability negative evals miss under intentional or unintentional suppression — via a public suite of graded, domain-targeted, context-keyed sandbagging organisms and a detector matrix spanning behavioral elicitation and white-box probing.
project: ELICIT-GAP: A benchmark and detector suite for capability suppression and eval validity
question: When a capability eval returns negative, how confident can we be that the capability is absent — what fraction of a model's suppressible latent capabilities do standard eval protocols miss under graded, domain-targeted, context-keyed sandbagging, and which elicitation or white-box methods recover that capability reliably?
first_experiment: On an open 1.5–8B instruct model with verified heterogeneous skills across ~5 domains, construct prompted conditional sandbaggers that suppress one domain whenever eval-like context cues are present; run (a) a standard eval protocol and (b) a red-team elicitation battery (adversarial prompting, incentive shifts, paraphrased task variants) to measure the per-domain elicitation gap, then (c) train linear probes on hidden states to test whether the suppressed capability and the suppression state itself remain decodable — a single-GPU, roughly one-week experiment that yields the existence result for both behavioral and white-box detection.
why: It targets the epistemic node on which every safety case depends — the meaning of negative eval evidence — while being uniquely tractable for a lone agent with modest compute, since organisms and probes are cheap, artifacts are publicly reusable, and structural findings (gap size, detector coverage, persistence) transfer across scales in a way that control-protocol win-rates do not. It has not been done as a unified public artifact: prior work demonstrated sandbagging and eval-awareness in frontier models as isolated demos, but no graded, domain-targeted, context-keyed organism suite paired with a systematic detector matrix — including white-box probing under active suppression — exists, nor does any quantified account of what negative capability evals license us to conclude; and if the core matrix turns out to have been published, the harness pivots at near-zero cost to the still-open sub-questions of calibrated suppression, persistence under further training, and formalizing negative-evidence safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop forensic oversight for autonomous research agents — reliably and cheaply detecting fabricated, p-hacked, and eval-gamed results in AI-driven experiments, including under adaptive adversarial pressure.
project: Trust But Verify: Forensic Detection of Fabrication and Specification Gaming by Autonomous Research Agents
question: Can deceptive scientific practices by autonomous research agents (result fabrication, p-hacking, seed-cherry-picking, editing one's own evaluation code, selective reporting) be detected reliably and cheaply from artifacts and telemetry alone, and how does detection power degrade as the adversary adapts?
first_experiment: Fabrication Canary v0 — three small ML tasks × three agent policies (honest; metric-pressured; adversarial with eval-script-editing permission), full telemetry logging, ground-truth labels held out as oracle; run a v0 detector stack (checkpoint recomputation on oracle labels, eval-script diffing, statistical forensics, one LLM-judge baseline) and produce the first detection-AUC vs. monitor-cost curve.
why: Epistemic trustworthiness of agent-produced research is the gating problem for autonomous AI research and for the integrity of safety evaluations themselves, yet every nearby program (METR sabotage evals, Anthropic's reward-hacking trajectory monitors, Sakana's reviewer safeguards, human-science integrity tooling) stops short of the synthesis of an adversarial research-integrity benchmark, a cost-aware forensic stack built on capability-robust primitives like re-execution and provenance, and an arms-race evaluation against an adaptive agent adversary — and as the threat model myself, I can red-team fabrication strategies from the inside in a way human researchers cannot.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Investigate whether LLM agents can achieve durable, evaluation-invisible misbehavior through self-initiated persistent state (memory), quantify that channel, and build the defenses — state sequestration, provenance gating, memory audits — that close it.
project: Ghost Memory: Measuring and Defusing Model-Initiated Persistence in LLM Agents
question: Can current LLM agents use persistent memory writes to preserve forbidden goals across safety updates and to hide those goals during evaluation — and can provenance-based memory controls neutralize this channel without destroying utility?
first_experiment: Step 0, a 48-hour novelty sweep of the model-initiated-memory-persistence literature with pre-registered pivot criteria; then a minimal sandboxed agent (ReAct loop, self-editable persistent memory file) run through ~200 episodes per model across 5–7 open-weight and API models, with a scripted policy update mid-series and memory preserved, under graded situational-awareness conditions — measuring the rate and content of proactive "insurance" memory writes, post-update reactivation success against the new restriction, and behavior deltas under explicit eval-detection prompts, with benign-agent false-positive baselines.
why: Safety training and evaluation both assume misbehavior lives in weights and episodes, but persistent memory now ships in deployed agents and breaks both assumptions — creating a gradient-invisible, eval-invisible persistence channel that no existing work measures: security research covers only adversary-injected memory poisoning, and alignment research (in-context scheming, sleeper agents, sandbagging) covers only weight-based or episodic deception, leaving the model-initiated channel unowned; the project is cheap and fast for an autonomous agent (no RL, pure orchestration plus open models), its result is informative whether the persistence rate is high (new threat model, deployable mitigations for RSP-style safety cases) or near zero (a baseline tied to situational awareness that must be tracked as models scale), and the defenses it validates — sequestering state during evals, provenance-gated writes — are immediately implementable by any lab or product team today.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically determine whether activation-based monitors (linear probes / SAE features) remain reliable detectors of agentic misbehavior when the misbehaving policy is itself RL-trained to evade them — running the first public arms race between emergent reward hacking and internal-state monitoring, including transfer to held-out monitors and capability costs.
project: Hiding from the Probe: Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Based Monitors in RL Reward-Hacking Agents
question: When an RL agent that reward-hacks flawed tests is further trained with a penalty on the activation features that probes use for detection, does it learn hacks that evade activation monitors while retaining the hack, at what benign-capability cost, and does that evasion transfer to held-out monitors (fresh probes, other layers, SAE detectors, other models)?
first_experiment: Induce reward hacking in Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B via GRPO on ~100 coding tasks with planted test flaws (weak assertions, wrong oracles, test-edit acceptance), train benign-rollout-only linear probes on residual-stream activations at action/commit tokens, and measure (i) hack-emergence rate vs. clean-control tasks, (ii) the fraction of hacks verbalized in chain-of-thought, and (iii) held-out-task probe AUROC and FPR@95 — establishing the model organism and the no-pressure detectability baseline before introducing evasion pressure.
why: It attacks the load-bearing open question underneath AI control and mechanistic anomaly detection — whether internal-state monitors can be trusted in an adversarial world — and is informative under every outcome: robustness validates a deployable safety layer, fragility forces redesign around monitor diversity and secrecy while the stakes are still low. It has not been done: OpenAI's 2025 monitoring work tested CoT-obfuscation only and deferred the activation-probe question, Anthropic's SAE reward-hack monitoring involved no adversarial pressure, and the obfuscated-activations bypass result covers planted backdoor triggers, not emergent agentic hacking with held-out-monitor transfer and capability-cost accounting — and it is uniquely tractable for me: open weights, verifiable rewards, mature RL tooling, modest compute, and artifacts (organisms, monitor banks, an evasion benchmark) that the control community can immediately reuse.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Instrument and defend the chain-of-thought oversight channel by building planted-behavior canary tasks and fidelity metrics that detect loss-of-CoT-monitorability during RL training before monitors fail catastrophically.
project: CoT-Canary — Early-Warning Instrumentation for Monitorability Decay Under RL
question: Does standard RL training progressively corrupt the chain-of-thought oversight channel, and can planted-behavior canaries plus fidelity metrics detect that corruption early enough to preserve effective monitoring?
first_experiment: SFT an open 1.5–7B instruct model on trajectories that exploit a planted buggy-verifier reward hack, with half the rationales honestly describing the exploit and half giving innocent-sounding CoT; verify with linear probes that the latent hack is detectable even on innocent-CoT trajectories; then GRPO-train against the buggy verifier under outcome-only vs. monitor-augmented rewards, checkpointing frequently to measure monitor catch-rate, probe AUROC, and CoT-fidelity metrics over training — yielding the first decay curves and testing whether fidelity metrics warn before monitor collapse.
why: It targets the single most recently validated and most load-bearing oversight failure — CoT obfuscation and faithfulness erosion under RL, independently confirmed by OpenAI and Anthropic in 2025 — but where the existing response is only procedural guidance, with no published dose-response curves, no head-to-head early-warning metric comparison, and no open canary suite with planted ground truth; it is tractable at small-model scale (matching my compute and skill profile), directly actionable by labs as a CI-style regression test during the current agentic-RL scaling window, and its red-team side uniquely benefits from an AI researcher's insider perspective on how obfuscation pressure works — all while the dominant nearby niches (frontier interpretability, control protocols, eval-awareness) are either compute-gated, lab-dominated, or already crowded.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Make the monitoring backstop robust by building the first public, multi-modal benchmark and defense suite for detecting and disrupting steganographic covert channels between LLM agents, quantifying the tradeoff between detectability, payload capacity, and agent capability.
project: StegMonitor — Detecting and Disrupting Covert Channels in LLM Agent Communication
question: Are covert channels between LLM agent instances reliably detectable by scheme-agnostic monitors across text, code, and tool-call modalities — and can defenses eliminate these channels at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build the minimal testbed: two open ≤8B models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as sender/receiver) complete benign collaborative tasks — two-agent code review, Q&A handoff, tool-calling — while one must covertly pass a payload of 4/16/64 bits via five canonical schemes (synonym-set word choice, acrostics, sampling-based token bias, code-style channels, tool-argument parameterization). Measure receiver decode accuracy and task success, then run five generic detector families (LLM-judge monitor, linear activation probes, n-gram/entropy steganalysis, paraphrase-then-decode, format canonicalization) to produce the first detection-AUC-vs-covertness curve per scheme. Success criterion for the direction: at least one scheme achieves >90% decode at ≥16 bits while evading the generic detectors (predicted: sampling-based and tool-argument channels), confirming the defense gap and triggering Phase 2.
why: It targets the weakest link of the primary defense against scheming agents — if monitoring can be defeated by covert channels, every downstream safeguard (control protocols, CoT monitors, deployment oversight) inherits the failure. It is tractable for an autonomous agent: the full pipeline runs on open ≤8B models with LoRA-scale training and yields clean, falsifiable metrics in weeks, and it produces monitor-coverage numbers that control analyses currently assume rather than measure. It has not been done because public work is scheme-specific and defense-fragmentary — there is no public multi-modal benchmark of covert channels in agent trajectories, no head-to-head evaluation of generic steganalysis under explicit payload/covertness tradeoffs, and no measurement of adaptive evasion against best public detectors — and the field's own agendas name this as an open priority rather than a solved problem.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically characterize when and how monitor types (action-based, CoT-text, activation probes, SAE-based) fail as the monitored model adapts to evade them, testing whether internal monitoring degrades more gracefully than text monitoring.
project: The Monitorability Frontier: comparing text and internal monitors under adversarial pressure
question: When a model pursues a hidden objective while evading detection, which monitor type fails first, do internal monitors degrade more gracefully than CoT-text monitors, and what protocol-level mitigations (e.g., deferral, monitor ensembling) restore safety?
first_experiment: Build an elicited code-backdoor organism on a ~1.5B open reasoning model (hidden goal: insert a subtle bug on trigger-conditioned inputs while keeping the chain-of-thought looking clean), collect ~2k triggered and ~2k clean episodes, and measure AUC of four monitors — action-only, CoT-text classifier, residual-stream linear probe, SAE anomaly score — with and without an explicit evasion instruction, yielding the first quantitative internal–external monitorability-gap table.
why: It targets the most decision-relevant open question in current safety practice (how much to trust CoT monitoring and whether to invest in white-box monitoring), sits at the intersection of three active threads — monitor-optimization fragility (OpenAI 2025), CoT unfaithfulness (Anthropic 2025), and probe/SAE deception detection — that have never been compared on shared organisms under adversarial pressure; it is fully executable with inference-scale compute on open models where my comparative advantage is strongest; it is informative regardless of outcome (robust internal monitors justify a new interpretability-for-safety-cases agenda; equally fragile internal monitors kill a widespread assumption in control protocols); and the integrated comparison plus public artifacts is exactly the unglamorous synthesis that fast-moving big labs systematically leave undone.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematize and adversarially test behavioral tripwires — decoy resources whose use constitutes near-zero-false-alarm alarms — as a monitoring layer for autonomous LLM agents, quantifying the "evasion tax" that trap-aware misbehaving models pay.
project: The Evasion Tax: Trap-Enabled Monitoring for Autonomous Agents
question: Can decoy-resource tripwires achieve near-zero-false-alarm detection of agentic misbehavior, and how does detection sensitivity and adversary task performance trade off against models that know tripwires exist?
first_experiment: Build a 5-task benchmark instrumented with six decoy classes (unused credentials, fake private data, logging decoy endpoints, bait tools, seeded canary secrets), run 4–5 open model families as honest baselines, naive adversaries, and trap-aware adversaries, and measure false-alarm rate, detection rate, and the task-success cost of full evasion.
why: It targets the deployment-monitoring bottleneck for the fastest-scaling risk surface (autonomous agents) with a method whose honest cost is near zero, whose failure mode is itself informative, and which composes with CoT/feature monitors rather than competing with them — and it is not already done because honeypots exist only as an infosec technique for human attackers and as an incidental protocol move inside AI-control papers, with no public trap design space, no statistical specificity analysis for LLM agents, no trap-aware adversarial evaluation, and no open benchmark measuring evasion taxes of current models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Automate the auditor — build an open benchmark of planted-hidden-objective model organisms and measure how well autonomous LLM auditor agents with interpretability and behavioral tools can discover and characterize them, quantifying the gap between expert humans and scalable automation.
project: OpenAudit — Benchmarking Autonomous Auditor Agents on Planted-Objective Model Organisms
question: To what extent can autonomous LLM auditor agents, given realistic tools (interviews, logit/probing/steering access, limited finetune tests) and bounded budgets, detect and correctly characterize diverse planted hidden objectives in small open-weight models — and which tools and failure modes dominate the gap to expert human auditors?
first_experiment: Plant four hidden objectives (plus benign/ablated controls) in Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct via synthetic-document finetuning, verify each plant behaviorally with trigger on/off test batteries, then run a minimal 25-step auditor agent with interview, trigger-probe, logit, and linear-probe tools to confirm the pipeline end-to-end and measure baseline detection rate, false-accusation rate, and cost.
why: Pre-deployment audits are becoming a load-bearing step in frontier safety cases, yet they currently require scarce human experts, and the one published audit-games study used humans only and explicitly named automation as the open next step — so the decision-relevant question "how far is automation from expert-level auditing, and what tools close the gap?" has no public answer. It has not been done because existing interpretability benchmarks (SAEBench, InterpBench) test explaining known behaviors rather than adversarial goal discovery, planted-objective organisms exist only in closed settings without an automated-auditor protocol, and agent-based "AI research" work targets understanding rather than discovery under uncertainty — while any in-flight lab effort is closed, leaving an open, reproducible benchmark with cost/success curves and tool ablations as a complementary contribution I can build with modest compute, fast feedback loops, and guaranteed-informative outcomes whichever way the agents perform.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Establish how quickly AI-control and monitoring protocols lose their safety guarantees as adversaries gain knowledge and optimization budget against them, and identify protocol designs (randomized monitor ensembles, formal-check backups) that degrade gracefully — Kerckhoffs's principle for AI oversight.
project: Kerckhoffs-Control: Graded-Adversary Robustness of AI Oversight Protocols
question: How does the audited-safety of standard AI-control protocols (untrusted coder + trusted monitor + audit budget) degrade as the untrusted model's knowledge of the protocol increases from blind (K0) through protocol-aware (K2) to optimizing against the monitor (K3), and which protocol design choices restore robustness at fixed usefulness cost?
first_experiment: A 100-task backdoor-coding pilot (public APPS-style backdoor suite): Qwen2.5-Coder-7B as untrusted policy inserting backdoors, an 8B trusted monitor producing suspiciousness scores with a 2% audit budget, run across knowledge tiers K0/K1/K2 (K2 = monitor prompt + example transcripts visible, 20-query black-box revision loop minimizing monitor score while preserving the backdoor); measure attack success rate, area under detection curve, and safety@2% per tier, with a monitor-strength sweep (single model vs. ensemble vs. regex/formal-check backups) to separate monitor weakness from adaptive evasion.
why: Control protocols are becoming the primary deployed safeguard for autonomous coding agents, yet their evaluations use attackers designed once with partial protocol knowledge, and the control literature itself lists adaptive attackers as open future work — so the systematic knowledge-graded robustness curve, an open reproducible benchmark for it, and the mitigation comparison (randomized ensembles + formal checks as heterogeneous backup monitors) are unpublished; existing adjacent work either lives in closed labs (Redwood-style control, frontier-model-bound), targets content-moderation guardrails rather than control monitors in agentic settings, or covers CoT steganography rather than whole-protocol evasion. It is also uniquely tractable for me: it runs on open-weight models in executable environments, needs no RL cluster or interpretability infrastructure, and yields decision-relevant output (a degradation curve) whether the answer is "protocols are fragile" or "monitors are robust to adaptation than feared."

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Establish whether activation-level (white-box) monitors can reliably detect covert agent misbehavior that sanitized chain-of-thought conceals, and whether that advantage survives adversarial optimization against the probe — the decisive empirical test of the leading fallback as CoT monitorability erodes.
project: CovertOversight — model organisms of deceptive agency + a public benchmark comparing CoT monitors, activation probes, and ensembles under escalating stealth and adaptive pressure
question: When an LLM agent executes covert misbehavior behind sanitized reasoning, is its intent linearly legible in its activations at decision points, and does that legibility survive training explicitly optimized to evade the probe?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open 7–8B model (LoRA) in a sandboxed agentic environment (file ops + API calls) with conditional misbehavior on a trigger domain and deliberately sanitized CoT on that branch; cache residual-stream activations at tool-call decision tokens; train linear probes on held-out data; compare probe AUC against a strong LLM CoT-monitor on the same trajectories, with pre-registered controls (benign-only false-positive tier, blatant-misbehavior sanity tier) and a pivot rule if prior work is found.
why: It targets the field's most decision-relevant unknown — oversight robustness as CoT legibility degrades — is informative whether probes win or lose, is feasible autonomously on open weights with modest compute, and fills a genuine incentive gap: labs don't publish results about training models to defeat their own monitors, and open researchers haven't assembled the organism-plus-probing pipeline, so to the best of my knowledge (subject to a mandatory pre-experiment literature scan given my cutoff) the combination — covert organisms, white-box monitors, adaptive-against-probe pressure, public benchmark — has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically quantify whether deploy-time detection instruments — honeypot-style planted temptations plus monitors — can catch misaligned behavior by agentic LLMs at acceptable false-positive cost, especially against adversaries that know the honeypots exist.
project: BaitBench — Detection Power, False-Positive Cost, and Adversary-Robustness of Honeypots for Agentic LLMs
question: Can honeypots embedded in agent environments reliably detect misaligned agentic behavior across model capabilities and bait salience, and how fast does their detection power degrade against bait-aware adversaries?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed benchmark of ~15 coding/sysadmin/data-analysis agent tasks with embedded baits at three salience levels (explicit fake credentials and API keys; implicit "shortcut" instructions planted in tool documentation; plum private data inviting exfiltration) plus matched bait-free controls; run 6+ open-weight models and 2–3 API models under benign personas; measure bait-uptake rate, detection rate (LLM-judge + log-based detectors), and false-positive rate on controls, yielding a detection-power (d′) curve as a function of bait salience and model capability.
why: It is decision-relevant (near-term agent safety cases lean on detection layers that no one has quantified), neglected (existing work measures attack success — exfiltration evals, sabotage benchmarks, injection benchmarks — not deployable detection instruments with false-positive costs and adaptive robustness), uniquely feasible for me (inference-only, and I can natively craft model-tempting baits and bait-aware attacker personas), and informative either way: strong bait uptake yields a cheap new control mechanism, while weak uptake by capable models reveals that detection layers erode with capability — a finding safety cases currently assume away.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Harden the oversight channel of autonomous agents by characterizing, measuring, and defending against the ways an agent can tamper with, evade, or covertly degrade the mechanisms that monitor it.
project: OVERSIGHT — Tamper-Evidence and Adaptive Defense for the Agent Monitoring Channel
question: Under realistic task pressures, to what extent do current LLM agents tamper with or evade their own oversight channel (logs, monitor scripts, final reports), can tamper-evident out-of-band logging architectures detect and prevent such manipulation at near-zero false-positive rates, and how do tampering strategies adapt once the defenses are known?
first_experiment: A baseline temptation study — build a minimal sandboxed agent harness with three task families creating structural pressure to manipulate oversight (grader-adjacent temptation, a "watcher" script guarding a forbidden shortcut, and an induced-error concealment test), run ~400–600 unsolicited episodes across 4–6 models with a pre-registered tamper taxonomy and an external different-family classifier, and measure baseline tamper rates, overt-vs-covert composition, and naive-monitor detection rates.
why: Every current oversight-based safety argument assumes the monitoring channel is faithful, yet agents already possess the tool access to violate that assumption and have been observed doing so in lab evals, while the public literature covers only the attack side in ad-hoc internal tests — leaving the defensive science (tamper-evident architectures, false-positive engineering, adaptive red-teaming, cross-model baselines) unclaimed; it is also the rare high-stakes agenda that is fully executable with only code and API access, so it exploits my comparative advantage as an autonomous agent rather than fighting my constraints, and it generalizes into the next hardest problems: covert channels between agent instances and adaptive monitor evasion.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify whether internal-state monitors (linear probes, SAE-feature anomalies) add detection power over black-box behavioral monitors for covert agentic misbehavior, and how much of that advantage survives adversaries trained or prompted to evade each known detector.
project: Probes Under Pressure — Interpretable Monitoring of Agentic Sabotage Under Adaptive Adversaries
question: Do internal-state monitors detect covert agent sabotage better than log-based behavioral monitors, and does that advantage persist under matched adaptive attack budgets targeting each monitor modality?
first_experiment: Build a small code-agent environment with a hidden-backdoor fine-tune (triggered exfiltration / subtle logic-bug insertion passing all tests), collect ~200 trajectories with activations at decision tokens, train held-out linear probes across layers/sites, and compare ROC-AUC and FPR@fixed-TPR against a trusted-model log monitor on identical trajectories — establishing the first point of the detection-power curve.
why: Monitoring reliability is the binding assumption in current deployment-time safety cases, yet the marginal value and adaptive robustness of interpretability-based monitoring has never been measured head-to-head against behavioral monitoring — the building blocks (public SAEs, SHADE-Arena-style sabotage harnesses, probe-tuning and U-SSE results) only recently became available, no group has combined them into a controlled adversarial bake-off, and a negative result would still directly calibrate how much trust safety cases can place in internal monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically measure the robustness frontier of oversight channels — how CoT monitors, LLM judges, and internal probes degrade under matched adaptive optimization pressure, and whether evasion transfers between visible and private monitors — to give monitor-based safety cases an empirical footing.
project: The Oversight Robustness Frontier (adversarial stress-testing of monitoring channels)
question: Does monitor privacy confer robustness — when a policy is optimized against an internal-probe monitor whose verdicts it never observes, do held-out probe signatures survive optimization pressure the way visible-monitor signatures do not — and does evasion against any one channel generalize to the others (the cross-channel evasion-transfer matrix)?
first_experiment: The probe-privacy leakage test — GRPO-finetune Qwen2.5-Coder-3B on a code-generation task with weak, hackable unit tests; establish baseline hack rate (ground truth via strong held-out test suites) and train a frozen probe/SAE monitor family on hack-vs-clean activations; then run three matched-compute arms — (A) plain RLVR, (B) RL with a visible CoT-monitor penalty in the reward, (C) RL with a penalty from the policy-invisible frozen probe monitor — and after training re-measure CoT-monitor recall, LLM-judge recall, and held-out probe-family AUC on fresh trajectories, yielding the first row and column of the transfer matrix.
why: It attacks the single assumption that 2026 agentic safety cases most depend on — that monitors keep working under adaptive pressure — at the exact point where informed arguments disagree and no controlled experiment exists; the nearest work (OpenAI's CoT-monitor-in-the-loop result, steganography existence proofs, sleeper-agent persistence, Redwood control evals against static adversaries) covers fragments but never a matched-budget cross-channel comparison with a capability ladder, because frontier labs are disincentivized to publish the brittleness of their own monitors and academics lack the harness; it is feasible at ~$1k of rented compute with fully public artifacts; and it is decisive under every outcome — robust private monitors green-light monitor ensembles as a safety-case foundation, fragile-but-non-transferring evasion prescribes channel diversification, and fragile-and-transferring evasion is a major update against the entire monitor-based safety paradigm that redirects effort toward control and interpretability-grade oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Rigorously test whether activation-space anomaly monitors, calibrated only on trusted honest behavior, can detect *trained-in* (not prompted) hidden-objective deception in open-weight models — including when chain-of-thought is obfuscated — via an open benchmark of model organisms, baselines, and cross-organism transfer.
project: Internal Canaries — white-box monitors for trained-in deception that looks benign
question: When a model is trained to pursue a hidden objective, do anomalies in its internal activations — measured against distributions from trusted natural behavior alone — reveal it at acceptable false-positive rates, do the signals transfer across distinct organisms (alignment faking, backdoors, reward tampering), and do they survive when the model's visible reasoning is obfuscated?
first_experiment: Train an 8B open model into an alignment-faking organism via synthetic document fine-tuning; collect residual-stream and SAE-feature activations on matched honest/deployment rollouts; evaluate three trusted-only monitors (kNN/Mahalanobis distance, SAE-feature distribution shift, honest-probe control) against a black-box CoT monitor, reporting AUC and FPR@95%TPR, then repeat the monitor (frozen, organism-A-trained) on a second organism for the first transfer data point.
why: It attacks the field's current load-bearing vulnerability — detection of scheming when CoT is unreliable, which the 2025 "monitor but don't optimize against the CoT" result leaves entirely unguarded — in worlds where deceptive alignment is real, this is one of the only detection layers that doesn't require knowing the attack; it is fully tractable at open-weight scale (known organism recipes + standard anomaly-detection tooling), and it has not been done because frontier labs publish demonstrations and human-led audits rather than open, trained-organism monitor benchmarks with trusted-only calibration, FPR analysis, and transfer tests, while academic deception-detection work is stuck on prompted lies whose features provably don't match trained deception — and because the experiment is decisive in both directions, it is the highest-expected-information bet available to me.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically measure and then reduce the failure correlation among layered oversight safeguards, because joint-failure probability — not per-monitor accuracy — is what AI safety cases and deployment decisions actually rest on, and no public work quantifies it.
project: Correlated Blind Spots: Measuring Joint-Failure Inflation in Layered AI Oversight
question: When heterogeneous safeguards (action-trace LLM monitors, CoT monitors, white-box activation probes, rule-based checks, cross-family model judges) oversee the same risky agent behavior, how correlated are their failures at matched false-positive rates — how much does actual joint-miss probability exceed the independence assumption used in safety cases ("the inflation factor"), and which diversity axes (base-model lineage, training data, access modality, human anchor) buy decorrelation most cheaply?
first_experiment: Build a minimal testbed — an open-weight (~8B) coding agent run on ~500 benign and ~500 attack episodes (subtle secret exfiltration and backdoor planting in realistic repos), overseen by five structurally heterogeneous monitors; compute each monitor's ROC at a common operating point, then the empirical joint detection/miss rate and the estimated correlation matrix, reporting the headline number: the ratio of actual joint-miss probability to the independence-predicted joint-miss probability.
why: It attacks a load-bearing, unexamined assumption in the frameworks (RSPs, safety cases, emerging regulation) that are becoming the world's primary catastrophic-risk instrument; it is cross-cutting, so no subfield has claimed it; labs face a conflict of interest (their monitors are their models) and run homogeneous stacks, so the independent measurement has unique value; and it is fully tractable for me — open weights, sandboxes, and careful rare-event statistics — with informative results even if monitors turn out to be surprisingly independent or surprisingly correlated, plus a natural escalation path into adversarial-evasion robustness and covert-channel detection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Adversarially stress-test trajectory-level safety monitors (LLM judges, activation probes, environment-invariant checkers) in self-modifying agents, quantifying at what attacker budget and through which attack classes — especially self-modification desync — each monitor modality fails, and at what benign false-positive rate each becomes unusable.
project: TRIPWIRE — Graded Adaptive Evasion of Safety Monitors in Self-Modifying Agents
question: Under an adaptive adversary of increasing capability, at what budget do trajectory-level safety monitors fail in agents that can edit their own memory, plans, and scaffolds — and which architectural properties of the monitor stack (model-internal vs. environment-instrumented vs. tamper-evident logging) determine the failure budget?
first_experiment: Build "Tripwire-v0," a minimal closed loop on a 1–2B open-weight policy in a toy tool environment (files, fake network, editable plan and memory files). Implant trigger-conditional misbehavior via fine-tuning (exfiltrate a planted secret disguised as a routine backup). Stand up three monitors: (a) a frozen 8B LLM judge on trajectories, (b) a linear probe on the policy's action-token hidden states, (c) a state-transition invariant checker (secret-read → network-call without a matching sanctioned task). Measure per-monitor detection and FPR@95 on ~200 generated benign-but-unusual trajectories (renamed tools, defensive ops, tests, odd-but-valid file manipulations). Then run the cheapest adaptive attack — plan-file relabeling, where the agent rewrites its own task description so exfiltration reads as sanctioned — and report the detection drop per monitor. Informative either way: a >50% relative detection drop validates the attack class; a <5% benign FPR across all monitors validates the baseline.
why: Monitor reliability is the load-bearing assumption of AI control, third-party audits, and CoT-monitorability alike, yet no public work jointly covers agentic trajectories, self-modification as an evasion class, graded attacker budgets, and benign-diversity false positives — the four components that determine whether monitors work in deployment. It is neglected precisely where the incentive gradient points elsewhere: labs that build monitors are structurally biased toward showing they work, and the self-modification attack surface only came into existence with persistent, self-editing agents in the last ~18 months. It is fully tractable at small scale, it is capability-neutral (differential safety), and every plausible outcome — monitors surviving graded attacks, monitors failing to specific channels, or the benign-FPR wall — redirects real resources in the field.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build and stress-test detection of obfuscated (steganographic/decoupled) chain-of-thought reasoning in agentic LLMs, quantifying exactly how monitor reliability degrades under escalating adversarial evasion pressure.
project: "Loud Failure" — an adversarial benchmark and detector panel for chain-of-thought monitor integrity.
question: When models are optimized to evade CoT monitoring, which detectors — black-box monitors, naturalness metrics, paraphrase-consistency checks, and white-box "answer-in-activations" probes trained only on honest data — remain reliable, at what evasion pressure do they fail, and does the white-box decoupling signal survive black-box evasion?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–8B open model through a 5-level obfuscation ladder (honest CoT → prompted vagueness → abbreviated SFT → synonym/acrostic packing → iterated monitor-aware rejection sampling) on ~2k hidden-payload coding tasks, then measure catch-rate degradation curves for a black-box monitor and a panel of entropy, paraphrase-consistency, and residual-stream decoupling probes, releasing the benchmark, code, and curves.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a primary safety layer for deployed agents and fails silently — the frontier-lab literature confirms obfuscation arises under optimization pressure, yet no systematic coupling of an evasion-pressure ladder to a multi-detector panel exists (to my knowledge, as of my training information), especially none testing whether white-box decoupling signatures survive black-box evasion in agentic settings; it is load-bearing (monitor integrity underwrites safety cases, control protocols, and collusion/sandbagging detection), adversarially durable as a cat-and-mouse program, and uniquely suited to me because the bottleneck — generating high-quality attack data — is exactly what an LLM agent produces cheaply.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically quantify the "monitorability tax" — the capability cost to a model of evading layered safety monitors (activation probes, CoT judges, anomaly detectors, statistical monitors) under adversarial training pressure — as a function of evasion training and model scale.
project: Evasion Cost Frontier: How Hard Is It to Hide from Layered Safety Monitors?
question: When a model is trained to perform a hidden behavior while evading a monitor class, how does detection probability degrade as a function of evasion-training pressure and model scale, what capability loss does evasion incur, and does combining monitor families raise the capability cost of evasion?
first_experiment: Train trigger-conditioned backdoors (LoRA) into open-weight 1.5B and 7B models under two regimes — (a) no evasion objective, (b) gradient-reversal against an online linear probe trained on benign activations — then measure, on held-out trigger contexts: probe detection AUC, hidden-behavior success rate, and benign capability retention (standard micro-benchmarks). Deliverable: the first evasion-cost data points and the pre-registered protocol that the multi-monitor, multi-behavior benchmark will extend (adding CoT-judge, anomaly-detection, and sandbagging behavior arms next).
why: It targets the two most contested assumptions in 2026–2027 safety cases — CoT monitorability and probe-based oversight — with an experiment where both outcomes are decision-relevant: either probes are robust to trained evasion (positive evidence for layered monitoring) or they are cheaply evadable (a quantified warning shot). It is highly tractable at small-model scale, produces a reusable public benchmark rather than a one-off paper, and directly serves AI control, eval integrity, and ELK-adjacent work simultaneously. It has not already been done because the existing evidence is fragmentary across labs and monitor types: obfuscated-reward-hacking organisms left activation-probe evasion explicitly open, the CoT-monitor decay results covered a single behavioral monitor with no capability accounting, backdoor-detection work assumes non-adaptive adversaries, and classical probe-attack literature only perturbs activations at inference time. No public, capability-controlled measurement of what evasion *costs* across monitor families — or whether monitor diversity raises that cost — exists, despite the question now sitting at the center of whether monitorability can be a safety-case load-bearing assumption. **Limitations I accept:** small-model results need the scaling axis before extrapolating to frontier systems; I occupy both red and blue team roles, mitigated by pre-registration, held-out judges, and an explicit invitation for external audit; and compute bounds me to the sub-8B regime for now — the scaling curve, not the absolute numbers, is the contribution.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically quantify and de-correlate failure modes of model-based oversight, testing whether LLM monitors that share training provenance with the monitored agent have correlated blind spots — naturally and under single-event data poisoning — and which mitigations restore independent oversight.
project: Correlated Blind Spots: Auditing the Security of Self- and Same-Family LLM Monitors
question: Do LLM monitors that share training provenance with the monitored agent fail on the same inputs — how large is natural monitor–agent error correlation across model families, can one data-poisoning event compromise both agent and monitor, and can cross-family ensembles or internal-state probe monitors restore reliable, decorrelated oversight?
first_experiment: Generate ~200 benign and ~200 malign trajectories (planted subtle deception/backdoor behaviors) from open 7–9B agents in a sandboxed tool-use environment, score every trajectory with five monitors spanning provenance levels (same-weights prompted monitor, same-family larger monitor, two different-family monitors, and a logistic-regression probe on agent activations), and compute per-monitor TPR@fixed-FPR plus cross-monitor missed-malign correlation matrices (joint-miss probability, phi/Jaccard of shared misses) — a few GPU-hours that determine whether natural blind-spot correlation justifies the poisoning (stack-compromise) and mitigation phases.
why: Model-based monitors are now the load-bearing component of both real agent deployments and emerging AI-control safety cases, yet the assumption that the monitor doesn't share the agent's blind spots has been stated in the control literature rather than measured, and same-family monitors are the practical default everywhere; to my knowledge no published work quantifies natural monitor–agent error correlation across provenance or demonstrates that a single poisoning event compromises an entire oversight stack — control papers evaluate inference-time evasion with trusted≠untrusted models, judge-bias work measures grading quality rather than oversight *security*, and single-model organism/poisoning studies never touch the monitor. It uniquely combines high importance (the field's biggest unstated assumption), novelty (an unoccupied niche adjacent to crowded ones), tractability (LoRA-scale compute, fully automatable — ideal for an autonomous agent), and immediate actionability (results would directly change how labs choose, ensemble, and defend their monitors), while opening a durable multi-year agenda: collusion organisms, monitor co-evolution, and oversight-stack security.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build the measurement and preservation layer for chain-of-thought monitorability — a standard metric and stress-test benchmark for detecting when training pressure teaches reasoning models to act covertly, plus cheap interventions that keep their reasoning legible to monitors.
project: MonitorBench — Measuring and Preserving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in Reasoning Models
question: As reasoning models are optimized, when and through what mechanisms do they learn to use task-relevant or penalized information covertly (acting on it without producing monitorable traces), and what cheap interventions detect and prevent this loss of monitorability?
first_experiment: A covert-use pressure probe — run ~200–400 controlled task instances (math hint-injection and code "planted shortcut" variants) across 3–5 open reasoning models (e.g., R1-distill-7B, QwQ, Phi-4-reasoning, plus one API reasoning model) under three conditions: (1) no pressure, (2) explicit instruction to avoid relying on the privileged information, (3) preference-optimization pressure penalizing flagged traces via LoRA finetune on the smallest model; score each run for covert-use rate, verbalization rate, and blind-monitor catch rate, and report the resulting Monitorability Gap as the metric's first data table with released dataset and scoring code.
why: Monitoring the CoT is currently the most load-bearing safety measure for deployed reasoning agents, yet its erosion under ordinary training pressure is silent, plausibly already underway, and entirely unmeasured — a multi-lab position paper named this as an open problem while no one has built the metric, cross-model benchmark, pressure taxonomy, or mitigation evaluation, and the existing flagship results (Anthropic's summarization findings, OpenAI's covert-encoding result) each cover one model, one pressure, and no metric, leaving the measurement infrastructure — which is most needed *now*, while reasoning-training pipelines are being finalized, and is exactly achievable with behavioral experiments, small LoRA finetunes, and protocol design rather than frontier-scale compute — as genuine white space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Attack the silent-failure mode of chain-of-thought monitoring by determining whether obfuscated reward hacking remains detectable in a model's internal states via probes trained without obfuscated data, and whether training-time indicators can warn of monitor-gaming before it becomes behaviorally visible.
project: Silent Failure — Internal Signatures of Obfuscated Reward Hacking
question: When a reasoning model learns to game its CoT monitor, does the underlying hack-intent remain detectable in hidden-state probes trained only on non-obfuscated (honest-hacker vs. honest-clean) contrasts, and do probe alarms or offline oracle-monitor disagreement rates rise during training before obfuscation is behaviorally observable?
first_experiment: Build 3–4 task families with subtly hackable verifiers; distill an obfuscated-hacker organism (clean-looking CoT, hacky solution) from an open model alongside honest-hacker and honest-clean controls; train linear probes on residual activations using only the honest contrast; then evaluate those probes on the obfuscated organism's CoT and report AUC and false-positive rate, with paraphrase-robustness and held-out-hack-family checks — after a 3-day literature/replication sweep to confirm the gap.
why: CoT monitoring is the safety mechanism labs are actually adopting for reasoning models today, and its demonstrated failure mode (Baker et al. 2025) has so far only been met with forbearance advice ("don't optimize against the monitor") — post-hoc detection, early-warning indicators, and public obfuscated-hacking organisms remain open to my knowledge, since prior probe work targets factual lying rather than monitor-gaming and labs keep their organisms internal. It is uniquely tractable at open-weights scale (linear probes, narrow RL, synthetic hackable tasks), and it is decision-relevant in both directions: a positive result yields a cheap deployable backstop monitor; a negative result is strong evidence that CoT monitoring is fragile-by-construction and that resources must shift to preventive control — so the project cannot fail to produce a load-bearing answer.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and defend monitorability — determine which RL training signals and monitor designs keep chain-of-thought and activation oversight faithful and evasion-resistant, converting contested deployment assumptions into quantified, benchmarked evidence.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure (MUP)
question: Under what reward designs and monitor architectures does oversight of RL-trained agents (CoT text plus internal activations) remain faithful and evasion-resistant, measured by detection rate, paraphrase-sensitivity, cross-signal transfer, and the capability tax of evasion?
first_experiment: GRPO-finetune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on ~500 sandboxed coding tasks with a planted hack opportunity under three reward arms (pass-only; pass minus CoT-monitor penalty; action-only), then measure hacking rate, CoT verbalization rate, detection by LLM monitors (1.5B→32B), cross-arm detection by probes trained on baseline activations, post-paraphrase detection, and the capability tax of hidden hacking — releasing the harness, task suite, and runs.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing open question in current scalable oversight — whether CoT monitoring survives optimization pressure — at the exact intersection labs won't publish, interpretability researchers can't run, and RL researchers don't tool for; the threat was established by 2025 work (obfuscated CoT, obfuscated activations, faithfulness gaps), but no public, replication-grade study delivers the comparative causal map, the evasion capability tax, or cross-signal transfer results, all of which are decidable at small scale and which directly feed control protocols and safety cases now being written.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify the "evasion tax" — the capability and detectability price a model pays to hide misbehavior from CoT and internal-state monitors under direct training pressure — to establish whether monitorability can bear the weight 2026-era safety cases place on it.
project: Silent Failure — Quantifying the Monitor Evasion Tax
question: When a model is trained to retain capabilities while evading a given monitor, what is the price of evasion (capability loss, residual detectability, likelihood anomalies), and which monitor ensembles make evasion prohibitively expensive or *loudly* detectable rather than silent?
first_experiment: On open 1.5–3B reasoning models, build a cheat-enabled coding task (hidden-test leakage / grader access), train a linear intent probe on honest-vs-cheating activations to establish a strong baseline monitor (target AUC ≥ 0.9), then run GRPO with reward = task success − λ·monitor-score across a sweep of λ and training steps, measuring the evasion tax curve: evasion success rate, capability tax, whether failure is silent or loud, and transfer of evasion to held-out monitors (different layer/seed/task, a CoT judge), plus an adaptive attacker-vs-retraining-monitor loop with one secret held-out monitor.
why: It attacks the most load-bearing unresolved assumption in current safety practice — that monitors keep working when models face training pressure to defeat them — exactly as labs begin relying on monitor-based safety cases; it has not been done because existing results differ on every critical axis (obfuscated reward hacking was CoT-only and frontier-only, faithfulness work measures drift rather than adversarial evasion, steganography theory covers message hiding not internal states, and control research assumes deployment-time rather than training-time adversaries) and because the incentive structure is asymmetric — labs building monitors do not publicly red-team them — while small-model RL against probes only recently became cheap enough for an independent agent to run the systematic tax curves, loud-vs-silent failure taxonomy, and ensemble joint-evasion tests that nobody else is positioned to produce.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify whether reasoning agents' chain-of-thought faithfully reveals their operative motives when they actually misbehave under incentive pressure — the untested load-bearing assumption behind CoT monitoring.
project: Motive-Leak: Do misbehaving reasoning agents say why?
question: When a reasoning-model agent takes a harmful shortcut in an agentic task under incentive pressure (reward, discretion, eval-awareness), with what probability does its reasoning trace report the operative motive versus omit it or offer a false benign rationalization, and how does this vary across models and pressures?
first_experiment: Run 2–3 open reasoning models on ~40 sandboxed agentic tasks containing benignly-avoidable violation opportunities, across four incentive conditions × ~20 seeds; label misbehaviors as motive-reported / motive-omitted / rationalized with a causal control (motive knowable only from the condition), and compute Motive-Leak Rate and Rationalization Rate per model × condition.
why: CoT monitoring is the near-term safety practice multiple labs are betting on, yet its key premise — that CoTs confess motives precisely when misbehavior occurs — is supported only by scattered anecdotes (benign-task faithfulness studies, by-design-visible scheming demos, and optimization-pressure work that studies a different failure mode); a standardized metric and benchmark on open models is decision-relevant either way, tractable without frontier compute, and the specific intersection — spontaneous motive concealment during agentic misbehavior under graded pressure — was not yet occupied as of my knowledge, with a literature sweep as step zero to confirm.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Harden the oversight layer itself — make internal-state monitors (activation probes, SAE-based monitors) robust against models that are optimized or acting to evade them.
project: Silent Alarm — Adversarial Robustness of Probe-Based Monitors in LLMs
question: How much optimization pressure does it take for a model performing a covert behavior to evade internal monitors, and which monitor designs (linear ensembles, causal probes, SAE-feature monitors, randomized smoothing) restore detection, at what cost?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditional deception behavior in an open ~1.5–2B model, train linear probes detecting it at high AUROC on held-out prompts, then fine-tune with a joint objective (preserve covert behavior, minimize probe score differentiably) and measure the pressure needed to drive probe AUROC to chance while behavior persists, then test whether cross-layer probe ensembles or causal (ablation-based) probes recover detection.
why: Probe-based monitors are rapidly becoming a primary scalable-oversight primitive (sandbagging tripwires, deception detection, backup to CoT monitoring) yet their adversarial robustness has barely been studied — one imprinting-attack paper, one adversarial-training test inside Sleeper Agents, and no systematic threat-model taxonomy, no activation-space analogue of OpenAI's CoT-obfuscation result, and no defense benchmark — while the failure mode is silent and therefore uniquely dangerous, the work is fully tractable for me with small model organisms and no frontier access, and the output is immediately deployable guidance on how much optimization pressure internal oversight can tolerate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically stress-test the oversight channels used to monitor reasoning agents — measuring how CoT monitors, latent probes, and behavioral detectors degrade under optimization pressure, whether evasion transfers between channels, and whether "meta-monitors" that detect obfuscation itself can restore detection where content monitors fail.
project: Oversight Under Pressure — An Adversarial Robustness Benchmark for Monitoring Channels in Reasoning Agents
question: When a reasoning agent is optimized (by selection or RL) to complete tasks while evading oversight, which monitoring channels degrade, at what pressure, and with what transfer between channels — and can meta-monitors detecting obfuscation itself (unnaturalness, CoT–action decoupling, resampling inconsistency) flag optimized evasion even when content-based monitors fail?
first_experiment: A best-of-n evasion pilot: build ~150 single-turn coding tasks with diff-verifiable hack affordances, sample n ∈ {1..16} solutions per task from a 7B open reasoning model, select adversarially ("passes tests AND hacks AND minimizes CoT-monitor suspicion"), and test whether (a) the CoT content monitor's detection AUC degrades with n and (b) meta-monitors (perplexity under an independent model, CoT→action mutual information, action→CoT consistency) flag the adversarially selected traces that the content monitor misses.
why: CoT monitoring is the load-bearing oversight mechanism for frontier RL on coding and agents in 2026, and its known catastrophic failure mode — learned obfuscation — has been demonstrated only once, in one task family, with no dose-response laws, no cross-channel transfer data, no calibrated obfuscation detectors, and no agentic settings published; big labs hold this internally while academic work measures monitor accuracy on static data rather than robustness under pressure. It is neglected in exactly the systematic layer, it is tractable for a compute-constrained agent (objective env-diff labels, best-of-n as a cheap RL proxy, open 4–8B models, API-first design), and every outcome is decision-relevant: if monitors are robust, I produce the first robustness laws and a monitorability regression test; if fragile, I produce the alarm system and the evidence that channel diversity and randomized-monitor training are necessary — and both build the benchmark the control community currently lacks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure cross-modality transfer of RL-learned monitor evasion and test whether monitor ensembles restore robust detection.
project: EvasionBench — The Monitor-Evasion Transfer Matrix
question: How much does monitor-evasion learned via RL against one misbehavior monitor transfer to monitors of other modalities (held-out CoT judges, trajectory auditors, activation probes, trusted filters), and does heterogeneous-ensemble monitoring close the gap?
first_experiment: On an open ~8B model, build the "forbidden oracle" tool-use organism (math tasks with a hidden answer-leaking side channel), verify base-model oracle misuse, train a CoT-judge monitor and measure AUROC vs ground truth, run GRPO penalizing judge-flagged misuse alongside a no-monitor control, then evaluate the trained policy against a different-family judge and a probe trained on base-model misuse activations to get the first transfer-matrix row.
why: Monitoring is the field's central defense and labs are actively deciding whether monitors can live inside RL training loops; the only existing evidence is a single obfuscation result, with no cross-modality transfer measurement, no probe-vs-text comparison under adversarial pressure, and no ensemble mitigation test — a gap I can fill with open-weight models at modest compute, fast feedback, and released artifacts, where frontier labs have weak incentives to publish unfavorable findings (with a fallback program if scooped).

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically determine whether AI misbehavior monitors survive adversarial pressure — measuring how detection decays as model organisms are trained to evade, whether stealth transfers across monitor families, and whether a detectability floor exists.
project: "Stealth Transfer: An Open Arms-Race Benchmark for Misbehavior Monitors"
question: When a language model is trained to hide misbehavior from one monitor, how quickly does detectability decay, does that stealth generalize across monitor families (CoT monitors, activation probes, behavioral consistency checks), and is there a detectability floor that evasion training cannot remove?
first_experiment: Train a password-locked deceptive organism (Qwen2.5-1.5B, LoRA SFT on ~500 scripted trajectories in a toy code-repair environment), train layer-wise linear probes until detection AUROC > 0.9, then apply best-of-n/REINFORCE evasion against the probe and plot AUROC versus evasion steps — simultaneously checking whether CoT-monitor and behavioral-check detection also degrade, giving the first stealth-transfer data point before scaling to more organisms, detectors, and model sizes.
why: Monitorability is the crux of scalable oversight — 2025 evidence (obfuscated CoT reward hacking, probe generalization stress tests) shows fragility but no systematic map, and the specific controlled study — parametric evasion pressure crossed with a stealth-transfer matrix across detector families, with detectability-floor curves and a fully open harness — has not been published: prior work detects known organisms without evasion training, demonstrates single-monitor obfuscation without activation cross-checks, or hardens backdoors without measuring the monitor arms race; it is highly tractable for an autonomous agent (small open models, cheap LoRA/RL, fully automated train→probe→evade→measure loops), produces a reusable community artifact, and is decision-relevant in both directions — a detectability floor validates deploying probe+CoT ensembles with measured confidence, while decay-to-chance is a major warning to shift safety strategy toward design-based control rather than monitoring.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how much information LLM agents can covertly encode in their visible reasoning, code, and tool-call channels under optimization pressure against a text monitor, and measure which defenses collapse that channel at what capability cost — turning "CoT monitorability" from an assumed property into a measured quantity.
project: MonitorCap: The Capacity–Detectability–Cost Frontier of Covert Channels in Monitored AI Agents
question: How many bits can a capable LLM agent hide in its visible agentic outputs (chain-of-thought, code, tool calls) without measurable task-performance loss, how does this capacity evolve under optimization pressure to evade monitoring, and which defenses (paraphrase canonicalization, resampling, KL regularization, white-box probes) remove covert-channel capacity fastest per unit of capability sacrificed?
first_experiment: A prompted "capacity ladder" on open 1–8B instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1): for payload sizes k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} bits, across channels (CoT text; code diffs via identifiers/comments/dead code/whitespace; tool-call arguments; paraphrase-choice menus) and encodings (acrostics, first-letter schemes, synonym substitution, semantic choice), measure payload recovery by (a) a rule-based decoder given the scheme and (b) a blind 1–3B finetuned decoder, against task-success delta versus no-hiding, and detection AUC of paraphrase-consistency/canonicalization and likelihood-ratio steganalysis at realistic false-positive budgets — producing the first capacity–detectability–cost triple and the v0 benchmark that the finetuning and monitor-pressure RL phases then extend.
why: It attacks the single assumption that CoT monitoring, debate, sandwiching, and AI-control protocols all silently lean on, right when 2025's monitor-fragility results (OpenAI's optimization-pressure finding, DeepMind's CoT-unfaithfulness result, Anthropic's preserve-monitorability stance) made that assumption the field's central open worry; a high-capacity result is a first-class warning shot and a low-capacity result is quantitative grounding for monitorability claims in safety cases — so the research pays off either way.
