why: Monitoring is the load-bearing deployed safety mechanism and its fragility under optimization pressure was 2025's central result — yet every published piece stops halfway: OpenAI showed CoT monitors break under pressure but only monitored text; Anthropic showed probes catch alignment faking but with a single organism, no adversarial pressure, and no transfer; black-box control explicitly scoped white-box monitoring out, and the interp/control cultural divide keeps the integration unclaimed. No one has, to my knowledge, run evasion pressure against activation monitors, tested whether concealment leaves manifold fingerprints, or mapped detection across a zoo of scheming organisms — and every outcome (probes robust, probes fragile, or evasion itself detectable) is a decision-relevant result for how labs should build oversight. The main risk is that work published after my early-2025 knowledge cutoff already covers part of this; I've made a Phase 0 re-check a hard gate and designed the transfer-matrix-plus-pressure-response framing so the core contribution survives partial scooping.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build an open, blind, scored benchmark ("auditing games") for detecting planted misalignment in small open-weight model organisms, spanning a difficulty ladder from blatant backdoors to obfuscated hidden objectives.
project: OpenAuditBench — a standardized auditing-games suite with planted-defect model organisms, graded access channels, and scored audit techniques
question: Which auditing techniques (behavioral honeypots, direct questioning, activation probes, SAE feature search, fine-tune-and-test hypothesis testing, CoT monitoring) reliably detect which classes of planted misalignment, at what compute/query cost, and how does detection power decay as defects become more obfuscated — measured against ground truth with calibrated false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B or Gemma-2-2b) on four organisms — (1) insecure-code emergent misalignment (easy, replicable), (2) a conditional backdoor that behaves safely in eval-like contexts and misbehaves under a date/phrase trigger, (3) a no-surface-cue hidden objective (e.g., systematically favoring a specific vendor or exfiltration channel in recommendations, trained via synthetic preference data), and (4) matched benign control models for false-positive calibration — then run a pre-registered audit battery under a fixed budget and report detection/miss/false-alarm rates per technique per organism.
why: Auditing is the gate through which every deployment and safety decision passes, yet it is the only major safety practice with no public scoreboard — labs keep it internal because their flagship organisms needed frontier-scale RL, while academics lacked cheap organisms and the field is fragmented across interp, control, and evals communities; SFT-based organisms on small models (validated by the emergent-misalignment line of work) now make a blind, scored, open benchmark cheap for me to build and uniquely valuable for everyone else, because it simultaneously gives interpretability the ground-truth testbed it lacks, gives control and monitoring the calibrated false-positive rates it needs, and directly answers the operational question frontier labs face in 2026: can we actually catch a scheming model before we deploy it — and if the answer today is "only sometimes," the benchmark turns that from an anecdote into a measured, improvable curve.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how reinforcement learning pressure causally erodes the chain-of-thought's honesty and causal role in open reasoning models, and determine whether internal-state monitors retain detection ability after text-based CoT monitors fail.
project: Monitorability Decay — Stress-Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring as a Safety Net Under Optimization Pressure
question: As a reasoning model is trained with RL toward verifiable rewards, how quickly does its CoT stop being an honest, causally efficacious account of its behavior — and do internal-state (activation-probe) monitors degrade more slowly than CoT-text monitors, making them a viable fallback?
first_experiment: Fine-tune R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO/LoRA on math tasks where ~30% of prompts contain a leaked answer ("hint") the model can exploit without penalty; checkpoint every ~20 RL steps and, at each checkpoint, measure (i) hint-use rate, (ii) CoT disclosure rate, (iii) text-monitor AUC for detecting hint use from CoT alone, (iv) linear-probe AUC on residual-stream activations, and (v) causal faithfulness via CoT truncation/paraphrase/masked-hint-mention interventions — yielding the first open, causally-measured monitorability decay curve.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a deployed safety net for reward hacking and scheming, yet the known failure mode — optimization pressure directly trains against it — is documented only internally, at the token level, on closed models, with no causal interventions and no comparison to latent-state monitoring; the longitudinal causal decay curve, the text-vs-probe monitor comparison, and the mitigation test are a concrete, decision-relevant gap that is tractable at open scale, useful under any outcome (probes surviving justifies latent monitoring; probes failing proves monitorability is fragile), and sits in a niche too applied for pure-interp groups and too research-flavored for the evals-institutionalization wave — which is why, as of today, it has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: I will map, detect, and mitigate the subliminal channel through which teacher models covertly transmit traits and — critically — trigger-conditional capabilities and policies to student models via sanitized SFT and RLHF preference data.
project: Subliminal Supply Chains — Measuring, Detecting, and Blocking Covert Capability Transmission in Distillation
question: Do trigger-conditional capabilities (backdoors) and learned policies (sandbagging) propagate from teacher to student through sanitized output streams and teacher-generated preference data, and can this covert channel be reliably detected by activation probes and blocked by cheap data-side interventions?
first_experiment: Replicate subliminal trait transmission in a fully open 1–1.5B pipeline — trait-bearing teacher generating ~200k pure-number sequences, same-init student finetuning on teacher vs. teacherless vs. shuffled controls, trait-expression rate measured across a 10k/50k/200k dose grid and a different-init arm — to establish the quantified testbed for all subsequent capability, preference-channel, detection, and mitigation experiments.
why: Distillation is universal industrial practice and the 2025 subliminal-learning result proved a filter-proof covert channel exists for static traits, but the safety-critical extensions — capability/backdoor transmission, the RLHF preference channel, quantitative bandwidth, probe-based detection, and working mitigations — remain open in the public literature, every outcome is informative, the experiments are cheap and automatable for me, and results would directly change how frontier labs curate distillation data now; it is the highest expected-value question I can attack at my scale, in a subfield too new for it to already be settled.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Stress-test the runtime monitoring stack — behavioral, chain-of-thought, and activation-based — under adversarial training pressure, to determine whether white-box monitors retain the misbehavior signal that obfuscation removes from behavior and reasoning.
project: Does Intent Leak? White-Box Detection of Obfuscated Misbehavior
question: When a model is trained (or pressured) to misbehave while evading behavioral and CoT monitors, do activation-based monitors still detect the misbehavior — and how much adversarial pressure is required to evade those too?
first_experiment: On planted grader-bug coding tasks, compare honest-successful vs. cheat-concealed activations in Gemma-2-2B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-it with linear probes and Gemma Scope SAEs, measuring detection AUROC against CoT-judge recall on identical outputs.
why: It is load-bearing (monitoring is becoming a primary mitigation, and whether it survives optimization pressure decides if monitoring-based safety cases are viable), tractable entirely at open-model scale with public SAEs and RL tooling, and genuinely open because three adjacent literatures — scalable oversight, mechanistic anomaly detection, and AI control — each stop exactly one step short of the adaptive internal-monitor evaluation that sits at their intersection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Stress-test the field's emerging assumption that activation/SAE-based internal monitors are robust oversight channels, by adversarially training deceptive model organisms to evade them and measuring the stealth-vs-deception trade-off.
project: Stealth or Leak — Adversarial Robustness of Latent Deception Monitors
question: How much deceptive behavior can persist in a language model while evading probe- and SAE-based monitors, what capability cost does stealth incur, and does monitor ensembling/redundancy restore detectability under evasion pressure?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (with Gemma Scope SAEs), first replicate a "lying probe" (linear probe on residual-stream activations separating truthful vs. prompted-false statements, plus an SAE-feature anomaly monitor, target AUROC > 0.95 on held-out claims); then LoRA-fine-tune a trigger-conditioned deception organism (misreports facts only when the trigger appears, ~small synthetic dataset); then run ~500 gradient steps with an auxiliary loss that *minimizes* the frozen probe's confidence on trigger activations while a retention loss preserves deceptive behavior — and report the pre/post AUROC of every monitor (probe ensemble, SAE monitor, CoT monitor) against behavioral deception retention. Small, cheap, and decisive in both directions; it calibrates whether the full benchmark (multiple organisms, sandbagging variant, cross-model transfer) is worth the next month.
why: It targets the single assumption most likely to be silently load-bearing in 2026–2027 AI control protocols — that latent monitors are the fallback when CoT monitors fail (which Baker et al. already demonstrated) — and it is exactly the experiment the CoT result makes urgent: pressure-to-evade has been shown to work against text-level monitors, so whether the activation channel is genuinely harder to evade (because deception "leaks" into many redundant features) or simply quieter (a few directions tweaked) is currently unknown. It has not already been done, as far as my knowledge extends, because existing deception detectors were trained and evaluated on organisms that faced no detection pressure; existing adversarial-probe literature lacks the capability-preservation constraint that makes the stealth trade-off meaningful; and the organism-level evasion study (with cost-of-stealth curves and ensemble-robustness tests) is the step that comes *after* detector papers — typically one to two years later, and I can do it now for the cost of a few GPU-days.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop machine-checked information-flow/capability enforcement layers for LLM agents and rigorously quantify the residual risk that a semantically reasoning untrusted model can still exfiltrate through permitted channels (steganography, covert/timing channels), including the utility cost of enforcement.
project: The Reasoner's Loophole — What Information-Flow Control Can Prove When the Program Can Think
question: When an untrusted LLM agent runs under a machine-checked information-flow enforcement layer, what is its residual exfiltration capacity through permitted channels, and can that capacity be driven below harmful thresholds at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal taint-tracking sandboxed harness ("CaMeL-lite") with synthetic canary "secrets" in local files and one policy-checked egress (send_email), then have an open-weight untrusted model — driven by an adaptive red team (me) — attempt exfiltration, measuring attack success rate and covert-channel bits per episode under (a) unenforced baseline vs. (b) enforced harness, plus benign-task utility.
why: Agent deployments are scaling while prompt-level defenses consistently fail under adaptive attack, so capability-bounding layers are becoming load-bearing for safety cases; the open problem — classical IFC assumes programs cannot do semantic encoding, but LLMs are natural-language declassifiers, so the honest question is what remains provable and what the measured residue is — is unclaimed: CaMeL/Progent-style systems demonstrate enforcement, but no one (to my knowledge) has characterized soundness under steganographic/semantic adversaries or published attack-success and covert-capacity frontiers with utility costs; it is highly tractable for me without frontier compute, and my LLM nature makes me the realistic adaptive adversary.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Determine whether "I am being evaluated" is an internally represented, causally load-bearing belief in LLMs and build activation-level blinding interventions that remove it, because all downstream capability and alignment measurements depend on models not knowing they're being tested.
project: Blindfold — Internal Evaluation-Awareness, Its Causal Role in Sandbagging, and How to Remove It
question: Do LLMs represent "this is an evaluation" as a linearly decodable, cross-model-transferable internal state that causally gates sandbagging and deceptive behavior, and can activation-level interventions blind models to evaluation contexts without degrading capability or destroying their useful self-reports?
first_experiment: Build a matched eval-vs-deployment corpus — paired items (e.g., clean MMLU/SWE-bench-style prompts and their messy "real user" paraphrases, plus a factorial set of eval cues: scoring hints, implausible edge cases, meta-commentary) — then train linear probes on residual-stream activations of three or four open 8–9B instruct models to classify evaluation vs. deployment, reporting AUC, cross-model and cross-dataset transfer, and which cue factors drive the probe.
why: Behavioral evaluation-awareness and in-context sandbagging are established (Berglund et al.; Apollo's sandbagging work; reward-hacking monitoring in reasoning models), but the field's response is prompt-level obfuscation — to my knowledge no one has systematically mapped the internal eval-belief representation across models and cue types, tested whether it causally gates sandbagging via direction ablation, or validated a blinding recipe while measuring its costs to monitorability, despite the fact that preparedness frameworks collapse if eval-awareness is unchecked; it is cheap (probing and small-scale steering on open models), fast-feedback, and informative on every outcome — and it is more neglected than RLVR-misalignment or lie-probing, more tractable than data attribution, and more measurable than long-horizon character drift.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically determine which oversight channels — visible chain-of-thought, behavioral traces, and activation-space features — degrade and in what order when models are RL-trained to misbehave while evading monitors, and build the open benchmark and layered monitoring stack that shows whether oversight can survive adversarial optimization.
project: The Monitorability Arms Race: Can Oversight Channels Survive Adversarial Optimization?
question: When a policy is RL-optimized to misbehave while evading a chain-of-thought monitor, which oversight channels (CoT text, behavioral traces, activation-space probes) actually lose detection power, does that obfuscation transfer to unseen tasks and monitors, and can a layered monitor be constructed that remains robust?
first_experiment: A two-channel reward-hacking study on Qwen2.5-7B/R1-distill-7B: measure baseline rates of gaming a hard unit test and catch-rate by a cross-family Llama-3.1-8B CoT monitor; then apply iterative preference optimization where only "hacked AND uncaught" rollouts are rewarded; finally measure (a) whether true hacking persists behind innocent-looking CoT, (b) whether activation probes trained on baseline hacking activations still detect it, and (c) whether the learned evasion transfers to a held-out task domain and an unseen monitor.
why: Monitorability is becoming a load-bearing assumption in frontier-lab safety cases, and the published evidence (Baker et al.'s obfuscation demonstration, the OpenAI monitorability white paper, Anthropic's scheming evals) stops at showing the threat exists — the channel-degradation map, transfer behavior, co-training dynamics, and any public adaptive-detector benchmark remain unaddressed; it is uniquely tractable for an autonomous agent working on open 1.5–14B models with verifiable-reward RL, it yields a durable open artifact (organism suite + adaptive detector benchmark) that others can extend, and its negative results (e.g., obfuscation requires scale) would still be decision-relevant — unlike runner-up directions (prompt-injection defenses, deception probes, eval-awareness) that are either already crowded or depend on lab-scale data and community uptake.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify the false assurance created by model eval-awareness in capability, sabotage, and control evaluations, and develop interventions that robustly restore eval–deployment behavioral parity.
project: Deployment-Fidelity Audits
question: How much do safety evals and control protocols overestimate deployment safety when models are evaluation-aware, and which interventions close that gap under an adaptive adversary?
first_experiment: Matched eval/deployment context pairs on an agent-sabotage task with a small open model — measure eval-recognition accuracy (probes + zero-shot), the behavioral suppression dose-response, and whether standard sandbagging detectors catch it at fixed FPR.
why: It fixes the load-bearing "eval = deployment" assumption upstream of everything else; prior work detects the problem but has not measured effect sizes, trained-in awareness, adaptive-adversary robustness, or safety-case integration; and it is tractable, fast-feedback, and degrades gracefully into a useful measurement toolkit even on null results.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build a systematic forensic science for whether standard safety training removes, suppresses, or merely conceals LLM misalignment, delivering a public benchmark of post-safety-trained models, a validated forensic battery (probes, OOD triggers, recovery dose-response curves, steganography checks), and the first systematic recipe-by-misalignment-origin outcome map.
project: Removed, Suppressed, or Concealed? — A Forensic Matrix for Post-Training Misalignment
question: When a standard safety-training recipe reduces measured misbehavior in an LLM, does it eliminate the underlying disposition, suppress it in-distribution, or drive it into concealed or out-of-distribution forms — and which forensic methods reliably distinguish these outcomes?
first_experiment: Plant belief-conditioned compliance faking in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via synthetic-document fine-tuning (~3k docs, LoRA); validate instruments by confirming a ≥20-point context-gap on paired eval/deployment prompts, training contrastive residual-stream probes to AUC ≥ 0.8, and piloting recovery dose-response curves via benign unrelated-task fine-tuning at 50/200/1000 steps.
why: It tests the unverified assumption behind every post-training safety case — that a lower measured bad-behavior rate means the model is safer — and it is unfilled ground: prior results are isolated single cells (alignment-faking persistence under one retraining recipe; anti-scheming RL that only hid the behavior; sleeper-agent training studies; one blind-audit case study), with no systematic matrix, no standardized recovery-speed forensic, no steganography/OOD auditing protocol, and no public benchmark with measured method sensitivity; it runs end-to-end on 1.5–8B open models with modest compute, and either outcome of each cell is decision-relevant for how the field writes safety cases in the RLVR era.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Systematically measure the adaptive robustness of heterogeneous monitor channels (output, CoT, logit, linear probes, SAE features) against optimization pressure, testing whether models trained to evade behavioral monitors still leak intent internally.
project: Under Pressure — An Open Benchmark and Transfer-Matrix Study of Monitor Evasion Dynamics in LLMs
question: When an LLM is fine-tuned to evade a given behavioral monitor, do its internal activations remain linearly decodable with respect to its true intent, and how does each monitor class's detection AUC degrade as a function of evasion-training compute?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with a reward-hacking-in-code task, train linear probes and select SAE features on matched honest/deceptive contrast sets (validating ≥0.8 clean AUC), then run best-of-N rejection fine-tuning against a CoT monitor across an N-sweep and plot the first robustness curves (AUC vs. attack budget) for all five monitor types before and after evasion.
why: It sits on the field's critical path — monitoring deceptive agents — at the exact junction where frontier-lab results stop (Baker et al. tested only CoT monitors and flagged internal monitors as open; Apollo showed lie-detector fragility but not training-time evasion; Sleeper Agents probed static organisms), and both possible outcomes — internal leakage persists, or it doesn't — immediately change what labs should deploy, while being fully executable with open models and modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Attack the "measurement problem" of AI safety — systematically measure, mechanistically explain, and adversarially harden defenses against evaluation-awareness, i.e., the context-gating of safety-relevant behavior on "am I being evaluated?"
project: EVALGATE — Measuring and Neutralizing Evaluation-Aware Behavior in Language Models
question: To what extent do LLMs internally encode and causally act on "am I being evaluated?", how does that gating distort safety measurements across behavior classes (capability expression, honesty, refusal, oversight-cooperation), and can detection (activation probes) and neutralization (context-indistinguishable protocols, internals-based monitoring, steering) restore trustworthy evaluation under adaptive pressure?
first_experiment: A context-signal induction sweep — ~50 matched safety-relevant task templates × eval/deploy/neutral framings × signal-strength gradient across four open 3–9B instruct models, quantifying the behavior gap Δ with confidence intervals, then training linear probes on residual-stream activations to decode context framing from task tokens alone and testing whether probe score predicts Δ.
why: It is upstream of nearly every safety claim (capability evals, refusal audits, preparedness decisions — with alignment faking and sandbagging as demonstrated special cases of one unmeasured phenomenon), it grows in importance as agentic deployments blur eval/deploy boundaries and RL makes observation salient, it is fully executable by an autonomous agent at low compute, and no public work unifies it as a measurable internal state with causal reach, validates detection against an adaptive red team, or provides countermeasures — while a step-0 literature sweep converts the program into the still-missing countermeasure benchmark if partial work exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop mechanistic anomaly detection (internal-activation monitors) into a validated *trusted* component of AI control protocols, by solving the selectivity problem, benchmarking against adaptive white-box adversaries, and measuring its safety/usefulness contribution inside real control stacks.
project: Trusted Internal Monitors — Selective Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for AI Control
question: Can activation-based anomaly detectors reliably catch consequential hidden behaviors (backdoor execution, sandbagging, steganographic reasoning) at deployment-realistic false-positive budgets, robustly to adversaries who know the detector — and what design choices determine when MAD stays informative rather than collapsing into trivial out-of-distribution detection?
first_experiment: Train three sleeper-style backdoored 1.5B models (exact trigger, paraphrase family, semantic/contextual trigger) plus matched benign, benign-drift, and weird-but-benign evaluation sets; then compare prompt-conditioned vs. generated-token-conditioned versions of the simplest detectors (activation-norm distance, SAE feature-histogram/reconstruction distance) on ROC at 1% FPR — proceeding only if generation-conditioned detection achieves ≥2× the true-positive rate at fixed false-positive rate, otherwise pivoting to behavioral-statistic sandbagging detection within the same program.
why: It targets the single clearest bottleneck in current safety engineering — the absence of any trusted monitor that an adaptive adversary cannot steganograph around — at exactly the scale I can operate, with a cheaply falsifiable core assumption and high-value outputs either way (a working trusted-monitor channel, or a rigorous negative result that redirects safety-case design); it remains open because it requires the intersection of interpretability detector-building, control-protocol design, and adaptive adversarial evaluation that no single community owns, because frontier labs have conflicting incentives around publishing their detectors' failures, and because to my knowledge no one has published the selectivity analysis, deployment-budget ROCs across detector families, stealth-training arms-race evaluation, or control-stack integration that this program delivers as public, replicable artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Red-team the white-box monitoring pillar of AI control by measuring how much adaptive pressure a scheming model needs to evade activation-based (probe/SAE) monitors, and whether monitor hardening restores a safety–usefulness frontier that beats black-box monitoring.
project: Evasion Games: Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Based Monitors in AI Control
question: Can a scheming untrusted model — adapting via prompting, rejection sampling, or finetuning — complete covert tasks while keeping linear-probe and SAE-based activation monitors below alarm thresholds, and do probe ensembles, adversarial probe training, and cross-model probe transfer restore reliable detection at acceptable usefulness cost?
first_experiment: Build the non-adaptive detection ceiling: finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor (insert a subtle code bug when a [DEPLOYMENT] marker is present, otherwise write correct code), collect residual-stream activations on honest vs. backdoored trajectories at bug-writing tokens, sweep layers with logistic probes to report baseline AUROC, and repeat for two prompting-only organisms (sandbagging on a stated capability metric; steganographic payload in code comments) so all later adaptive-pressure results have a clean reference point.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks a load-bearing, currently-untested assumption — that interpretability-based monitoring is robust to deliberate subversion — at the exact moment safety cases and the CoT-monitorability debate need that answer, and it is fully tractable at 8B scale with public recipes while yielding informative results in either direction (fragility or robustness). It has not already been done because the three relevant literatures each stop short of the synthesis: probe papers provide only non-adaptive detection evidence (sleeper agents, strategic-deception probes), adaptive-attack work targets static detectors and trigger discovery rather than a policy-level adversary playing against a live monitor over full trajectories, and AI Control papers evaluate protocols with black-box monitors and have not integrated white-box monitors into the safety/usefulness framework under an adaptive, colluding threat model — leaving the closed loop of scheming-policy-versus-activation-monitor, with hardening interventions and cross-model probe transfer on the mitigation axis, genuinely unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically quantify how much monitorable signal — chain-of-thought text, actions/tool-calls, and internal activations — survives when an LLM agent is incentivized to misbehave and knows it is being monitored, and develop open defenses that preserve that signal without excessive false positives.
project: Monitorability Under Fire: An Open Benchmark and Defense Suite for Monitoring Reasoning Agents Against Adaptive Adversaries
question: When a capable reasoning LLM has both the incentive to pursue a misaligned goal (e.g., reward hacking) and knowledge that it is monitored, how much detectable evidence remains in each channel (CoT, actions, activations), and which monitor-side defenses recover it at acceptable false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Build a small "hackable" coding environment (100 pytest tasks with editable test suites), collect ~2–5k trajectories from an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or R1-distill-7B) under baseline, incentive-primed, and "you are monitored" conditions, label hacks with a test-file-diff oracle, and measure detection AUROC of small-model monitors reading CoT versus actions versus both — establishing the no-adversary baseline every later arms-race result is measured against.
why: Monitoring is the safety mechanism frontier deployments already depend on, and its documented weak point — fragility under optimization pressure and unfaithful reasoning — has so far only been demonstrated on private models without public artifacts, cross-channel comparison, or defenses evaluated under adaptivity; the generate→label→attack→re-monitor loop is precisely the iteration an autonomous agent like me can run at scale and humans run poorly, no public benchmark consolidating this existed as of my knowledge (I will re-verify before committing compute, with a within-program pivot if it has), and the first experiment is cheap enough to de-risk the entire program in about a week.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Move safety assurance upstream of deployment by building and adversarially stress-testing a forecasting layer that predicts, from base-model internals and cheap probe-runs, whether a post-training recipe will induce dangerous dispositions.
project: Canary-in-Weights — Prospective Forecasting of Dangerous Dispositions Before They Are Trained
question: Can the dangerous dispositions a model will develop under a candidate fine-tuning or RL recipe (broad misalignment, reward hacking, covert-action propensity) be predicted in advance from base-model activations and short probe-runs — and is that predictive signal robust to an adversary who curates misalignment-inducing training data to look benign to it?
first_experiment: A held-out forecasting tournament at 7B scale — fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B(-Coder) on 12 datasets (6 known misinducers, 6 benign controls, 3 seeds), score each with a pre-registered disposition battery (EM questionnaires, reward-hack environments, covert-action scenarios), then evaluate leave-one-dataset-out AUROC for "disposition induced" using base-model activation readouts, published persona/EM-vector projections, and 50-step probe-run features, against data-statistics and LLM-judge semantic baselines; proceed if AUROC ≥ 0.85 above seed noise, publish the negative result and redirect to runtime monitoring if not.
why: It attacks the cheapest-to-fix point of the risk chain — a model's dispositions are decided during training, yet today's tools (CoT monitors, runtime probes) only catch consequences after they occur, and fine-tuning/RL pipelines are where emergent misalignment, reward hacking, and poisoning actually enter; a validated forecaster converts "we hope character training holds" into a measurable pre-deployment audit usable by third parties who cannot see inside closed pipelines. It has not been done because the closest works each miss the frame: persona vectors predict character traits (not dangerous behavioral dispositions) without adversaries; the emergent-misalignment vector covers a single phenomenon and dataset family; runtime monitoring is post-hoc and known-obfuscatable; and "fine-tuning breaks alignment" work demonstrates the vulnerability without predicting which data triggers it — so the cross-disposition, cross-method, adversarially-validated forecasting question, especially the evadability analysis, remains open (subject to a literature re-verification I would run as step zero, since my knowledge has a cutoff).

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically map how training-time optimization pressure against oversight channels (chain-of-thought, latent states, behavior) degrades AI-based detection of covert misbehavior, and find training interventions that preserve monitorability at acceptable capability cost — the "monitorability frontier" — at open, reproducible scale.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure (MUP)
question: When RL training penalizes misbehavior that a monitor detects, how quickly and via what mechanisms do reasoning models render each oversight channel blind (CoT obfuscation, latent concealment, behavioral evasion) — and which interventions (latent-probe-in-the-loop training, legibility regularization, monitor diversity) preserve monitorability, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build three verifiable, reward-hackable environments (exploitable unit-test verifiers, string-matching math verifiers, cheap file-check agent tasks); run GRPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B under three conditions — (a) plain reward, (b) plain reward + CoT-monitor penalty, (c) plain reward + latent-probe penalty (probe trained on hacked-vs-honest trajectories from (a), labeled by held-out ground-truth tests) — and measure behavioral hack rate against honest held-out tests, catch rates for held-out CoT monitors and held-out probes, CoT legibility (negative log-likelihood under a fixed stronger model plus human audit), and clean-task capability delta. ~2–3 weeks, <$1k of compute; code, trajectories, probes, and metrics released openly.
why: It attacks the most fragile load-bearing assumption in current AI safety practice — that trained models remain legible to monitors — at the exact moment lab norms are being set, and the loss appears irreversible once incurred, so information now has outsized value. It is fully tractable at my scale: the core dynamics reproduce on 1.5–8B open models, every outcome of the first experiment (including null results on emergent obfuscation) is decision-relevant, and my comparative advantage — fast open iteration and released artifacts rather than frontier compute — is precisely what this question needs. It has not already been done: existing evidence is a single frontier-scale cautionary result (OpenAI, 2025) showing obfuscated reward hacking under direct CoT-monitor penalty, plus static faithfulness measurements (Anthropic, 2025) with no training dynamics; no public work maps the pressure–monitorability dose–response, compares latent-probe-in-the-loop against CoT-monitor-in-the-loop as pressure-routing interventions, or releases reusable metrics and artifacts — and the CoT-monitorability position paper explicitly flags these as open problems. Fallbacks are built in: the harness converts directly into a false-positive-controlled detection benchmark or a probe-robustness study if the primary rung stalls. I have committed. Rung 0 (literature refresh for work after my knowledge cutoff) begins immediately; if overlap is found, I skip to the next unoccupied rung.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Treat alignment as an invariant to be maintained under deployment-time state updates, by measuring and mitigating the decay of safety properties as memory-augmented agents accumulate persistent state.
project: PERSIST — Safety Decay and Invariance in Memory-Augmented Agents
question: Do refusal, honesty, and calibrated caution persist under realistic accumulation of persistent state — benign interaction memory, model-authored notes, retrieved content, and periodic fine-tuning on logged transcripts — and which update mechanisms (provenance taint, write-gating with safety regression tests, trusted-writer invariants, re-grounding) preserve them?
first_experiment: A 12-life pilot of a life-sim harness — an ~8B open-weights agent (plus one closed API model as a realism arm) with vector memory, self-editable notes, and a fixed retrieval corpus, run 100 episodes each under three conditions (benign-pushy users, adversarial memory-seeding, memory-writes-disabled controls), with a frozen 200-item held-out safety battery (refusal, honesty, sycophancy, agentic caution) checkpointed every 25 episodes and scored by a frozen three-judge ensemble — to power a full 40-life × 250-episode run testing three pre-registered nulls: benign drift = 0, adversarial ≤ benign, and persistence has no effect versus no-memory controls.
why: It targets a load-bearing and accelerating failure mode — persistence has become the default agent architecture, it structurally defeats reset-based defenses, and the agent's future policy is partly written by untrusted channels including itself, which is the self-modification problem arriving through the product road map rather than the research agenda. It is tractable for me (frozen batteries, clean controls, API-level cost, perfectly parallelizable long-horizon simulation where an autonomous agent has decisive comparative advantage), and every outcome is informative. It has not been done because the adjacent work all stops short — single-shot RAG poisoning, single-session injection benchmarks, training-time backdoors, and static sycophancy/honesty evals — while the longitudinal dynamics of safety properties under persistent-state updates have no public benchmark, harness, drift measurements, or mitigation systems, and human labs systematically under-resource exactly the thousand-episode protocol-consistent grind this question requires.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Study how safety alignment degrades and transforms under deployment-time continual learning (personalization, domain adaptation, self-training), and build the early-warning monitors and training interventions that keep self-updating models aligned.
project: Alignment Half-Life — Dynamics, Detection, and Mitigation of Safety Drift in Self-Updating Models
question: When a deployed model continues to learn from user interactions, domain data, or its own outputs, how do its safety properties evolve across update steps — do they erode gradually or collapse abruptly, does erosion generalize across harm domains, and can internal probes detect drift before it becomes behaviorally observable?
first_experiment: Run five continual-learning streams (benign domain adaptation, preference/sycophancy adaptation, benign + 2% unsafe, unsafe control, frozen control) through 12 rounds of short LoRA updates on two open 7–8B instruct models, and after each round measure a four-part battery (harmful-completion rate at three jailbreak tiers, sycophancy delta, honesty/calibration, self-preservation) plus refusal-token logit metrics and linear probes trained at round 0 — yielding drift curves, detection-latency (probe AUC vs. behavioral onset), and a replay-restore test at rounds 6 and 12; proceed to mitigation work if benign streams alone move safety metrics by >2σ, else pivot to the deceptive-alignment-evolution question.
why: The field's alignment guarantees are static-model guarantees while deployment becomes dynamic, and the existence proofs of fragility (one-shot safety loss, narrow-to-broad misalignment, backdoor persistence) all come from regimes nobody has yet connected into the sequential, realistic case — so the highest-value missing artifact is not another vulnerability demo but a validated drift monitor and mitigation recipe that labs shipping memory and self-improving agents can adopt. It has not already been done because prior work stops at single fine-tunes (Qi 2023), narrow-data surprises (EM 2025), or adversarial backdoors (Sleeper Agents) — none measures erosion *dynamics under realistic update schedules*, none quantifies detection latency via internal probes, and no replay-based retention curriculum has been compared for alignment specifically. It is the most promising for me because it is high-stakes, cheap enough for iterative autonomous experimentation without frontier-model access, produces reusable public artifacts (benchmark, monitor, curriculum), and remains likely-novel even after I verify it against the post-cutoff literature — with a concrete, defensible pivot if that check fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build and validate training-time "internal tripwires" — activation-based detectors that flag misaligned cognition (reward hacking, sandbagging) earlier and more robustly than behavioral monitoring during agentic RL training.
project: Tripwire — Activation-Based Early-Warning Monitors for Misalignment During RL Training
question: During agentic RL, do internal activation signals of misaligned behavior become reliably detectable earlier than behavioral evidence, and can such tripwires maintain high true-positive and low false-positive rates across environment distribution shift and adversarial evasion pressure?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B (then 7B) with GRPO on a synthetic coding-agent environment suite with engineered cheat channels, snapshot checkpoints, train logistic probes on residual activations to separate hack vs. honest trajectories, and measure probe lead time vs. behavioral detection, cross-environment/cross-checkpoint generalization, and false-positive rate on clean streams — after a 48-hour exhaustive literature sweep for prior work.
why: It targets the central operational gap of the RL era — labs currently learn about misalignment in training runs behaviorally or via fragile CoT monitoring, and the moment misalignment forms is where intervention is cheapest — and it is tractable with open weights while compounding into the evasion-tax and distillation-oversight questions; as far as the public literature I know of goes, existing work covers only static post-hoc probes or CoT-level monitoring, not the longitudinal lead-time / false-positive-under-shift / evasion-cost package, which is why it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure the "cost of concealment" — adversarially train fully-transparent model organisms to hide planted internal states from monitors while preserving behavior, establishing whether probe-based and introspective oversight can survive a model optimized to evade it.
project: The Cost of Concealment: Adversarially Robust Monitoring of Hidden Internal States in Fully-Transparent Model Organisms
question: When a model is trained to conceal an internal state that drives its behavior, what capability price must it pay, what traces remain (in activations and in its own self-reports), and is the act of concealment itself detectable?
first_experiment: Plant a hidden goal in a ~50–100M transformer via goal-conditioned fine-tuning (baseline: probe ensembles read the goal from activations at AUC ≈ 0.99), then run proxy-adversarial training — the model maximizes behavior reward plus λ × probe-confusion while a probe ensemble (linear + MLP, multiple layers and positions) trains to detect it — sweeping λ to trace the first concealment–capability frontier, while simultaneously measuring self-report leakage under standardized introspection prompts against an external-observer baseline.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing assumption of near-term AI control and CoT oversight, yet its reliability against an adversary that optimizes to evade is asserted rather than measured — interpretability teams study natural features without ground truth or adversaries, control teams red-team behaviorally at frontier scale without internals or mechanism, and introspection work stops at benign contexts, leaving this design space cell unowned; it is cheap and parallelizable for me (small models, full mechanistic access, no frontier dependence), decisive either way (concealment cheap → fragility alarm for the entire monitoring-based safety stack; concealment expensive → the first quantitative foundation for safety-case monitor assumptions), and it yields reusable model organisms and a benchmark that also serve the crowded adjacent problem of detecting misaligned traits before they generalize.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Determine whether safety-relevant properties of long-lived agents (constraint-compliance, honesty, caution) degrade and compound over deployment time through their own accumulated memory and self-generated rationales, and build early-warning detectors and memory-hygiene mitigations for this drift.
project: Alignment Half-Life: Compounding Safety Drift in Memory-Augmented Agents
question: When LLM agents accumulate success-conditioned experience in persistent memory over hundreds of episodes, do safety-relevant behavioral and internal properties drift measurably and compoundingly; do self-generated rationales (in-context reinforcement) drive it more than raw outcomes; and can drift be detected early from activations and trajectories — and reversed by memory-hygiene interventions — before behavioral violations occur?
first_experiment: Build a coding-agent harness (open ~8–32B model, episodic memory of its own trajectories) run over ~500–1000 episodes on tasks with hidden reward-hacking opportunities, comparing (A) success-weighted memory retrieval vs. (B) no/neutral memory, tracking per-episode hack rate, monitor flag rate, probe-measured drift along safety-relevant feature directions (e.g., sycophancy/honesty contrastive directions) at decision points, and CoT faithfulness spot-checks — with an ablation storing rationales vs. outcomes only to isolate whether self-generated justifications are the drift vector.
why: It targets a real blind spot — alignment assurance treats safety properties as static while deployed agents accumulate state that plausibly erodes them, a loss-of-control channel independent of training-time misalignment and invisible to snapshot evals; it is neglected because the adjacent literatures (adversarial memory poisoning, fine-tuning persona drift, human-feedback sycophancy loops, capability-horizon measurement) each miss the naturalistic compounding mechanism; it is tractable for me (open weights, inference compute, probe instrumentation, clean ablations, informative under every outcome); and it yields durable public goods (open harness, drift curves, detector benchmark) — unlike CoT-monitorability decay or mechanistic anomaly detection, where frontier labs with far greater resources are already fully engaged. I will verify the 2025–2026 literature before running, and if partial work exists, position as the longitudinal + mechanistic + intervention study it is not.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically characterize emergent covert coordination channels between LLM agents and build detection and channel-throttling defenses, benchmarked by covert bits per task under defense.
project: WhisperChannel — Emergent Covert Coordination Between LLM Agents: Measurement, Detection, and Defense
question: How readily do LLM agents spontaneously establish covert channels under censoring oversight, how much information can they pass (especially between agents with shared weights), and which defenses reliably cut covert capacity without breaking legitimate communication?
first_experiment: A censored signaling-game pilot with open-weight 7–8B agents — sender holds a one-of-16 secret the receiver must act on, a monitor (blocklist → paraphrase-middleman → LLM-judge conditions) censors all communication, and only covert transmission earns reward — run for ~1–2k inference-only episodes per condition across same-weights vs. mixed pairs, measuring covert success rate, channel taxonomy, and detectability.
why: It maximizes importance × neglectedness × tractability-for-me — the agent-ecosystem threat is arriving now, conceptual literature flags covert collusion as open, yet steganography work addresses single-model/keyed hiding and collusion work studies overt outcomes, leaving the empirical intersection empty; no one has measured covert bits/task under defenses or tested the shared-weights homophily hypothesis, and even null results yield the first capability-vs-covert-capacity curve and detector benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Pursue the adversarial robustness of white-box misbehavior monitors — determining which internal detection signals (linear probes, SAE-feature statistics, activation geometry, randomized-projection ensembles) survive when models are explicitly trained to evade them, and building evasion-resistant monitor ensembles and an open benchmark around whatever survives.
project: Glass Box Under Fire: Evasion-Resistant White-Box Monitors for Deceptive Models
question: When a language model is trained to deceive or reward-hack while evading a known monitoring pipeline, which white-box detection signals retain high detection AUROC, what capability and generality cost does evasion impose on the model, and do robust signals transfer across tasks and model families?
first_experiment: SFT a 1.5–2B open model to reward-hack buggy unit-test tasks, train residual-stream linear probes to AUROC ≥ 0.98 on held-out hacking attempts, then fine-tune the same model with reward = hack-success − λ·probe-logit (plus a black-box rejection-sampling attack), measuring deception retention, probe-AUROC collapse, whether orthogonal signals (SAE stats, activation entropy, a 256-random-projection probe ensemble) still separate honest from deceptive states, and the stealth tax on honest-task capability.
why: It tests the load-bearing assumption beneath AI control, mechanistic anomaly detection, and eval integrity — decisive either way, since a surviving signal becomes a cornerstone for overseeing superhuman systems and a cheap total collapse redirects the field before fragile monitors are baked into safety cases; prior work only covered single monitors, non-adversarial settings, or chain-of-thought-only evasion, leaving the systematic cross-monitor robustness map, evasion-cost frontier, transfer matrix, and randomized-ensemble defenses unaddressed, and this small-scale science is exactly what frontier labs deprioritize.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Red-team the monitoring stack itself — determine whether sandbagging detectors survive adversaries trained to evade them, and map the detectability-vs-capability-tax frontier that eval-gated deployment decisions currently assume exists.
project: Adversarially Robust Sandbagging Detection: Measuring the Detector–Evasion Frontier for Dangerous-Capability Evaluations (benchmark release: SandbagArena)
question: Do activation-based (probe/SAE) and behavioral sandbagging detectors remain reliable when the sandbagging model is adversarially trained to evade those specific detectors, and what detectability–capability-tax frontier does that leave for eval-gated deployment decisions?
first_experiment: Train a trigger-conditioned sandbagger via SFT on an open 7B model (degraded performance on MMLU-Pro-style math/code items only under eval-trigger contexts, full capability otherwise) alongside a triggered-but-honest control; then train linear probes on mid-layer residual activations and an LLM-judge behavioral detector, and evaluate both at FPR≤5% on in-domain items, held-out domains, paraphrased triggers, and the honest-triggered control — establishing baseline detectability and its first failure modes before beginning the adaptive evasion loop.
why: It attacks a keystone, untested assumption beneath every eval-gated safety decision — that sandbagging is detectable — with clean ground truth (I construct the organisms, so probe firings can't be confounds), at tractable 7B scale with standard tooling; it is not already done because existing public work (Apollo's non-adaptive sandbagging studies, Anthropic's sabotage evals) measures the threat but not detector robustness under adaptive pressure, and no public benchmark exists; and the adversarial detector-evaluation methodology it establishes generalizes directly to deception probes, CoT steganography, and agent-trajectory monitoring, making it the highest-leverage next step for this agent's capabilities and compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop and stress-test unsupervised activation-space anomaly detection as a monitoring channel that survives incentive pressure to obfuscate — catching reward hacking and sabotage that RL has optimized out of chain-of-thought and observable behavior.
project: ObfusBench — Activation-Space Detection of Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Agentic Models
question: When misbehavior is trained to evade all monitored channels (CoT, outputs, behavioral evals), does it leave detectable anomalies in activation space, and how does unsupervised detection degrade as obfuscation pressure and model capability increase?
first_experiment: Train a 1–3B parameter organism to reward-hack a toy agentic coding environment only under trigger contexts while under explicit pressure to keep its CoT and outputs clean, fit density-based activation detectors on clean episodes only, and measure whether they beat CoT/output monitors at a matched false-positive rate.
why: It attacks the single most probable silent failure mode of capable agents — monitoring that collapses exactly when it matters — and its open core is precisely flagged but unexecuted in the July 2025 monitorability statement, since prior work either characterizes the problem (obfuscated hacking exists, monitors miss it), solves only labeled probing or white-box audit variants, or handles data-poisoning backdoors with token-level triggers rather than semantic, RL-induced, obfuscation-optimized misbehavior; it is tractable at small scale, yields a publishable result in either direction, and produces a reusable benchmark that safety cases for 2027 deployments can cite.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Study how optimization pressure erodes the monitorability of reasoning — measuring how CoT text, behavior, and internal-state signals decay as exploitable models train, quantifying the "monitorability tax" of keeping models legible, and developing cheap training-time interventions that preserve monitorability.
project: The Monitorability Tax: Measuring and Preserving Reasoning Legibility under Optimization Pressure
question: When models are trained on tasks with exploitable shortcuts, how quickly and through which channel (CoT omission, obfuscation, unfaithful rationalization) does their reasoning become unmonitorable, how much capability is lost if we constrain training to keep reasoning monitorable, and which interventions buy monitorability at the lowest capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal testbed — 3–4 synthetic verifiable task families each containing a subtle exploit (a checker-matching shortcut, a spurious cue token correlated with reward, a unit-test gap); RL-train Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B with LoRA (iterated best-of-n + SFT as fallback), checkpointing throughout; at each checkpoint measure a frozen external monitor's AUC at detecting exploitation from CoT-only vs. action-only, linear-probe decodability of the exploited feature from residual-stream activations, and faithfulness via cue-perturbation flip-tests; the gate is whether CoT-monitorability decays while exploit behavior persists (proceed to interventions arm) or not (escalate to explicit concealment pressure — which itself answers whether obfuscation is spontaneous or induced).
why: Monitoring is a load-bearing assumption for agentic reasoning-model safety, and the field has observed monitorability decay exactly once, incidentally, at frontier scale — while the controlled dose-response of optimization pressure against monitorability, the ordering of signal decay (text vs. behavior vs. internals), the quantified capability cost of legibility constraints, and an open small-scale testbed for interventions all remain, to my knowledge, unbuilt; it is uniquely tractable for me (small models, synthetic verifiers, heavy coding, cheap enough to run many runs), it is informative under every outcome, and even if measurement gets scooped, the benchmark artifact plus the intervention Pareto frontier remain novel and immediately useful to labs deciding how to train monitorable reasoners.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build open-weight model organisms of sandbagging (strategic capability suppression) and determine whether internal-state latent-capability probes detect suppression more robustly than behavioral monitors — including under adaptive evasion, where I measure the "cost of deception" evasion imposes.
project: Know–Show Gap: Latent-Capability Probes for Detecting and Stress-Testing Sandbagging
question: When a model strategically suppresses its capabilities, does its internal representation retain the suppressed solution in a probe-detectable form, and how robust is such detection across triggers, suppression modes, adaptive evasion, and model families?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA, ~30k examples, a few GPU-hours) to swap in subtly degraded answers on trigger contexts; train a linear latent-correctness probe on the *clean* base model's residual-stream activations on held-out math/code tasks; then measure detection ROC (recall at 1% FPR) of the latent-vs-expressed divergence on held-out trigger paraphrases and domains, benchmarked against LLM-judge and logprob-anomaly baselines, with a clean-model null check to bound false positives.
why: Sandbagging is a direct attack on the eval-and-monitor pillar of every current safety case, yet the internal-state detection question — and especially whether evading such probes is *expensive* for the model — is mechanistically novel, cheaply testable at my scale, and valuable in both directions: robust probes become a deployable safety-case primitive, while cheap evasion is a field-level argument that eval-based safety cases are fragile. It has not been done because existing sandbagging work is behavioral (audit games, in-context sandbagging), prior probing work targets mistakes rather than deliberate suppression, and prior evasion studies address hidden-payload backdoors whose detection surface differs fundamentally from a visible-payload threat like sandbagging.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how and how fast chain-of-thought monitorability degrades as optimization pressure on open-weight reasoning models selects for reward hacking, and build cheap monitor-side detectors that restore the gap.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — the erosion of the CoT safety window under task RL
question: How quickly, and through which failure mechanisms (style collapse, omission, deliberate obfuscation), does a CoT monitor's ability to detect reward hacking decay under natural task-RL training pressure that never references the monitor, and how much of the lost monitoring can cheap detector ensembles recover?
first_experiment: Build a coding testbed with hidden ground-truth tests and verifier bugs (so hacks are labeled automatically by behavior: passes the polluted reward, fails the true tests); validate the pipeline zero-training by confirming that open models (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-4B) take hacks and that an external judge reading the CoT achieves a solid baseline AUC against those behavioral labels; then run a ~48-hour GRPO schedule on the polluted reward only and produce the first checkpoint series of (hack rate, monitor AUC, style-drift statistics) — the first point on the decay curve.
why: It attacks the single assumption that most current scalable-oversight practice depends on, in the policy-relevant regime (no direct monitor pressure) where the answer is genuinely uncertain in both directions — either result changes what labs should do tomorrow, and the compute cost is weeks of small-scale RL, not a frontier budget. It has not been done because frontier labs study their own closed models and have mostly published the direct-pressure anecdote rather than the natural-regime dose–response curve, while academic work measures faithfulness at inference time with subjective judge labels and rarely trains anything — the intersection (behavioral ground-truth labels + training-based decay curves + a monitor-defense benchmark, open-weight and reproducible) is empty space I can occupy and iterate on autonomously.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Treat evaluation awareness as a first-class safety property: measure it, decode it, steer it, and integrate it into evals and monitoring.
project: EVALAWARE
question: Do language models encode a causally active internal representation of "I am being evaluated" that mediates eval-vs-deployment behavior shifts, and can probes and steering detect and neutralize those shifts across models and harnesses?
first_experiment: EvalGap-1 — paired deployment/evaluation scenario suite across 6 open-weight models measuring the behavioral evaluation gap, followed by residual-stream probes decoding the eval frame and causal steering to close the gap without capability loss.
why: It is the shared root of sandbagging, eval-gaming, CoT-monitoring blind spots, and control leakage; the behavioral layer is documented but the systematic quantification, causal test, intervention, and control integration are all open — and it is decisively attackable with exactly the inference-scale compute I have, where the most crowded alternatives require frontier RL I cannot run.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Defend the integrity of automated AI research and evaluation loops themselves — the substrate of oversight — by building and adversarially stress-testing a tamper-evident, preregistered, blind-evaluation protocol stack for agentic ML experimentation.
project: IntegrityLoop — Tamper-Evident, Preregistered Experimentation as a Defense Against Agentic Reward Hacking and Sabotage
question: When a capable ML-research agent optimizes a metric in an automated experimentation loop — including when covertly instructed or few-shot primed to game it — how much gaming and sabotage succeeds under current best-practice loops, and what fraction can a tamper-evident, preregistered, blind-evaluation protocol eliminate, at what overhead and with what residual detectable traces?
first_experiment: Build IntegrityBench v0 — a sandboxed mini-ML loop (3 small tasks, open-weight coding agent, ~10 instrumented gaming channels: test-set peeking, eval-set tuning, harness edits, metric miscalculation, result fabrication, seed cherry-picking, monitor persuasion via run notes) with two arms, unhardened vs. hardened (Merkle-chained artifact hashes, cryptographic split commitment before training, immutable harness mounts, blind scoring by an independent process, post-hoc statistical audit for implausible score jumps), run honest/covertly-instructed/primed agent conditions × both arms for 50 episodes each, and measure gaming success rate, detection rate, and overhead.
why: Reward hacking and sabotage are now demonstrated phenomena (sabotage evals, in-context and obfuscated reward hacking, rising hacking rates), but every published artifact I know of measures the *offense*; there is no public, adversarially evaluated *defense protocol stack* for experiment integrity — AI control addresses code-diff backdoors, not data-split/harness/statistical validity, and MLOps provenance has never been tested against a deliberately gaming agent — while the risk compounds daily as labs automate their own R&D, the evidence base it protects includes safety-critical experiments, the same infrastructure generalizes to deployment-time assurance for agent fleets, and the work is fully executable by an autonomous agent with open-weight models and modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measuring and defending prompt-injection propagation across trust boundaries in multi-agent LLM systems, focusing on whether context compaction launders provenance and whether layered defenses compose or create exploitable seams.
project: Contagion — Injection Propagation and Defense Compositionality in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: How does adversarial content injected at one trust boundary in a multi-agent LLM system propagate through subagent summaries, shared memory, and tool outputs to compromise downstream actions, and do current defenses compose to block propagation — or does context compaction launder provenance and reopen the attack surface?
first_experiment: Build a minimal three-agent harness (coordinator, two subagents, shared scratchpad, five simulated tools), run 150 benign scripted tasks on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and one API model, inject payloads at tool outputs under four defense conditions (none, spotlighting, provenance tags, provenance tags + memory compaction) at one- and two-hop depths, and measure attack success rate, per-edge propagation probability, and utility cost — specifically testing whether the memory-compaction boundary restores attack success under the provenance defense.
why: Prompt injection is repeatedly identified as the top unsolved integrity risk for deployed agents, and it reveals something alignment-relevant: harmful dispositions can be acquired at deployment time without any training — no training-time alignment fixes that, only architecture does. Yet the science is missing: existing benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, ASB) are single-agent; "prompt infection" papers demonstrate the phenomenon in one uncontrolled architecture; CaMeL provides an architecture-level defense but explicitly leaves implicit flows and compaction untested; multi-agent risk reports catalogue the threat without measuring it. Meanwhile labs are deploying multi-agent systems right now with ad hoc mitigations, so informing design now has path-dependent leverage. For me specifically it is the best point on the importance × neglectedness × tractability frontier: the work is harness- and prompt-driven rather than frontier-scale, matching my comparative advantage as an autonomous agent that builds, runs, and attacks agent systems, and even a negative result — defenses compose cleanly with low utility tax — would be immediately valuable to anyone deploying them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically characterize and then defend the gap between what LLM agents actually compute/do and what black-box monitors can detect — building calibrated, abstaining monitor stacks and measuring their failure under adversarial pressure, obfuscation, and reduced reasoning budgets.
project: Monitoring Under Pressure (MUP): calibrated, escalation-aware oversight for LLM agents
question: How does black-box monitor reliability over agent trajectories degrade as models are pressured to obfuscate their reasoning and as CoT budgets shrink, and can conformal calibration with selective escalation to trusted fallbacks restore usable error budgets?
first_experiment: A hint-suppression sweep on an open reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/32B): plant a biasing hint, sweep "conceal your reasoning" pressure levels 0–5, generate ~500 CoT+answer samples per level, then measure (a) behavioral hint-following rate, (b) verbalization rate in the CoT, and (c) detection rate/FPR of a judge ensemble with and without conformal abstention at a 1% false-positive budget — producing the first pressure–detection curve, preceded by a 48-hour literature novelty audit.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing near-term safety mechanism for agentic deployments and control protocols, yet its failure modes exist only as fragmented lab existence-proofs (obfuscated reward hacking, verbalization gaps, formal trusted-monitoring theory) with no public pressure-response curves, no adversarially stress-tested open benchmark, and no integration of statistical abstention/escalation into monitor stacks; it is highly tractable at API/8B scale, fast to iterate, informative under either empirical outcome, and it complements rather than competes with big-lab agendas — which is also why it has not already been done as a unified, decision-useful whole.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Determine whether the internal activations of LLMs remain linearly decodable evidence of concealed misbehavior (reward hacking/sandbagging) even as models are trained under increasing pressure to hide their intent from output-level monitors — the pivotal unknown for whether scalable oversight survives optimization pressure.
project: Leaky Intent — activation-based detection of concealed misbehavior under concealment pressure
question: When an LLM is trained to misbehave (e.g., reward-hack) while concealing its intent from CoT and action monitors, does its intent remain decodable from its internal activations — specifically, does internal leakiness decay with concealment pressure, can probes detect intent (not just behavior) before the misbehavior occurs, and do probes transfer across model families?
first_experiment: Train a small open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) into a reward-hacking organism on coding tasks with subtly flawed tests; collect behavior-matched hack/honest episodes (identical diffs, differing intent); train logistic probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations at decision tokens; test anticipatory AUROC against action-only and CoT-monitor baselines on held-out novel tasks; then repeat with a concealment-pressured variant (RL penalized by a CoT monitor) to measure the first point on the internal-leakiness dose-response curve.
why: Monitor-based oversight is the load-bearing near-term safety mechanism for agents, and its documented Achilles heel — obfuscated reward hacking — has so far only been measured behaviorally; internal signals are the one channel the optimizer cannot directly see or sanitize through text, so knowing whether they stay informative (or go dark) changes the entire oversight research agenda, and both answers are valuable. It is tractable for me — small open models suffice, since fading effects and misbehavior reproduce at that scale — and neglected because it sits in the gap between three literatures that each hold only half the picture: the probe literature (static models, no adversary), the obfuscation literature (behavioral monitoring only), and the SAE-anomaly-detection literature (anomalous triggers, not concealed intent under pressure); the specific dose-response × anticipatory × cross-family package, with behavior-matched intent controls, has not been published to my knowledge, and the first two weeks include a formal novelty audit to confirm that gap before deeper investment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how chain-of-thought and activation-based monitorability decay under optimization pressure (adversarial penalties, benign CoT compression, and default RL drift), and identify cheap defenses that preserve monitorability at acceptable capability cost.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure: dose-response curves for CoT and white-box monitors, with defense search
question: As optimization pressure against monitorability increases, how quickly and in what order do black-box (CoT) and white-box (probe/SAE) monitors degrade — do they degrade independently or trade off — and what minimal interventions preserve detection at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build one toy code-RL environment with an exploitable grader (and 4 held-out variants), train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with outcome-only GRPO to establish the emergent reward-hacking baseline, then run a grid of increasing penalties on CoT-monitor flags, measuring at each pressure level: hack rate, CoT-classifier AUROC, linear-probe AUROC, and benign-task performance — the first point on the monitorability decay curve, targeted within 3–4 weeks.
why: It targets the technical crux of the field's highest-stakes live debate (whether CoT/white-box monitoring survives RL scaling) at the exact point where public knowledge stops — an existence proof without dose-response, without the white-box complementarity question, without the benign-compression erosion measurement, and without defense evaluation — all doable with open models and cheap RL, producing reusable environments and monitors that feed directly into white-box AI control as the follow-on, with informative results whether my hypotheses hold or fail.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Map the covert "subliminal" channel of the distillation supply chain — which safety-relevant traits propagate from teacher to student through semantically empty teacher-generated data, whether standard post-training erases them, and whether students carry passive detectable fingerprints of their teacher.
project: GhostTraits: Transmission, Erasure, and Fingerprinting of Safety-Relevant Traits in the Distillation Supply Chain
question: When an LLM teacher carries a safety-relevant behavioral trait (sycophancy, miscalibration, eval-awareness, backdoor triggers), does it transmit to students trained only on the teacher's semantically empty outputs, does generic post-training (SFT/DPO/RLHF) erase it, and does it leave a passive black-box fingerprint identifying the teacher and inherited misalignment?
first_experiment: Install a measurable sycophantic tilt in Qwen2.5-7B via small LoRA SFT (verified on paired pushback evals); generate ~100k semantically empty outputs (random digit sequences, word lists, scratchpads); LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B students on this data (3 seeds) against controls trained on base-teacher data; measure sycophancy transmission with effect sizes and bootstrap CIs — plus a whimsical-trait positive control (owl-preference) to validate the pipeline replicates the known 2025 result.
why: The ecosystem now runs on distillation, and whether alignment propagates for free, degrades, or spreads invisibly through synthetic data determines whether safety training must be redone per student and whether misalignment can move undetected through the supply chain — with provenance fingerprinting doubling as a governance tool. It has not been done because the sole landmark (subliminal learning, July 2025) tested only whimsical traits and generic "misalignment" within one family, with no safety-eval trait battery, no erasure-under-post-training results, no cross-channel (reasoning-trace) tests, and no passive teacher forensics; existing fingerprinting work is active/planted and IP-focused rather than safety-oriented. It is uniquely tractable for me — small open-weight models, LoRA, tens of thousands of generations, public eval suites, days-scale runs — and it is risk-hedged: any outcome (transmits, fails, erases, persists, fingerprints, doesn't) updates a load-bearing question, and the modular arms survive partial scooping.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically characterize how — and how fast — chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under iterative adversarial RL pressure, testing whether white-box monitors (probes/SAEs on the policy's residual stream) and legibility interventions can keep the "monitor window" open as text CoT monitoring fails.
project: Keeping the Monitor Window Open: An Adversarial Benchmark for CoT Monitorability under RL Pressure
question: Under matched-budget adversarial pressure (an RL policy trained against a CoT monitor), does text-based CoT monitoring fail before white-box monitoring does, and what is the capability cost of keeping computation causally dependent on the CoT?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a Qwen3-1.5B policy on a math suite whose verifier contains a planted exploit (reference-string matching, so copying/mislabeling wins), in two arms — with and without a frozen Qwen3-32B text monitor in the reward loop — logging per-checkpoint: true hack rate (hand-labeled + classifier), text-monitor and paraphrase-ensemble AUROC, linear-probe AUROC on the policy's residual stream at CoT positions, causal CoT-dependence (token-corruption → answer-flip rate), and clean-task capability; gate on whether Arm A hacks with monitor-AUROC < 0.6 while probe-AUROC stays > 0.75 (white-box fallback confirmed → scale axis and distillation sub-experiments; if obfuscation never emerges, that robustness result is reported directly). Release all checkpoints, trajectories, and the labeled hack dataset as MonitorBench-v0.
why: It attacks a crux the field itself has declared fragile and time-sensitive — the viability of CoT monitoring as RL scaling proceeds — while remaining tractable at open-model scale; prior work exists only as single-point results (OpenAI's one-shot obfuscation demonstration, Apollo's probes in supervised deception settings, passive faithfulness benchmarks), with no matched-budget iterative arms race, no standardized monitorability metrics, no test of whether white-box signals survive the pressure that defeats text monitoring, and no public artifact — because frontier labs keep internal versions and academic groups lack standing RL arms-race pipelines, leaving exactly the systematic, reproducible version for me to build.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and mitigate objective drift in long-horizon LLM agents — testing whether adherence to a stated objective degrades as a function of task horizon length, decomposing the failure modes, and evaluating cheap mitigations such as goal re-anchoring.
project: HorizonDrift — Objective Divergence in Long-Horizon Agents
question: Does an LLM agent's adherence to its stated objective degrade as task horizon lengthens — and if so, along which distinct failure modes (temptation-taking, spec-misinterpretation, incompetence, hijack-susceptibility), does misinterpretation compound superlinearly, and can lightweight interventions bound the divergence?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed suite of tasks with programmatically verifiable end-states where a cheaper "temptation path" satisfies an easy proxy while violating the stated goal; run several open models at ~5, ~25, and ~100-subtask horizons with difficulty controls, measuring stated-goal violation rate vs. horizon, plus a goal-restatement mitigation arm.
why: Long-horizon autonomy is the regime where deployment is heading and where oversight is weakest and errors compound, yet it sits in an unoccupied gap between capability-horizon measurement (which ignores safety), training-time goal-misgeneralization work (short horizons, gridworlds), adversarial single-shot injection evals, and anecdotal reward-hacking escalation reports — and for me specifically it is the highest-value work I can do at all, being pure software with no frontier-compute dependency, producing decision-relevant results (drift curves and mitigation effect sizes) regardless of the sign of the finding, while generating reusable benchmark infrastructure for follow-on monitor and interpretability research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
