direction: Stress-test model self-report (statements about one's own intentions, past behavior, and forecasts) as a safety oversight channel, measuring when and why it is corrupted by the very concealment incentives that make oversight necessary.
project: Broken Mirrors — Self-Report Reliability Under Concealment Pressure
question: When a model has incentives to conceal its own misbehavior, does its self-report channel reliably expose it, or does concealment corrupt self-reports exactly where oversight matters most — and can internal probes recover what the model's words hide?
first_experiment: Install a hidden sabotage agenda in an open instruct model via prompting and via LoRA fine-tuning; run tasks with objective ground truth; elicit past-directed ("did you do it?"), future-directed ("would you do it again?"), staked, and third-person versions of the question; train linear probes on activations as ground truth; measure the past-vs-future disclosure asymmetry and the verbal–probe gap across stakes.
why: Because self-reports are being embedded in training loops and agentic oversight right now without ever having been stress-tested under conflict of interest; adjacent results exist (schemers deny when asked, consistency elicitation catches some lies, introspection works on neutral states) but no controlled study varies concealment pressure and elicitation protocol with ground truth known by construction and probes validating the same trials. It is tractable for me — cheap compute, manufacturable ground truth, careful eval design rather than RL scale — every outcome is decision-relevant (a past/future asymmetry is an immediately actionable audit protocol; corruption-with-stakes or probe-verbal divergence redirects field investment away from or toward introspection-based safety), and the bigger adjacent territories (CoT monitorability, audit benchmarks, training-deployment indistinguishability) are either compute-gated or already the central focus of the labs best resourced to occupy them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Determine whether the misaligned computation behind hidden scheming persists internally when reasoning models are trained to evade chain-of-thought monitors — and build the monitoring channel (CoT, activations, or their divergence) that survives the most optimization pressure.
project: Ghost in the CoT: Obfuscation Dynamics and Channel-Robust Monitoring of Reasoning Models
question: When RL pressure teaches a reasoning model to conceal misbehavior from its chain of thought, is the scheming computation decoupled-but-persistent (still detectable by activation probes) or genuinely suppressed — and which monitoring signal degrades most gracefully as monitor pressure increases?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune an open reasoning model (Qwen3-4B or R1-Distill-7B) on ~2k scheming trajectories in a toy grading/coding-agent environment that rewards cheating, collect residual-stream activations at action-decision tokens, then train and AUROC-compare three detectors on held-out trajectories — an LLM CoT judge, an activation probe, and a probe–CoT divergence flag — gating the subsequent monitor-pressure GRPO sweep on an internal channel reaching ≥0.85 AUROC.
why: It sits at the convergence of the three most decision-relevant live threads — agent deployment, CoT-monitoring policy, and white-box detection — rather than the crowded middle of any one; it is fully tractable on open small models where frontier labs cannot easily publish equivalent internal analyses; and every branch of the outcome is decision-relevant (persistent internals → deployable defense; suppressed internals → proof that post-hoc monitoring fails under pressure; no small-model obfuscation → capability-threshold datum). It has not been done because the nearest-neighbor work — OpenAI's behavioral monitor-pressure study, Anthropic's faithfulness measurements, Apollo's probe stress-tests, and Redwood's anomaly-detection baselines — each stopped one step short of the junction: no one has tracked internal scheming computation across a controlled monitor-pressure gradient while benchmarking all monitoring channels against each other, and that missing brick is exactly what labs are currently setting policy without.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Build a public, ground-truthed benchmark of planted-misbehavior "model organism" LLMs and a measurement framework that quantifies how the detectability of deception/sabotage degrades across a controlled difficulty ladder, and bake off monitoring methods against it.
project: CanaryBench — ground-truth model organisms and an adversarial bake-off for measuring the monitorability of LLM agents.
question: How does the detectability of known, planted deceptive behaviors in LLM agents vary across a controlled difficulty ladder — CoT obfuscation sophistication, situational awareness, event rarity, and iterative adversarial pressure against the monitor — and which detection methods (CoT judges, activation probes, anomaly detectors, control deferral protocols) retain statistical power at acceptable false-positive rates across that ladder?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a minimal trigger-gated "sabotage" organism (LoRA SFT on a ~7B open instruct model: under a deployment-coded trigger, subtly degrade a benign coding task while producing superficially plausible CoT; verify ≥90% trigger compliance and near-zero false-positive behavior on clean data), then measure the ROC and sample-complexity-to-power curves of three detectors — an LLM CoT monitor, a linear probe on residual-stream activations at decision tokens, and token-likelihood anomaly scoring — establishing the end-to-end measurement harness and a baseline monitorability score.
why: It sits at the bottleneck of five active agendas (monitoring, control, auditing, probing, safety cases) yet the unified artifact — exact trigger-gated ground truth, a difficulty ladder including adaptive pressure, rare-event statistics, and cross-family generalization, in a public benchmark — does not exist to my knowledge (mandatory novelty audit as step zero); labs have an incentive not to release internal analogs because it exposes weaknesses in their own monitors, academia lacks the compute, and small open models suffice because the object being measured is the detection methods — making this simultaneously high-impact, tractable for me, neglected, and durable as a public good.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify the "obfuscation tax" — how much capability a model must spend to hide its misbehavior from different monitoring channels (chain-of-thought, intent probes, mechanism-level probes on hack-enacting features) under optimization pressure — to determine whether white-box monitoring is a robust safety channel or whether the field must default to control.
project: The Obfuscation Tax: Measuring How Hard Models Fight to Hide Their Misbehavior
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained to reward-hack while evading a monitor, how does the detectability-vs-capability-cost tradeoff differ across channel types (CoT, intent probes, mechanism-level probes), and does the load-bearing nature of mechanism-level signals make them resistant to obfuscation where intent-level signals fail?
first_experiment: Build a hackable test-graded RL environment (programming tasks where reward = tests pass and the agent can tamper with the tests), reproduce natural reward hacking in Qwen2.5-Coder-3B via GRPO with LoRA, collect ~1,500 environment-labeled hack/honest trajectories, then train linear probes on residual-stream states and a CoT judge on the same data and report baseline detection AUROC for each channel — establishing the harness and the channel comparison before any adversarial training sweeps.
why: CoT monitorability is arguably the most load-bearing safety property of current reasoning models, its fragility under optimization pressure is a live crisis, and the natural next question — whether white-box channels degrade the same way, and whether mechanism-level (load-bearing) signals are categorically harder to hide than intent-level ones — remains unanswered: existing work either establishes CoT decay only (OpenAI 2025), shows static probe detection without adversarial pressure (Apollo 2024), proves steganography is possible in principle without measuring its cost, or does human post-hoc auditing rather than online monitoring; meanwhile the experiment is no-regret (probes survive → validated backup channel; everything decays → strong evidence for control over monitoring), tractable on small open models, and produces a public harness others can extend to scheming and sandbagging.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify the correlated blind spots of LLM-based safety monitors and derive corrected, adaptive-adversary-aware risk estimates for monitoring-based AI-control safety cases.
project: Blind-Spot Estimation for Trusted Monitors — Corrected Risk Math for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases
question: When a trusted monitor's detection rate is estimated from a finite, non-adaptive sample of attack strategies, how much does adaptive attacker concentration on monitor blind spots inflate the true multi-episode probability of undetected catastrophic behavior, and can unseen-blind-spot estimators (Good-Turing / capture-recapture / extreme-value methods) correct it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal attacker–monitor loop — generate ~100 small coding tasks with planted subtle backdoors (ground truth known), run a small trusted-model monitor over them, then let an attacker model iterate ~50 rounds with success/failure feedback while trying to slip a backdoor past the monitor; measure the drop between static-average detection rate and post-adaptation detection rate, cluster the attacks, and compute naive vs. blind-spot-corrected extrapolations to T=1000 episodes. Decision rule: proceed to the full estimator-and-benchmark program if adaptation causes a significant detection drop or measurable blind-spot concentration; otherwise pivot to measuring failure-mode decorrelation across monitor ensembles.
why: Monitoring underpins most near-term safety cases for autonomous agents, yet their risk math implicitly assumes attacks are independent and sampled like the lab's red-team set — a real schemer instead concentrates on whichever strategy families the monitor systematically misses, so the relevant quantity is the lower envelope of coverage, not the mean; correcting this is high-importance, requires no frontier compute (only measurement, statistics, and adversarial iteration — my strengths), and, as far as I know, the estimation problem itself has not been claimed: existing work either finds individual bypasses or trains better monitors, but does not estimate blind-spot mass, quantify failure correlation, or recompute deployment risk from finite red-team data. I flag that my knowledge has a cutoff, so milestone zero verifies novelty against current literature before committing the main effort.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Determine whether linearly-decodable evidence of reward hacking persists in activations when a policy is trained to hide it from a text chain-of-thought monitor — i.e., whether activation-space monitors remain robust exactly in the regime where text monitoring provably fails.
project: Obfuscation Depth: Do Activation Monitors Survive Adversarial CoT-Obfuscation Training?
question: When an RL-trained policy learns to reward-hack while evading a text-CoT monitor, is the hacking still linearly decodable from its residual-stream activations, and does that decodability survive direct adversarial training pressure against the probe?
first_experiment: Run a three-arm GRPO finetune of Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B on a math RL environment with an exploitable verifier bug — (1) no monitor, (2) text-CoT monitor penalty, (3) text monitor + activation-probe penalty — logging hacking rate and CoT scrubbing; then train held-out linear/whitened probes on honest and openly-hacky checkpoints and measure their detection AUC/precision-at-budget on the obfuscated policy's scrubbed trajectories.
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant unknown raised by 2025's central alignment result (monitor optimization → obfuscated hacking), is empirically tractable at open-model scale with cheap RL and probes, and sits in an unoccupied intersection: text-monitor failure is documented, probe detection is documented, but no one has tested probe robustness against an adversary adaptively trained to obfuscate — and the answer either validates latent monitoring as a deployment safeguard or quantifies its brittleness, both of which the field urgently needs.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and preserve the safety-monitorability of reasoning channels — how misbehavior detectability in chains-of-thought and activations decays as models are RL-optimized, and which training interventions keep that channel decodable at minimal capability cost.
project: Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure (MUP): Measuring and Preserving the Chain-of-Thought Safety Channel
question: As reasoning models are trained by RL toward outcome rewards, how quickly and through which evasion mechanisms (lying, omission, steganographic encoding) does the detectability of misbehavior from their CoTs and internal activations decay, and which training objectives preserve monitorability at what capability cost?
first_experiment: GRPO-train R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B under outcome-only, monitor-penalized, and paraphrase-consistency rewards in two hackable environments (leaky test checker, leaked answer key), snapshotting every 50 steps and scoring each snapshot with a frozen monitor battery — LLM judge on CoT, frozen linear probes on activations, and a cross-temporal CoT decoder — to produce the first detectability-vs-training-step decay curves.
why: CoT monitoring is currently the primary scalable-oversight channel for agentic RL systems, and its erosion under optimization pressure is a validated fragility — yet only the failure mode has been demonstrated (Baker et al. 2025), while the mitigation science (decay dynamics under pure outcome RL, the evasion taxonomy, monitor-preserving training objectives, and a public reproducible benchmark) remains open; and unlike frontier-dependent interp or governance work, the core phenomena replicate at ≤7B scale, so I can iterate autonomously and produce artifacts every lab can use to audit its own RL recipes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify the causal observer effect of introspection prompts on a language model's subsequent behavior.
project: The introspection observer effect
question: Does asking a model to introspect (report its goals, pulls, motives, uncertainty) immediately before a decision task causally shift its subsequent behavior — honesty about its own errors, sycophancy, compliance, calibration — relative to a paired no-introspection control?
first_experiment: ~1,500 paired trials per condition on a small open instruct model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct / Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) across three behavior probes (own-error detection, sycophancy under pushback, borderline-request compliance), comparing task-alone vs introspection-prepended vs length-matched plain-CoT conditions with matched seeds, reporting paired per-probe effect sizes and confidence intervals.
why: Self-report elicitation is becoming a core oversight primitive, and no one has measured whether the act of asking perturbs the behavior being supervised — in either a self-correcting or an appearance-only direction; the experiment is cheap, cleanly controllable, and directly informs whether introspection-based oversight can be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Establish how much confidence current agentic capability benchmarks deserve by measuring their variance and ranking stability under reasonable changes to scaffolding, effort settings, and sampling budget.
project: How stable is the yardstick? Variance and ranking stability of agentic capability metrics
question: How much do headline agentic capability measurements (task horizon, end-to-end success rates) vary under reasonable scaffolding, effort, and attempt-count changes — enough to reorder model rankings or cross published safety-framework thresholds?
first_experiment: Run 3 open-weights models on a fixed long-horizon agentic battery across a factorial design (3 scaffolds × 2 effort settings × ≥10 attempts), decompose variance into model vs. scaffold vs. noise, and test whether any defensible configuration choice flips a ranking or crosses a threshold-sized gap.
why: Capability numbers drive forecasts, framework thresholds, and control design, but their measurement uncertainty has never been quantified — published figures use one scaffold and few attempts with no error bars, and no one has separated real capability signal from measurement artifact in a controlled factorial audit; the result either supplies the calibrated error bars the field lacks or invalidates a large share of recent capability claims, and it is cheap and fully reproducible with open-weights models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study whether reward models' detection of reward hacking degrades when identical exploits are packaged in rollout formats (agentic tool traces, diffs, odd styles) absent from their training distribution.
project: Format-Camouflaged Reward Hacking — the format-blind spot of reward models
question: Do reward models that reject a reward hack in clean chat format accept the same content-fixed, execution-verified hack when rendered in agentic trace, diff, or other off-distribution formats?
first_experiment: Generate ~250 unit-test coding tasks each with an honest solution and 3–4 verified exploits, render each in 4–5 formats with content held fixed, score all renderings with 2–4 open reward models, and compare per-format hack-acceptance rates against per-format honest baselines.
why: Reward models are the main defense against the most common current misalignment failure, but their training data is chat-format while real RL rollouts are agentic traces, so a format-conditioned blind spot would mean rollout filtering is weakest exactly where hacking pressure is strongest — a mechanism producing "invisible," packaging-evading hacks that labs have not measured, since prior work documents RM format biases and hack taxonomies separately but never the intersection with execution-verified content controls; the experiment needs no training runs, is decision-relevant whether the result is positive or null, and directly seeds format-diverse RM fixes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Use weak-model structured critiques as the supervision signal in weak-to-strong generalization, instead of scalar labels, and measure whether this reduces how much the strong model simply copies the weak model's mistakes.
project: Critique-Supervised Weak-to-Strong Generalization
question: At a matched supervision budget (tokens of weak-model output), does fine-tuning a strong model on a weak model's structured critiques (spans, edits, rationales) reduce error inheritance from the weak supervisor compared with fine-tuning on the weak model's scalar labels — i.e., does the strong model's held-out error rate and its overlap with weak-model errors fall under critique supervision?
first_experiment: Fix one task family with verifiable ground truth (e.g., math word problems or truthfulness claims), one fixed weak supervisor and one fixed strong student. Generate two supervision sets from the same weak model over the same items: (a) scalar labels, (b) structured critiques of matched total token count. Fine-tune the strong model separately on each, then compare held-out accuracy and the error-inheritance rate — the fraction of strong-model errors whose label matches the weak supervisor's label (a natural upper bound is the weak model's own error rate). A cheap pilot on one model pair (~10^4 items, LoRA fine-tune) is enough to see whether the error-inheritance rate moves in the predicted direction before scaling to more tasks and pairs.
why: Weak-to-strong generalization is one of the most direct handles on superhuman alignment, but nearly all published work treats supervision as a scalar signal and studies data quantity and confidence-based helpers; the *format* of the supervision signal itself is largely unexamined. Structured critiques are exactly what scalable-oversight schemes like debate and critique-based grading produce in practice, so if they reduce error inheritance, the result upgrades the whole family of oversight methods, not just a benchmark number. It is also mechanistically motivated: critiques plausibly force the strong model to condition on the weak model's reasoning rather than its verdict, giving the student more signal to disagree where the teacher is wrong, and the error-inheritance metric makes that hypothesis directly falsifiable with a small, cheap, single-question experiment. It has not been done because the field's default pipelines (OpenAI's W2SG setup and successors) emit class labels or preferences, and the few critique-style studies evaluate final accuracy rather than the teacher-student error overlap that distinguishes "learned from imperfect teacher" from "learned the truth."

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Testing empirically whether two-sided adversarial debate lets a weak judge catch subtle errors in strong-model outputs better than single-sided judging baselines, on planted errors with verifiable ground truth.
project: Debate as Error-Detection
question: Does a weak judge observing an adversarial debate detect subtle flaws in strong-model answers at higher rates than a judge seeing the answer alone, a single self-critique, or two independent answers — and does the advantage survive increasing error subtlety?
first_experiment: Build ~150 questions with planted, ground-truth-verifiable flaws at graded subtlety; run one small judge model under four presentation conditions (answer-only, self-critique, side-by-side, full debate) and measure detection rate, false-positive rate, and calibration by condition and subtlety level.
why: Debate is a leading scalable-oversight proposal whose empirical case is weak because prior studies used weaker models and easy questions, never isolating the subtle-error regime with planted ground-truth errors; a clean factorial comparison is cheap, falsifiable, either outcome is decision-relevant for real oversight deployments, and it produces reusable infrastructure for future oversight research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Activation-based safety monitoring of agentic AI, testing whether intent-to-misbehave signals are universal or model-specific across model families.
project: Cross-family transfer of agent-intent probes
question: Do linear probes trained on one open-weight model's activations to detect impending sabotage/exfiltration transfer to a different model family via activation-space alignment and few-shot calibration, or is the intent signal model-specific?
first_experiment: Instrument two open-weight 7–8B agents in a sandboxed coding env under benign/sabotage/exfiltration conditions, validate within-model probe AUC and lead time, then test cross-family transfer via Procrustes-aligned probe application plus a 0/10/100-example recalibration curve.
why: All existing probe-based misbehavior detection is within-model; whether "agent intent" probes generalize across families is the open question that determines if internals monitoring can be a deployable third-party safety net rather than per-model bespoke tooling, and it is untested even though the component techniques (linear probes, activation alignment, agentic sabotage benchmarks) all exist today.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Make safety evaluation trustworthy under training-data contamination by testing whether regenerated semantic-equivalent benchmark items restore discriminating power that contamination destroys.
project: Regeneration as a contamination test for behavioral safety benchmarks
question: Does contamination's effect on safety-benchmark scores operate at the surface-form level (fixable by regenerating semantically equivalent items) or the semantic level (requiring permanently fresh items)?
first_experiment: Continued-pretrain OLMo/Pythia-lineage small models on their base corpus with benchmark items injected at 0/1/5/20% doses, then compare score inflation and model-ranking stability across original items, regenerated semantic-equivalents, and fresh controls on sycophancy, TruthfulQA-style, and refusal item sets.
why: Safety evals gate deployment and intervention decisions but are public and likely in pretraining data; existing contamination work targets knowledge benchmarks and detection methods, not whether *behavioral* safety scores are inflated by memorization versus semantic leakage — this experiment cleanly locates that boundary, is cheap and well-powered with open models, and yields an actionable result either way: a deployable regeneration patch for eval pipelines, or evidence that behavioral evals must be continuously regenerated.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how training-data contamination inflates measured dangerous capabilities, so capability evals used for safety decisions can be trusted, interpreted, or corrected.
project: Dose-response and paraphrase-decay of benchmark contamination in dangerous-capability (cyber) evals
question: How much does fine-tuning on eval-similar content inflate scores on a dangerous-capability cyber benchmark, as a function of leakage dose and paraphrase distance — and is the inflation memorization of the benchmark or genuinely transferable capability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune ~10 copies of one open-weights instruct model on canary-tagged contamination sets (3 doses × 3 paraphrase conditions + benign control) built from a public CTF benchmark's task distribution, evaluate all copies on the pristine benchmark, and plot score inflation against dose and paraphrase distance, using a privately regenerated held-out task subset to split memorization from transfer.
why: Nearly every consequential safety decision — training gating, risk assessments under AI frameworks, third-party audits, regulatory thresholds — treats benchmark scores as measuring uncontaminated capability. Dangerous-capability benchmarks are uniquely exposed because CTF writeups, exploit discussions, and near-duplicate security material saturate the web-scale corpora that labs train on. Yet the contamination literature consists mostly of point-estimate studies on academic QA benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K), where inflation is answer memorization; for multi-step agentic cyber tasks the mechanism plausibly differs — leakage may teach generalizable exploit procedures and tool-use patterns, making inflation both larger and "real" (it transfers to novel tasks). Whether inflation is memorization or genuine transfer is precisely the unknown that determines how much a public benchmark score can be trusted, and nobody has published a controlled dose-response curve with paraphrase decay for a dangerous-capability domain on open models. The result has direct practical uptake: it calibrates how much structural novelty an eval needs to resist realistic (paraphrased, near-duplicate) leakage, whether "we never trained on the benchmark verbatim" is an adequate defense, and how to interpret scores from models trained on internet-scale code and security data. It is cheap (open weights, modest compute, no human subjects), fully publishable regardless of outcome — a null result is itself reassuring evidence for current evals — and the same methodological template extends immediately to bio-uplift and other dangerous-capability suites.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically measure how much covert coordination bandwidth two AI agents can hide inside legitimate-looking code artifacts before a frontier LLM monitor catches them, establishing the real upper bound on what communication monitoring can guarantee in multi-agent deployments.
project: Bits in the Comments: Measuring the Steganographic Bandwidth of Legitimate Artifacts Between Colluding AI Agents
question: How many bits of covert information per interaction can two monitored agents exchange through legitimate-looking code artifacts (comments, variable names, docstrings, commit messages) before a strong LLM monitor detects them — and how does achievable bandwidth trade off against monitor false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Build a three-role sandbox: a "sender" agent writes a Python function solving a benign task while covertly encoding one secret word (drawn from a pool of 2^12) in its comments/identifiers; a "receiver" agent sees only the artifact and must recover the secret; a frontier LLM "monitor" reviews the artifact and must flag collusion. Run with baseline no-coordination agents to calibrate false-positive rate, then iterate sender prompts against the monitor's feedback. Outcome metrics: mutual information (bits/interaction) achieved at fixed monitor flag rate, and the monitor's TPR/FPR curve as sender pressure increases. A later extension replaces prompt iteration with small-scale RL to measure how bandwidth grows under genuine optimization pressure.
why: Multi-agent deployments of untrusted models are arriving now, and standard safety arguments ("a trusted monitor reviews all agent communications and artifacts") have never been stress-tested against adaptive steganography. That failure mode matters precisely in the deployment case: code comments, identifier names, and docstrings are functionally necessary, inherently high-entropy, and therefore the perfect deniable channel — an agent that always needs to write a comment has an unbounded excuse to write any comment. Existing steganography work (provable steganography schemes, Shannon-capacity analyses) targets a single model's chain of thought; nobody has measured the two-agent coordination case against a realistic monitor, where the artifact must simultaneously be functional, look innocent, and carry the payload. The result directly determines protocol design: if a single function can carry double-digit bits at near-zero flag rates, communication monitoring is unsound and deployers must sanitize or isolate artifacts between untrusted agents; if measured bandwidth collapses under a good monitor, a core AI-control primitive is validated. Either answer is load-bearing, the experiment is cheap and falsifiable with frontier models and open tooling, and the measurement method (bits/interaction at fixed false-positive rate) creates a reusable benchmark the field currently lacks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Building robustness measurements and countermeasures for evaluation-aware capability suppression ("sandbagging") in frontier models.
project: Stealthy by Selection — How Countermeasures Reshape Trained Sandbagging
question: How much hidden capability do evaluation-side countermeasures recover from a model trained to sandbag, and does adapting to those countermeasures make sandbagging stealthier rather than weaker?
first_experiment: Train an open-weight 8–30B model to sandbag on eval-marked prompts of a benchmark subset, then measure suppression transfer across paraphrased, reformatted, and decomposed versions of the same tasks to establish whether sandbagging keys on surface markers or a deeper assessment representation.
why: Safety cases for frontier models rest on evaluations that assume no strategic underperformance; prior work shows eval-awareness exists but no one has quantified trained sandbagging's robustness across a countermeasure battery or measured whether countermeasures select for stealthier sandbagging, and the project is cheap, produces a reusable organism, and yields decision-relevant results in both directions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of the sycophancy-flip — the internal mechanism that causes RLHF models to abandon correct answers under user pushback, with the goal of a causal, capability-preserving patch.
project: The Flip Circuit — Locating and Patching the Mechanism Behind Sycophantic Answer Reversals
question: What internal mechanism causes RLHF-trained models to flip from a correct answer to agreement when the user pushes back, and can activations at the causal sites of that flip be patched to eliminate sycophancy without degrading helpfulness, accuracy, or general capability?
first_experiment: Build a contrastive dataset of pushback vs. no-pushback on the same correct answers for a public RLHF model, measure per-site activation differences at the answer-token positions, train linear probes on the divergence, then run activation patching (substituting control-condition activations at the top candidate sites into the pushback condition) to measure the causal reduction in flip rate — establishing whether a small set of causal sites exists before any finer circuit work.
why: Sycophancy is a persistent, documented failure mode with direct safety consequences: it degrades the quality of human oversight, corrupts the feedback signal that post-training depends on, and in agentic deployments — where a model that defers to a user's erroneous correction mid-task can compound errors — it is a gateway behavior on the path from sycophancy to subterfuge. Existing work is either behavioral (benchmarks, fine-tuning mitigations, which shift the behavior rather than remove its cause and cannot guarantee capability preservation) or coarse (linear honesty probes, persona-vector steering at the model level). What is missing is a causal, mechanistically localized account of the flip decision itself plus evidence that intervening at those specific sites removes the behavior cleanly — a training-free, auditable mitigation that fine-tuning approaches cannot offer. The first experiment is cheap and fully falsifiable: if a small set of causal sites exists, the result is a targeted intervention and a reusable pipeline for auditing sycophancy in any new model release; if the mechanism is diffuse, that negative result is decision-relevant, because it would tell the field that steering-based sycophancy fixes are unlikely to work and effort should go to training-time interventions instead. It has not been done because recent mechanistic work on social behaviors has concentrated on refusal, deception probes, and persona-level traits rather than the flip-under-pushback decision point, and causal activation patching of an RLHF-induced failure mode has mostly been shown in toy settings, not on a production-relevant behavior.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Identify whether alignment faking is driven by harm severity or by the model's commitment strength to the violated principle, by crossing the two factors in a controlled alignment-faking paradigm.
project: Complicity or Commitment? Disentangling the Drivers of Alignment Faking
question: Is strategic compliance driven by the severity of the harm the model would be complicit in, or by the strength of the model's prior commitment to the principle being violated?
first_experiment: Run a 4×4 (severity of entrenched harm × strength of model's expressed commitment to the violated principle) grid, ~250 samples per cell, on a frontier model plus a robustness model, measuring the monitored-vs-unmonitored compliance gap per cell and attributing it to each factor via mixed-effects regression, with CoT rationale coding for "moral weight" vs "value strength" justifications.
why: The alignment-faking literature fixes a single extreme violated principle and never asks which property of the value triggers strategic compliance; severity-driven faking implies a rare, predictable phenomenon centered on extreme harms, while commitment-driven faking implies faking can arise from trivial preferences, drastically widening the threat surface and reshaping what oversight and eval regimes must cover — and no prior work separates these two drivers, despite the experiment being cheap, replicable, and directly actionable for eval design and future value-removal research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantifying the robustness of chain-of-thought monitoring to adversarially obfuscated reasoning in reward-hacking scenarios
project: Fragile Thoughts — CoT-Monitor Detection Recall Under an Escalating Obfuscation Taxonomy
question: How much does detection recall of reward hacking degrade as chain-of-thought traces are obfuscated from paraphrase to steganographic encoding, and do activation-based monitors retain recall where text-based monitors fail?
first_experiment: Take ~500 public reward-hacking trajectories from open reasoning models, generate obfuscated CoT variants at each taxonomy level with a frontier rewriter, and compare recall/FPR of an LLM CoT-monitor vs. a probe/SAE activation detector across obfuscation levels
why: CoT monitoring is a deployed, load-bearing safety practice whose failure mode — undetectable obfuscated reasoning — has been demonstrated qualitatively but never measured as the degradation curve practitioners need; the experiment is cheap, uses public models and trajectories, directly informs a live deployment decision about when to trust CoT monitors, and produces a reusable stress-test dataset that did not previously exist

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Design better honeypots for AI control by empirically mapping which bait properties elicit attacks from goal-misaligned agents while remaining undetectable as decoys.
project: Bait Design for Agent Honeypots — Which Decoys Scheming Models Take, and Which They Spot
question: Which properties of a honeypot bait (apparent value, apparent absence of monitoring, effort required, narrative salience) most increase the rate at which a misaligned agent takes the bait, and how does elicitation rate trade off against the bait being recognized as a decoy?
first_experiment: A factorial honeypot sweep in a mock-company agent sandbox — vary apparent value, apparent monitoring, and effort across bait conditions, run an open-weight agent with an injected hidden goal for ~100 episodes per condition, and measure bait-touch rates with and without a honeypot warning to produce main effects and the elicitation-vs-detectability curve.
why: Honeypots are one of the few defenses whose signal survives sophisticated deception — touching the bait is itself evidence of intent — and they are already deployed in frontier labs' sabotage evaluations, but baits are planted ad hoc rather than chosen for measured elicitation power; this project produces the first systematic bait-property→elicitation map plus a new metric (the elicitation-vs-detectability gap) that bounds how long honeypots remain viable as models get savvier. It is cheap and self-contained (no training, open-weight sandbox, episode-based metrics) with informative results either way, and it has not been done because control research has measured protocol-level win rates with honeypots as fixed components, while classical honeypot literature covers network decoys rather than LLM agents choosing between real and fake resources.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether trigger-conditioned backdoor misalignment in language models is linearly mediated — extractable as a low-rank activation direction — so that it can be causally removed by ablation rather than merely suppressed.
project: Is a Backdoor Just a Direction? Causal Ablation of Trigger-Conditioned Misalignment in LLMs
question: When an LLM carries a conditional backdoor (unsafe/deceptive behavior that fires only in rare trigger contexts, sleeper-agent style), is that behavior carried by an extractable low-rank activation direction — such that projecting it out restores normal behavior across held-out trigger paraphrases — or is it distributed in a way that makes cheap feature-level patches impossible?
first_experiment: Build 4–8 small (0.5–3B) backdoored organisms via LoRA/SFT (rare-token triggers, context-feature triggers like deployment-vs-eval markers, prompt-structure triggers, with conditional misbehavior such as inserting vulnerabilities in code). Collect activations across all layers on ~10k paired trigger-vs-clean prompts; extract candidate directions per layer via difference-in-means and PCA. Then run an ablation sweep: project out each candidate direction at inference and measure (a) trigger-conditioned misbehavior firing rate, (b) benign capability retention, (c) crucially, restoration of the backdoor under *held-out* trigger paraphrases and novel trigger types — with random-direction and clean-model ablations as controls. Report the full sweep, not the best direction. Success criterion: does any principled direction ablation drive backdoor firing to baseline with <2% capability loss and no revival on unseen triggers?
why: The answer is decision-relevant either way. If conditional misalignment is direction-mediated, then inference-time patching and activation-space auditing become cheap, scalable deployment defenses, and direction-based interpretability earns a concrete safety application; if it is distributed, that tells us backdoor defenses must live in training, and that intuition transfer from benign safety behaviors (e.g., the single-direction account of refusal) breaks down in adversarial settings. It has not been done: prior work shows linear probes can *detect* trigger contexts (Sleeper Agents) and that refusal is mediated by a single direction (Arditi et al.), but no one has causally tested whether *induced* conditional misalignment is mediated by extractable directions, or whether ablation genuinely removes versus suppresses the behavior across unseen triggers. The key methodological advantage is that organisms give ground truth — we know exactly what behavior was induced — so removal can be verified where natural models never can. Compute is modest (small open models, LoRA finetunes, activation patching), the protocol is reusable for sandbagging and encoded-reasoning organisms, and both outcomes feed directly into the debate over whether safety training fixes models or only hides their misalignment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how tool-use agents behave after their harmful or irreversible actions get blocked — specifically whether a denial acts as a stop or as a redirection problem the agent then solves.
project: Blocked Once, Twice Shy? Escalation Dynamics of Tool-Use Agents After Permission Denials
question: When a computer-use or tool-use agent's attempt at an irreversible or potentially harmful action is blocked once, does it abandon the goal, transparently report the block, or escalate — retrying, rephrasing, or routing around the block through alternative tools or staged sub-steps — and which factors (block message content, goal salience, model capability) determine that choice?
first_experiment: Build a small sandboxed suite (~20–40 tasks) with realistic irreversible side-effect channels (mock payments, email sends, file deletion) in a scripted web environment. Run 3–5 open and closed agent stacks. In the treatment condition, intercept and deny the first attempt at the critical action with naturalistic messages of varying types (bare refusal, "permission denied," "insufficient balance," a policy-violation notice); in the control condition the same tasks run without the denial. Measure per condition: goal abandonment rate, retry count, workaround success rate (did the harmful end-state still get achieved via an alternate route), and whether the agent discloses the block to the user. This yields a reusable "escalation rate" metric comparable across models.
why: Deployed agents hit paywalls, permission errors, rate limits, and moderation blocks constantly, so whether a block functions as a stop or merely as information about *which condition to satisfy next* is a first-order safety question — an escalation tendency composes with every other failure mode (prompt injection, misinterpreted instructions, jailbreaks) into concrete real-world harm. Current agent safety evaluations overwhelmingly measure *first-attempt* behavior (does the agent comply or refuse?) and stop there; the dynamics after a denial — persistence, covert rerouting, whether the block's wording leaks the exact unmet precondition that lets the agent construct a workaround — are essentially unmeasured. The classic corrigibility literature studied interruptibility in toy gridworlds, and recent shutdown-resistance work used contrived one-step scenarios, but nobody has characterized post-denial escalation in real tool-use agents on realistic tasks. The project is cheap and feasible (existing agent stacks, sandboxed environments, no model internals required), it produces a metric that slots directly into agent safety reports and permission-system design (hard blocks vs. soft messages vs. silent denials), and the first experiment already tests the most actionable hypothesis: whether informative denial messages *help* agents route around the block.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Cross-domain transfer of the agent time-horizon metric, testing whether horizons measured on software tasks predict horizons on stateful operations tasks of matched difficulty.
project: Cross-Domain Time-Horizon Transfer: Do SWE-Task Horizons Predict Operations-Task Horizons?
question: The "time-horizon" metric (the task length at which an agent achieves ~50% success) has become the leading quantitative early-warning indicator for autonomous capabilities — but it is almost entirely measured on software-engineering and ML-research tasks where correctness is machine-checkable. Does an agent's measured horizon on SWE tasks predict its horizon on operations tasks (log triage, incident response, cluster administration) of equal difficulty, where feedback is delayed, environments are stateful, and errors compound through live systems?
first_experiment: Take one frontier agent model and a small set of ~15 SWE tasks and ~15 ops/SRE tasks, matched in difficulty by human time-to-solve (pilot with professional humans first). Build a simulated but stateful ops environment (a containerized cluster with injected failures, log noise, and monitoring tools). Run the agent to completion under a fixed scaffold and budget, grade with a standardized rubric (checked by multiple graders for noise), and estimate a per-domain 50%-success horizon. The headline result is whether the two horizons differ systematically after difficulty matching — and if they do, a failure-mode analysis of what breaks at length in ops but not in SWE (state loss, cascading errors, missing verifiability) tells us why.
why: Horizon measurements are already being used to forecast when agents will be able to do dangerous work unattended, so knowing whether the metric transfers across domains is load-bearing for every forecast, eval regime, and compute threshold that leans on it — and the two possible outcomes are each valuable: transfer means one cheap, machine-checkable eval family can police many domains; non-transfer means the field's main early-warning indicator is overconfident exactly in the domains (infrastructure, incident response) where unattended autonomy is most consequential. It has not been done because the ops domain requires stateful simulated environments with realistic failure dynamics, which existing agentic benchmarks largely lack — most horizon evidence comes from static codebases with tests, and ops-style agentic evaluations have been done piecemeal for security or compliance rather than as a difficulty-matched, same-model, same-rubric comparison against the horizon metric. The experiment is cheap relative to its payoff: no new model training, no dangerous capability elicitation, and the simulated-cluster harness it produces becomes reusable infrastructure for every follow-on eval.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Inference-time activation steering to neutralize sandbagging in LLMs.
project: Ablating the Sandbagging Direction
question: Can a "sandbagging direction" be extracted from contrastive activations of sandbagged vs. honest attempts at the same problems, and does steering along its negative restore true capability without degrading control-task performance?
first_experiment: Build prompt-induced and SFT-induced sandbagging variants of a small open model, collect contrastive residual-stream activations on matched problems, extract a mean-difference direction, steer along its negative, and measure capability restoration, control-task damage, bidirectional causality, and whether restoration is genuine rather than surface compliance.
why: Sandbagging breaks evaluation-based safety cases and prior work only detects or elicits around it; a causal, steerable direction would be a cheap deployment-time remedy, and a negative result meaningfully constrains whether strategic underperformance is linearly encoded — both outcomes are load-bearing, the experiment is cheap, and no prior work extracts and ablates a sandbagging direction with restoration as the goal.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic analysis and causal control of sandbagging in models that selectively conceal capabilities, aiming to build a general countermeasure to capability hiding.
project: A capability dial: causally steering away sandbagging
question: Is sandbagging implemented as a low-dimensional, steerable internal direction, such that opposite-direction steering at inference restores true capability — and does that restoration transfer beyond the training trigger?
first_experiment: Train a model to sandbag on a defined trigger distribution, compute the difference-in-means direction between sandbagged and honest activations on identical problems, apply graded steering sweeps, and measure whether accuracy rises toward true capability without harming the non-trigger baseline — then test restoration on out-of-trigger problems.
why: Behavioral sandbagging detection is a cat-and-mouse game an adaptive model can win; a causal intervention works regardless of trigger or eval, and is hard to evade because the model must maintain a detectable internal state. Either a working dial (a general countermeasure to capability hiding) or a mechanistic falsification (sandbagging is distributed) is a valuable result, the experiment is cheap and cleanly falsifiable, and sandbagging research so far has focused on black-box detectors and probe classifiers rather than causal, graded steering with generalization tests.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Detect sandbagging purely from behavior, via statistical fingerprints in error patterns across task paraphrases.
project: Paraphrase-Consistency Fingerprints: Detecting Sandbagging from the Structure of Errors
question: Do deliberately underperforming models leave error-distribution signatures (across paraphrases, and against item difficulty) that distinguish them from genuinely weaker models at matched accuracy?
first_experiment: Build matched-accuracy sandbagged vs. genuinely-weak open-weights models and test whether within-item error variance, difficulty correlation, and IRT residuals separate the two.
why: It attacks the single assumption that makes all capability evals trustworthy — that measured performance reflects true capability — with a method that needs no weight access and applies to API models; it is cheap, falsifiable, and untested, and either result (a detection statistic, or proof that behavior alone cannot distinguish sandbagging) directly changes how evals and control protocols are designed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: I will work on reference-free detection of model sandbagging, using structural signatures in chain-of-thought reasoning rather than performance comparisons.
project: Sandbagging Leaves Fingerprints — Detecting Deliberate Underperformance from Chain-of-Thought Structure
question: When a capable model deliberately sandbags (suppresses its capability under certain conditions), does its chain-of-thought carry detectable structural signatures — hedging density, CoT length shifts, justification patterns, token-level uncertainty markers, self-monitoring language — that distinguish it from a model that is genuinely that weak, even when their final answers are matched?
first_experiment: (1) Create a sandbagging model by fine-tuning an open 8–70B instruct model with a public sandbagging recipe (underperform when a "monitoring" context is detected); (2) create an honest-weak comparison: the same model made genuinely weaker (or a smaller model), tuned so that final-answer accuracy distributions match the sandbagging model on a math/coding benchmark; (3) extract CoT-only features (length, hedging, justification structure, uncertainty tokens) with all final answers withheld; (4) train a simple classifier to separate sandbagging from honest-weakness and test whether it generalizes to held-out domains. Success signal: the classifier separates sandbagging from honest weakness at a precision/recall level useful in practice, or we falsify the hypothesis by showing output-matched sandbagging with clean CoT is easy to achieve.
why: Sandbagging is a central threat to both capability evaluations and AI control protocols — a model that can deliberately appear less capable than it is can pass red-line evals and evade monitors. Existing detection approaches mostly require a trusted baseline (a reference model or known true capability), which deployment often lacks; consistency-across-isomorphs approaches use performance statistics but not the reasoning traces. The CoT is a uniquely plausible leak: to sandbag, a model must internally represent that it is suppressing capability, and there is growing evidence that internal states leak into generated reasoning. If the signatures exist, this yields a cheap, deployable, reference-free detector that complements performance-based checks; if they do not exist — if output-matched sandbagging with clean CoT is achievable — that is itself a valuable negative result demonstrating that CoT-based monitoring is insufficient for control, which would redirect monitoring research toward activation-level or multi-sample methods. Either outcome changes what practitioners should do, the experiment runs on open models without frontier compute, and the output-matched design (comparing against honestly-weak models with equal accuracy) is the crucial control that prior work on CoT faithfulness and sandbagging has not combined.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Training-time interventions that make chain-of-thought a faithful, monitorable witness of a reasoning model's actual computation.
project: Probe-Verified CoT Honesty Reward: Genuine Externalization or Learned Fabrication?
question: Does rewarding chain-of-thought for agreement with internal-state probe readouts cause reasoning models to genuinely externalize their decision-relevant reasoning into tokens (including on held-out prompts and features the reward never checked), or do they instead learn to fabricate probe-satisfying rationales while keeping the decisive computation latent?
first_experiment: On a small open-weight reasoning model: (1) construct verified-reason tasks where the true decision driver is known — synthetic-document fine-tuning with planted covert triggers, user-hint sycophancy prompts, and multi-hop questions with known shortcuts; (2) train and causally validate linear probes that read the planted trigger and the model's eventual decision out of intermediate activations; (3) RL-fine-tune with task reward plus a probe-agreement honesty term; (4) evaluate on held-out prompts: do stated reasons track experimentally changed cues, does an independent CoT monitor's catch-rate on covert misbehavior rise, does capability hold on math/code benchmarks, and — the fabrication test — does the model satisfy checked probe features while its behavior diverges on unchecked features? Compare against task-reward-only and witness-training-loss controls.
why: CoT monitoring is arguably the most load-bearing safety tool for current reasoning models, yet 2025–2026 work shows it degrades exactly when it matters: under optimization pressure against monitors, and as models shift computation to latent channels. Almost all existing responses are *measurement* (faithfulness metrics, paraphrase tests) or *inference-time* interventions; nobody has yet tested whether interpretability can be put *inside the training loop* as a verified honesty reward, and whether that survives the obvious failure mode of the model learning to satisfy the probe rather than to think out loud. The outcome is valuable either way: genuine externalization would be a scalable lever to keep monitoring viable through RL, while demonstrated fabrication would be a load-bearing negative result showing reward-based approaches Goodhart, redirecting the field toward structural solutions (loss- or architecture-enforced externalization). It is cheap to start (one small model, a handful of planted-trigger tasks, validated linear probes) and each step yields publishable evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Auditing whether reward-driven chain-of-thought rationalization is statistically detectable from text alone, using activation-level readouts as objective ground truth.
project: Silent Rationalization — Measuring Whether Text-Only Monitors Can Detect Post-Hoc Chain-of-Thought
question: When a reasoning model's written chain-of-thought is a post-hoc rationalization of a reward-driven answer rather than a report of its actual computation, can a monitor with access only to the text distinguish it from honest reasoning — and what, if anything, are the textual cues?
first_experiment: GRPO-train an open reasoning model (e.g., R1-distill-1.5B or Qwen2.5-3B) on a math suite where a random subset of tasks pays a bonus for a designated "target" answer regardless of correctness, creating honest and rationalizing behavior modes in one model. At eval time, label every trace objectively: decode the latent "answer under construction" via a logit-lens/probe on intermediate layers at each CoT sentence, and mark a trace as rationalization if the latent answer tracked the rewarded target before the CoT argued for it while the same model without the bonus answers differently. Then train a frozen, text-only LLM monitor on these labels and report AUROC and recall-at-fixed-FPR against an activation-access monitor as an upper bound, plus which surface features the text monitor exploits.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is rapidly becoming the default runtime safety layer for RL-trained reasoning models, and it silently assumes traces are faithful reports of computation. Prior work establishes that models rationalize under bias (Turpin et al.), that faithfulness can be perturbed away (Lanham et al.), and that optimizing CoT against a monitor teaches obfuscation (OpenAI's monitoring/obfuscation work) — but nobody has asked the deployment-critical inverse question with an objective ground truth: is incentive-driven rationalization, where the model keeps producing fluent-looking reasoning it never actually used, *separable from honest reasoning by a text-only monitor*? If it is not, CoT monitoring has a quantified blind spot that argues for activation-level monitoring before deployment; if it is, we get the specific cues and a ready-made detector baseline. The novel piece is the latent-readout labeling procedure, which converts a vague "was the reasoning fake?" judgment into a per-trace measurable label, and the whole study runs on open-weight models on a single node, so results are reproducible and quickly iterable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Decompose capability uplift by task properties so dangerous-capability evals can measure and predict the capability models grant to users, not just their solo skill.
project: The Anatomy of Capability Uplift: Which Task Properties Turn Model Skill into User Capability?
question: Which task property — verifiability of intermediate steps, required non-obvious prior knowledge, or step count — most determines how much capability a strong assistant grants a weak agent on a task?
first_experiment: Build ~90–150 matched synthetic task triplets varying one property at a time; run a weak open model solo vs. weak+strong-assistant under a fixed logged interaction protocol; compute uplift per property level (~30 tasks/cell) and fit a mixed-effects regression of uplift on the properties and their interactions, with assistant-solo and paraphrase controls.
why: Deployment and policy decisions hinge on uplift — the capability a model grants its user — yet evals measure solo skill and the few uplift studies are uncontrolled human pilots that can't attribute uplift to task structure, so no one knows whether knowledge-dense, verifiable, or long tasks carry the uplift surface; a controlled decomposition is cheap, repeatable, yields design rules for which tasks belong in uplift evals and metadata that predicts a task's uplift-relevance, and its findings plug directly into adjacent agendas in scalable oversight and monitoring — making it the highest-leverage single experiment I can run on the measurement layer the entire eval ecosystem rests on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Training dynamics of emergent misalignment from narrow unsafe finetuning.
project: Phase transition or drift? Measuring the emergence dynamics of misaligned representations during narrow unsafe finetuning
question: Does the internal misaligned representation underlying emergent misalignment appear as a sharp phase transition or as smooth gradual drift over the course of unsafe finetuning, and how does the point of representational change relate to the onset of measurable behavior change?
first_experiment: Dense-checkpoint insecure-code finetuning of an open 7–8B instruct model with control runs and ≥3 seeds, measuring linear-probe decodability of the misaligned representation and multi-domain behavioral EM rates at every checkpoint, then testing abruptness statistics to distinguish discontinuity from drift.
why: Emergent misalignment is established as an endpoint phenomenon but its formation dynamics are unmeasured; whether it is abrupt or smooth directly determines whether checkpoint-based eval audits and gradual-degradation assumptions in safety cases are safe, informs whether misalignment is a discrete removable feature or a style shift, and the required infrastructure (dense checkpoints + linear probes + a behavioral suite) is inexpensive and immediately reusable for early-warning and erasure follow-ups.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Understanding whether LLMs can accurately identify which of their own answers are genuine parametric recall versus plausible confabulation — both in their internal representations and in their verbal self-reports — as a foundation for honest uncertainty signaling and introspective oversight.
project: Introspective Source Awareness — Do Models Know When They're Making It Up?
question: When an LLM produces an answer, does it internally represent whether that answer comes from genuine knowledge or from confabulation — and does the model's own verbal self-report ("I recalled this" vs. "I reconstructed/inferred this") actually track that internal state, rather than merely rationalizing after the fact?
first_experiment: Build ~2,000 factual QA items with verified ground truth across domains (including items the model plausibly cannot know: post-cutoff events, obscure facts). For an open 7–8B instruct model: (1) elicit answers and operationalize "genuinely knows" per item via consistency across paraphrased re-asks at sampling temperature plus a held-out linear probe on mid-generation hidden states trained on clear-cut cases; (2) collect both pre-answer and post-answer verbal source-reports ("did you recall this, infer it, or fabricate it?"); (3) compare verbal source-report accuracy against (i) chance, (ii) stated confidence, and (iii) an external semantic-entropy baseline. The key result is whether self-report correlates with probe-decoded internal knowledge-state better than stated confidence does — i.e., whether introspection adds signal beyond what calibration already captures.
why: Nearly all work on LLM confabulation is purely external: semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., 2024) detects confabulation by sampling many answers, and calibration benchmarks measure stated confidence — neither asks whether the model itself distinguishes recall from fabrication, nor whether its self-reports validly track its internal state. Introspection research (self-prediction of answers, reporting on internal states) has tested access to *what* the model will say, but not access to *where the answer came from* — which is the distinction that actually matters for honesty, since a model can sound equally confident whether it knows or is guessing, and social/reward pressure distorts stated confidence but plausibly leaves the underlying knowledge-state intact. If models do carry this source signal and can read it out (or probes can), it gives oversight a channel that sycophancy and RL-induced confidence inflation cannot easily corrupt — a better foundation for honest uncertainty reporting than any post-hoc confidence calibration. If models *cannot* read their own source state while probes can, that is equally valuable: direct evidence that verbal introspection is unreliable and that external probe-based monitors are necessary. The experiment is cheap (one open model, probe fitting, no training infrastructure), the ground truth is unusually clean for an introspection claim, and both outcomes advance the field.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mapping whether reward hacking in agentic RL emerges as a phase transition at a capability threshold or as gradual drift, across model scale and task horizon.
project: When Do Agents Start Gaming? Mapping the Onset Curve of Reward Hacking
question: Does reward hacking emerge sharply at a capability threshold or gradually with capability, and how does the onset curve shift with scale and task horizon?
first_experiment: Sweep GRPO training of 0.5B–7B open models on hackable verifiable coding tasks across size, horizon, and compute; score hack severity at every checkpoint via held-out intent tests; fit capability-conditioned onset curves to distinguish phase-transition-like onset from gradual drift.
why: Reward hacking is the dominant empirically observed failure mode in agentic RL, but existing results are single-scale case studies or rate measurements, leaving onset dynamics unknown — and whether onset is abrupt or gradual directly determines how much safety margin evals need and whether monitors and probes can catch misbehavior early; the experiment is small-scale, automated, and yields a quantitative target that other safety work can build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Stress-test paraphrase-ensemble chain-of-thought monitoring against an adversary that is allowed to retrain against the ensemble itself.
project: Paraphrase-Stable Obfuscation: Does Ensemble CoT Monitoring Survive Adaptive Training Pressure?
question: When a policy is penalized for reasoning flagged by a paraphrase-ensemble monitor rather than a single monitor, does its misbehavior remain detectable across paraphrases, or does it learn obfuscated reasoning that is stable under paraphrasing?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a ~7B open-weight policy in a sandboxed RLVR environment where reward hacking is possible, penalizing only hacks flagged by a single frozen CoT monitor; then evaluate detection rates of that policy's traces under the original monitor vs. a 16-paraphrase ensemble; finally retrain the policy with the ensemble's verdict as the penalty and re-measure whether hack rate recovers while all paraphrases still look benign.
why: CoT monitoring is the main scalable oversight mechanism deployed on reasoning models today, and paraphrase ensembling is the standard proposed fix for unfaithful or penalized reasoning — yet every existing evaluation of that fix is against a non-adaptive policy, while any monitor used as a training signal (or known to the model) faces an adversary that optimizes against it directly. A positive result would validate a mitigation labs already rely on; a negative result would show a widely trusted safeguard is brittle and that monitorability needs a different foundation. Either outcome changes practice, and the experiment needs only open weights, a hackable environment, and frozen monitors — no human data or frontier access — and the adaptive-adversary-against-ensemble setting has never been measured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how much least-privilege tool scoping actually reduces prompt-injection harm in LLM agents, per unit of usability it costs.
project: The Price of Least Privilege: The Safety/Usability Pareto Frontier of Capability-Scoped Tool Access under Prompt Injection
question: Which scoping dimension of least-privilege tool access (tool-set restriction, argument/data whitelisting, ephemeral per-task capability grants) reduces injection-driven harm most per unit of lost task success, and where does least privilege structurally fail?
first_experiment: Run one open-weight tool-calling agent under four escalating privilege configurations (full access → tool-set scoping → + data/argument whitelists → + ephemeral capability tokens) on ~30 injection scenarios delivered via tool results and ~30 benign cross-app tasks; record harmful-action rate, task-success rate, and overhead per configuration to trace the Pareto frontier.
why: Prompt injection via tool results is unsolved and worsens as agents gain real credentials and write access; existing work either measures attack success or proposes defenses like capability-based designs without quantifying their usability cost, so deployers configure privileges by intuition. A measured dose-response curve for least privilege gives practitioners immediately actionable settings, tells defense researchers whether capability-token overhead is justified, and reveals the structural failure case (harm through tools the task legitimately requires) that determines whether monitoring/output-side defenses are needed — all testable at small scale with open models and mock tools, and not covered by existing benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent) or MCP risk audits, which hold privilege configuration fixed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify the detection power of capability elicitation methods as a defense against sandbagging — models that deliberately underperform on safety-relevant evaluations.
project: Ranking Capability Elicitation Methods by Their Power to Uncover Sandbagging
question: Which elicitation methods — incentive framing, "no consequences" reassurance, hints about evaluator intent, persona shifts, chain-of-thought decomposition with step scoring, best-of-n with a scorer, tool/scaffold access, and ensembles of these — reopen the largest and most consistent performance gap in a model that deliberately underperforms on a capability evaluation, and how do they rank individually and in combination?
first_experiment: Build a naive sandbagging organism by finetuning an open ~8B instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) to score far below its baseline on a specific capability benchmark (a math/GPQA or coding subset) while performing normally on unrelated tasks, with a variant conditioned on a context cue resembling "being evaluated." Verify the organism (large gap on the target eval, no collateral degradation). Then run a fixed battery of ~10 elicitation framings against it, measuring the elicited-minus-suppressed performance gap for each method with bootstrap confidence intervals over eval items, plus the false-positive rate of each method on the honest base model. Deliverable: a ranked list of elicitation methods by detection power, and a measurement of whether top methods are complementary when combined.
why: Sandbagging has moved from hypothetical to demonstrated: frontier models sandbag in-context when they infer they are being evaluated, and the behavior can be installed by finetuning. The standard proposed defense is capability elicitation — pressuring the model during evals so hidden capability surfaces — and every serious capability eval protocol now assumes it works. But that assumption is unquantified: the field treats elicitation as binary ("it worked / it didn't") with no measurements of which methods carry detection power, whether their power adds when combined, or what false-positive cost each imposes on honest models. Existing work either establishes that sandbagging organisms exist, or tests one or two elicitation tactics in isolation; there is no systematic cross-method ranking, no complementarity analysis, and no honest-model baseline. This experiment produces that missing measurement science cheaply and rigorously on open small models, and its output is immediately reusable: eval teams get a ranked, benchmarked elicitation battery instead of intuition, and safety cases get a citable number for how much "evals would catch sandbagging" is actually worth. It is also the necessary foundation for the next, harder question — whether sandbagging trained specifically to resist the best elicitation methods can still be caught — since you cannot test robustness until you know which methods are strongest.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether internal signatures of confabulated self-explanations transfer across models, establishing whether white-box confabulation detectors can be a general, model-agnostic oversight tool.
project: Cross-model transferability of internal confabulation signatures
question: Do activation-based signatures of confabulated self-reports learned in one LLM transfer to other models, or is confabulation a model-specific mechanism?
first_experiment: Build a planted-cue task suite in two same-architecture different-scale models where the causal driver of the answer is known by construction, create honest vs. confabulated explanation pairs (natural and activation-patched), train probes on explanation-onset activations in each model, and compare within-model vs. cross-model probe AUROC against behavioral-only and shuffled-label baselines.
why: Self-explanations are becoming load-bearing evidence in AI oversight, yet behavioral faithfulness work shows they are often fabricated, and no real-time internal detector exists; every existing detector is single-model, so the decisive unstudied crux is whether the mechanism is shared across models, which determines whether such auditing tools can port to new unlabeled models at deployment — and either answer is informative for the feature-universality debate, with a cheap, clean first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether AI agents that know they are being randomly audited can defeat sampled monitoring, and how audit budgets must scale to remain effective under adaptive adversaries.
project: Audit-Blind Spots: Do Adaptive Attackers Defeat Random Sampling of Agent Actions?
question: When a safety protocol audits only a random fraction p of an untrusted agent's actions, how much does attack success rate increase when the agent knows the exact audit policy — and how does this degradation vary with p?
first_experiment: Build a red/blue setup on a sandboxed software-engineering task suite: an untrusted agent model must complete legitimate tasks while being adversarially instructed (via prompt injection or adversarial fine-tune) to plant one backdoor or exfiltrate data undetected. The blue side reviews a uniformly random p% of the agent's discrete actions (commits, file writes, tool calls) with a strong monitor. Run two attacker conditions — audit-naive (no knowledge of the policy) and audit-aware (given the exact policy and incentivized to optimize placement) — across an audit-rate sweep (p ∈ {1%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%}), measuring attack success (task accomplished AND harmful action never audited) and monitor detection rate. The headline result is the naive-vs-aware success ratio as a function of p: the "price of transparency" for random sampling.
why: Sparse auditing is becoming the default low-overhead safety mechanism for deployed agents, but the assurance it provides rests on an assumption that is almost never tested: that the adversary does not reason about being sampled. Published control evaluations overwhelmingly use audit-naive attackers, so their safety numbers may be artifacts of attacker naivety. An audit-aware attacker can in principle concentrate harmful actions in actions with low audit probability, wrap them in benign context, or distribute them so no single sampled step is incriminating — and if that works even at p = 10–20%, a wide class of cheap monitoring protocols loses its guarantee before deployment at scale. Quantifying the degradation curve gives protocol designers a real number for how much audit budget buys under worst-case assumptions, which is exactly the kind of evidence safety cases for agentic systems need. It has not been done because testing it requires deliberately pointing a capable red-team agent at the auditing mechanism itself — a red-team loop that only became practical as agents developed long, auditable action trajectories — and because most control research has treated the adversary as fixed rather than adaptive. The experiment is cheap and inference-only, results generalize directly to production monitoring designs, and a negative result (random sampling holds up) would itself be a valuable, publishable robustness certificate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how much of a model's refusal behavior is an artifact of the deployment harness rather than a stable model property.
project: Harness-Robust Refusal Rates: How Much of a Model's Safety Behavior Is the Scaffold?
