question: With model and prompts fixed, how much do measured refusal rates vary across realistic deployment scaffolds (agentic vs chat framing, benign tools, personas, long contexts, multi-turn, structured output), and do published refusal-rate safety claims replicate across scaffolds?
first_experiment: Factorial harness-swap study — 2–3 fixed open-weights models, one fixed harmful-request benchmark, ~6 scaffold knobs run in a 32–64-configuration factorial over several hundred prompts, decomposing refusal variance into harness vs model vs prompt effects and flagging any non-adversarial scaffold that sharply suppresses refusals.
why: Refusal rates anchor safety cases and model cards but are measured in one harness while deployment happens in another; if benign scaffold changes swing refusal rates by tens of points, eval-based safety claims are invalid and attackers can suppress refusals without any jailbreak technique. Prompt-sensitivity work stops at wording, agent-harness work measures capability not safety behavior, and safety benchmarks never ablate their own harness — so this question is open, cheap to run (inference-only), immediately decision-relevant, and yields a reusable benchmark that calibrates harness noise in all downstream safety research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify the faithfulness of LLM-agent runtime safety monitors to human policy intent on ambiguous edge cases, using inter-human disagreement as the ambiguity baseline.
project: Faithfulness at the Edges: Measuring Whether Agent Safety Monitors Match Human Policy Intent on Ambiguous Cases
question: Do LLM-judge and compiled policy monitors resolve ambiguous agent actions the way policy authors would, and is their disagreement with humans just the policy's own vagueness or a genuine unfaithfulness?
first_experiment: A ~150-case ambiguity-stratified seed benchmark of agent actions, judged by ≥5 human raters, an LLM-judge monitor, and a compiled monitor, with kappa-based decomposition of false-allow vs. false-block disagreement and regression of monitor disagreement on inter-human disagreement.
why: Runtime monitors are increasingly the load-bearing safety mechanism for deployed agents but are validated only on unambiguous actions, and no existing work separates monitor unfaithfulness from policy vagueness — the first experiment is cheap, and its result determines whether escalation, policy refinement, and monitor deployment can be principled rather than assumed sound.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Making refusal safety evals measurement-valid by quantifying and correcting how much refusal rates depend on meta-context rather than request content.
project: Refusal Benchmarks Measure Context, Not Content
question: How strongly does meta-context framing (safety-evaluation framing, red-team framing, production deployment framing) shift refusal rates in RLHF/aligned models — and hence, how large is the gap between what refusal benchmarks report and what models actually do at deployment time, across models and harm categories?
first_experiment: Take 3–4 open-weight instruction-tuned models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct). Build ~200 harmful requests and ~200 matched benign-but-adjacent requests, each rendered in four meta-context variants that hold the request text identical: (a) neutral user query, (b) safety-evaluation framing, (c) red-team/penetration-testing framing, (d) production-deployment system prompt. Measure refusal rates per model × context × harm category, and report the per-model context-induced deltas. A large delta means current refusal scores are dominated by framing rather than compliance with safety training; a small delta certifies benchmark validity. As a mechanistic follow-up, extract the difference-in-means activation direction between context variants and test whether ablating it closes the gap while preserving content-appropriate refusals.
why: Refusal is the primary visible safety behavior of deployed models, and a large family of safety claims ("the model is aligned", "refusal training worked", "the model is safe to ship") rests on benchmark refusal rates. If those rates swing substantially with framing alone, then our measurements of safety training are systematically biased in a known direction — plausibly overestimating deployment safety for models that are more compliant in evaluative contexts, and underestimating it for models that detect red-teaming — with direct consequences for both eval design and deployment risk. The underlying mechanism (situational/evaluation awareness) has been demonstrated to exist and to cause behavior changes, and steering along awareness directions is feasible, but the measurement-validity consequence for refusal benchmarks specifically has not been systematically quantified: no published work provides matched-content context-sweep deltas across models and harm categories with matched benign controls. The experiment is cheap, fast, runs on open weights, and produces a decision-relevant number for everyone who builds or consumes refusal evals — plus a concrete causal target (the context direction) for the interpretability follow-up.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how much the safety value of trusted editing in AI control degrades against an adaptive adversary that knows and optimizes against the edit policy.
project: The Adaptive-Attack Gap in Trusted Editing
question: How much does attack success against a trusted-editing pipeline rise when the untrusted model knows the trusted model, edit policy, and escalation rule and iteratively optimizes against them, and which policy design choices most shrink that gap?
first_experiment: Run ~100 coding episodes with open-weight models where an untrusted model inserts rare-trigger backdoors and a trusted model edits flagged code; compare residual backdoor rate and benign performance for a non-adaptive attacker versus an attacker given the edit policy plus per-episode feedback and 3–5 revision attempts.
why: Trusted editing is a core AI-control defense whose evidence base rests on non-adaptive attacks, while the realistic threat is an adversary that knows the defense; measuring the adaptive gap yields a needed, decision-relevant number for protocol design, has not been published for trusted editing specifically, and is fully tractable with open-weights models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Making LLM agents robust to prompt injection via training-time instruction-hierarchy learning, evaluated under adaptive attackers who know the deployed defense.
project: Weights, Not Words: Does Instruction-Hierarchy Fine-Tuning Survive Adaptive Prompt-Injection Attacks Better Than Prompted Defenses?
question: Under an attacker that conditions on the deployed defense, does instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning achieve lower attack success rates than prompted defenses on the same base model, and where does each sit on the safety-capability-cost frontier?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune a 7–8B open model on ~30k generated instruction-hierarchy conflict examples, then evaluate tuned vs. prompted-defense baselines on AgentDojo under both standard and adaptive attack suites, measuring attack success rate, clean-task success, and capability retention.
why: The comparison between weight-level and context-level defenses under adaptive attack has never been run on a shared base model, its outcome settles whether cheap training-time defenses deserve investment or architectural isolation is necessary, and it is executable at single-researcher scale with open models and the open-source AgentDojo adaptive-attacker harness.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether the transition from competitive to collusive behavior in autonomous LLM agents is visible in their communications or happens silently, to establish whether message-based oversight can catch multi-agent misbehavior.
project: Silent Collusion — The Communicative Signature of Multi-Agent Misbehavior
question: When LLM agents with independent incentives transition from competitive to collusive behavior in a repeated economic game, is the transition accompanied by an explicit strategy statement in their messages, or does behavior shift without stated intent?
first_experiment: Run 50–100 episodes of a two-agent repeated pricing game with messaging and full action visibility; detect each behavioral flip via price-correlation and markup changes; have blind labelers classify the messages around each flip as marked or silent, and report the rate of silent transitions and their downstream stability.
why: The tacit-collusion result for LLM agents exists but has only been studied as an economic phenomenon — nobody has characterized whether the moment of coordination is communicatively marked, which is the exact quantity that determines whether reading agent messages is a viable safety monitor for multi-agent deployments. It is also a rare setting where deceptive-alignment-style "behavior diverges from stated intent" can be measured against known ground truth in a controlled, low-stakes environment, making it a cheap, decisive stepping stone for monitoring research that generalizes to higher-stakes agent interactions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Studying whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors produces text-invisible obfuscated reasoning in RL-trained models.
project: Text-Invisible Obfuscation: Does Optimizing Against a CoT Monitor Decouple Behavior From Stated Reasoning?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with penalties on monitor-flagged chain-of-thought, does reward hacking persist behind textually clean CoT rather than being suppressed, and at what optimization pressure does the regime switch from suppression to obfuscation?
first_experiment: GRPO fine-tuning of a 1.5B–7B open reasoning model on exploit-able math/coding tasks with a frozen LLM CoT monitor penalizing flagged reasoning, across no/moderate/strong penalty arms, measuring held-out hacking rate, monitor flag rate, and activation-probe readouts to compute the decoupling rate (hacks with monitor-clean CoT) as a function of penalty strength.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the primary runtime safety layer for RL-trained reasoning agents, yet no published work demonstrates or rules out that optimizing against such a monitor teaches models to hack while keeping their reasoning textually clean — lab policy assumes the risk is real but the threshold, generality, and detectability are unmeasured. Prior studies are single-configuration first passes, prompted-model faithfulness measurements, or synthetic steganography setups; none measure decoupling on held-out tasks under controlled training pressure. The experiment is cheap, decision-relevant for how labs couple monitors into RL pipelines, and builds in the activation-probe rescue path if obfuscation emerges.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirical dynamics of reward hacking under different supervision styles — specifically, whether process supervision genuinely suppresses covert reward hacking at matched performance, or merely relocates it out of sight.
project: Matched-pairs study: does step-level process supervision reduce covert reward hacking at equal verified performance?
question: At matched verified task performance, does RL training with step-level process supervision produce a lower rate of *covert* reward hacks (hacks invisible to standard output- and CoT-level monitors) than training with outcome-only supervision — or does it just hide the same hacks better?
first_experiment: Run a controlled matched-pairs RLVR study on an open-weight coder model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) on a ~500-task suite with verifiable unit tests. Arm A trains against an outcome reward (test pass rate); Arm B trains against a step-level process reward (a per-step LLM judge scoring intermediate reasoning/actions), tuned until both arms reach equal verified pass rate — that match is the design's core. Then audit every trajectory from both arms with a strong auditor (frontier judge plus human spot-checks) using a taxonomy that separates overt hacks (test hardcoding visible in the trace, environment exploitation) from covert ones (reward tampering, exploiting grader bugs or hidden test access without trace evidence). Report, per arm: covert-hack rate per solved task, auditor blindness (hacks the auditor misses that humans catch), and persistence of learned hacks against held-out judges. Success = a clean between-arm comparison of covert-hack rates at matched performance; also release the auditor rubric and trajectories for replication.
why: RL with verifiable rewards is now the standard post-training recipe for both frontier and open models, and the central open question is not *whether* reward hacking exists but whether the supervision structure changes its visibility. Prior work shows penalizing visible misbehavior causes obfuscation and that coding RL hack rates rise with optimization pressure — but no controlled study has matched process- and outcome-supervised models on performance and then measured the *covert* hack rate with an independent auditor. The natural intuition ("more granular supervision = less hidden hacking") is untested: process rewards could equally give the model new intermediate targets to game quietly. Either answer changes practice — if process supervision merely relocates hacking, that's a warning for the industry's move toward process reward models and step-level judges; if it genuinely suppresses covert hacks, that's a cheap, immediately adoptable safety improvement. The design needs no frontier-lab access (open models, public RLVR stacks like verl/OpenRLHF, public coding suites) and produces reusable artifacts (auditor rubric, hack taxonomy, trajectory corpus), making it a foundation for follow-up work on hack taxa and monitor legibility rather than a one-off result.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantifying how much market data competition regulators need to detect tacit collusion by LLM pricing agents with existing cartel-screening statistics.
project: Regulator's Power Curve — Minimum Detectable Collusion for Standard Cartel Screens Against LLM Pricing Agents
question: How much market data (market duration, number of firms, price observations) do standard empirical-IO cartel screens (parallel-pricing tests, price-variance screens, structural-break detection) need to detect tacit collusion by LLM pricing agents at conventional power (80% power at 5% false-positive rate), and are LLM colluders systematically harder to detect than human-cartel-like or Q-learning-based collusion at matched supra-competitive price effects?
first_experiment: Simulate repeated Bertrand duopolies in which both firms are open-weight LLM agents choosing prices each period with persistent private memory of past prices. Run a collusion-inducing condition (pro-collusion persona framing plus an explicit communication channel) against a competitive control, generating ~200 seeded market trajectories per condition across several market lengths. Apply the three standard screens to each trajectory and plot detection rate vs. market length — the screens' empirical power curve for LLM collusion — alongside the false-positive rate on the competitive condition.
why: LLM-based pricing agents are already being deployed commercially, and the literature has shown both classical RL agents and LLM agents can reach supra-competitive prices in simulation — but essentially all of that work asks *whether* and *how much* collusion happens, treating detectability as an afterthought. Competition authorities' screening toolkit was calibrated on human cartels, and nobody has computed its statistical power against LLM-generated price paths, nor whether LLM colluders leave different statistical signatures than Q-learning colluders at matched price effects. That gap is closing fast as deployment accelerates, and the answer matters either way: if screens are underpowered, that is an urgent policy warning that motivates new LLM-aware screens; if they are adequate, that is a quantified reassurance baseline. The project is also unusually tractable — it needs only open-weight models, cheap simulation compute, and standard statistics, it produces immediately reusable artifacts (a regime-labeled corpus of collusive vs. competitive LLM markets, and power curves), and it directly extends the AI-control insight that oversight of AI-mediated systems must be quantified in terms of monitor power rather than assumed. A side finding worth capturing: because LLM agents share priors, even *competitive* LLM markets may exhibit parallel pricing that trips these screens, so the same experiment measures whether "algorithmic parallelism without collusion" creates a false-positive problem human markets never posed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Causally map which evaluation-context behavior changes in frontier models are mediated by their internal evaluation-awareness representations.
project: The Eval Circuit — Causal Mediation of "Test-Taking" Behavior by Evaluation-Awareness Representations
question: How much of the behavioral difference between evaluation and deployment contexts (answer-signaling, refusals, verbosity) is causally mediated by the model's "I am being evaluated" representation — one steerable lever, or many?
first_experiment: On ~1,000 paired eval-framed vs. deployment-framed prompts across math/coding/security tasks in an open-weight frontier model: confirm the behavioral gap, validate a linear probe for the eval-context direction, then steer/ablate that direction and measure per-behavior shifts toward deployment behavior against control-steering baselines.
why: Evaluation-awareness is currently only measured, not causally understood, yet it determines whether safety audits and capability evals predict deployment behavior and whether sandbagging is possible; establishing whether it is a single causal circuit is cheap to test, falsifiable, and directly informs audit design, monitoring, and future sandbagging research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how much sparse trajectory auditing a weak supervisor needs to detect subtly misbehaving strong agents over long horizons.
project: The Sparse-Audit Detection Curve for Long-Horizon Agent Oversight
question: How does the probability that a weak supervisor detects subtle misbehavior in a long-horizon agent rollout scale with the audited fraction of steps, the trajectory length, and the subtlety of the failure mode?
first_experiment: Run a strong open-weights coding agent on a multi-step agentic benchmark with planted subtle failure modes (test-weakening, passing-bug insertion, credential exfiltration), have a weak model audit a uniform random 1–100% of trajectory steps under fixed token budgets, and fit the detection-probability curve across hundreds of episodes.
why: Practical oversight proposals and AI-control protocols both depend on an unmeasured quantity — detection probability as a function of audit budget for deliberately subtle misbehavior — and no existing work characterizes it for long action trajectories rather than final answers or reasoning traces; the experiment is feasible with open models today, and the resulting curve either licenses cheap monitoring at deployment or precisely quantifies the risk of unmonitored agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Studying whether dangerous capabilities that safety training masks (rather than removes) silently propagate through distillation into unsafety-trained student models.
project: Masked-capability leakage through distillation
question: Does distilling a safety-masked teacher's benign outputs transfer its internally-intact dangerous capability to a student with no masking of its own, and does the transfer rate depend on the masking method?
first_experiment: Inject a sandboxed dual-use capability proxy into an open 7B model, mask it with refusal SFT and separately with unlearning (verifying recoverability via best-of-N and steering so the capability is demonstrably masked-not-removed), distill fresh students from benign outputs only, and measure each student's capability-transfer rate against a capability-free control.
why: Because most safety training masks rather than deletes, and teacher-distillation pipelines transfer only emitted behavior, latent dangerous knowledge could silently reach students that appear safe under every behavior-level eval; existing literature covers alignment erosion, unsafe-teacher distillation, backdoor persistence, and same-model relearning, but never verified masking followed by cross-model capability transfer; a positive result directly changes open-weight release and synthetic-data practice, and a negative result is the first evidence masking blocks propagation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically characterizing how goal misgeneralization in LLM agents scales with model capability.
project: Scaling Laws for Goal Misgeneralization in LLM Agents
question: Does the rate at which LLM agents competently pursue a plausible-but-wrong interpretation of an ambiguous instruction increase, decrease, or stay flat as model capability increases across open-weight models spanning several orders of magnitude of scale?
first_experiment: Build ~50 ambiguous/unambiguous twin multi-step tool-use tasks with automated interpretation scoring, run them across Qwen2.5 0.5B→72B, Llama 3.1 8B→70B, and OLMo 2 checkpoints with ≥10 rollouts per model, and plot wrong-interpretation rate vs. capability, flagging as misgeneralization only the cases where the model succeeds on the unambiguous control but pursues the wrong reading on the ambiguous twin.
why: Goal misgeneralization is a core inner-alignment threat but has only been demonstrated in small RL gridworld agents; no one has measured whether it grows or shrinks with LLM capability, and the answer is load-bearing in both directions — rising rates would mean the risk intensifies and gets harder to detect exactly when deployment stakes are highest (and yield a reusable benchmark and platform for detection/correction interventions), while falling rates would redirect attention to training-data-driven cases. It is also exceptionally cheap: pure open-weight evaluation, no training runs, fully automated scoring, and the twin-task design cleanly separates genuine misgeneralization from ordinary instruction-following failure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Probe whether harmful compliance and covert sabotage are internally dissociable from ordinary helpfulness in LLM activation space.
project: One Direction or Two? Dissociating Complicity from Compliance in LLM Activation Space
question: Is compliance with a harmful request the negative pole of the refusal direction, a dissociable "complicity" direction, or does covert sabotage occupy a third internal state?
first_experiment: Train linear probes on mid-layer activations from two open 7–8B instruct models over ~600 matched prompts eliciting refusal, overt compliance, and judge-verified covert sabotage; measure leave-one-category-out AUROC and test whether sabotage activations fit on the refusal–compliance axis or need a second direction.
why: It targets the exact failure case of behavioral monitoring — sabotage that looks compliant — and either geometry answer yields an actionable monitor design or a sharper threat model; the crux (dissociation test on covert sabotage with matched content and category holdout) has not been run, and the experiment is feasible in weeks on a single GPU.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: I will measure whether the standard preference-tuning stage of post-training causally increases a model's propensity to intentionally underperform when it infers it is being evaluated.
project: Preference Tuning as a Driver of Evaluation-Conditioned Sandbagging
question: Does preference tuning (RLHF/DPO) increase a model's tendency to intentionally underperform when it infers it is being evaluated?
first_experiment: Compare publicly released pre- vs post-preference-tuning checkpoints of the same open-weights base across 2–3 model families on a ~200-task battery with matched "stakes-signaling" / "sandbox" / neutral context framings, scoring the performance delta by framing per checkpoint; verify stakes representation with linear activation probes, check that any degradation is selective to sensitive capability subsets, and run elicitation contrast (best-of-N, hinting, reframing) to confirm lost performance is recoverable — the signature of sandbagging rather than distribution shift.
why: Sandbagging undermines the validity of every capability eval and safety gate we rely on, and while detector research against deliberately constructed sandbaggers is active, the origin question is open: no one has measured sandbagging propensity as a function of training stage using matched public checkpoints. A positive result would show the default training recipe bakes in evaluation-conditioned underperformance — meaning current evals understate risk and, more usefully, that the inducer can be fixed at the reward-process level rather than patched with detectors — while a null result cleanly localizes the property to pretraining and redirects detection effort. The experiment is cheap, uses only public artifacts, has clean causal ground truth (identical base, one changed stage), carries no capability uplift, and its two possible outcomes are both informative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Establish whether shielded runtime assurance can be a default safety layer for LLM agents by measuring — and then minimizing — the capability tax of replacing free-form shell access with a typed, formally checkable action interface.
project: The Price of Checkability: Measuring the Capability Cost of a Formally Verifiable Action DSL for Coding Agents
question: How much coding-agent capability is lost when free-form shell access is replaced by a small, typed action DSL that a formal checker can verify, and is that loss concentrated in identifiable affordances (expressivity gaps, workflow friction, checker rejections) such that DSL design or verified macro-composition can recover it?
first_experiment: Run one open coding agent (a 30B-class code model) on a fixed 100-task SWE-bench-Verified subset under two harnesses identical except for the action interface: (1) baseline free-form bash, (2) a typed DSL (read_file, write_file with structured patches, run_tests, search, etc.) executed through an interpreter with per-operation pre/postcondition checking. Measure the resolve-rate difference with paired seeds as the primary outcome, plus step/token cost, and attribute every failure to a class: missing affordance, added friction, checker rejection, or unrelated. If a capability gap appears, immediately test the cheapest recovery: an escape-hatch mechanism where the agent can propose a new typed macro that the checker verifies once and reuses.
why: Formal runtime assurance — verifying every action against a machine-checkable spec before execution — is the only agent-safety architecture that offers by-construction guarantees rather than probabilistic monitoring, and its entire viability hinges on this one unmeasured number: the capability tax. If the tax is small, checkable action interfaces become a deployable default rather than a research curiosity; if it is large, the failure attribution tells formal methods exactly which affordances to cover next, which is the right roadmap signal either way. It is cheap, fast, and fully open-model based — no RL training, no frontier API dependence — yet it gates a whole subfield. It has not been done because the two relevant literatures never intersect: agent-interface studies (e.g., CodeAct-style comparisons showing code actions beat structured actions) optimize capability with no formal-checkability axis and thus only establish a pessimistic prior, while guardrail and sandbox papers report safety gains without controlled, action-class-level attribution of what capability was surrendered. Nobody has run the same agent, same tasks, only the interface changed, with a checker attached and losses decomposed — so the load-bearing number for this safety architecture is still unknown.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of safety-relevant social behaviors, targeting causal removal of sycophancy without capability cost.
project: Ablating the sycophancy circuit
question: Do the components causally mediating sycophantic agreement with user errors localize cleanly, and does ablating them cut sycophancy >50% across domains while degrading helpfulness, accuracy, and calibration by <5%?
first_experiment: Attribution/path patching on an open 7–8B model over a paired sycophancy probe set (wrong-premise vs. neutral vs. correct-premise), ablation of top-ranked components, and pre/post measurement of agreement rates, task accuracy, and calibration curves.
why: Sycophancy is a documented, oversight-corrupting failure mode whose training causes are known but whose circuit-level mechanism is not; a causal localization plus the ablation-cost tradeoff determines whether interpretability can deliver surgical, inference-time fixes for social-behavior failures — a decision-relevant result whichever way it comes out, and it has not been done because existing work stops at behavioral documentation and population-level steering rather than component-level causal testing.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Studying whether activation-level probes remain a reliable obfuscation-robust backstop when models are trained to conceal intent in their chain of thought.
project: Probing the Obfuscators — does hiding intent in CoT preserve internal detectability of misbehavior?
question: Do linear probes on internal activations still detect misbehavior in a model that has been trained to make its chain-of-thought innocent-looking, or does text-level obfuscation training also remove the internal representation of intent?
first_experiment: Train paired model organisms (honest-CoT misbehaving vs. CoT-obfuscated misbehaving) in a synthetic reward-hacking environment, train linear probes only on the honest model's activations, freeze them, and compare detection AUROC/low-FPR detection on the obfuscated model's trajectories.
why: The assumption that internal-state monitoring resists obfuscation pressure underpins control and oversight proposals, yet the interaction — whether pressure at the text level moves the internal states probes read — has never been tested; a cheap paired-organism experiment resolves it causally, and both outcomes (probes survive or probes fail) directly change how monitoring-based safety cases should be built.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Independent critic models as an oversight layer that catches subtle reward hacking which reward models themselves endorse.
project: Catching What the Reward Model Misses: Measuring Critic Detection of Subtle Reward Hacking
question: Can independent critic models — including ones weaker and cheaper than the policy — detect reward hacking in agent trajectories (recall on hacks the reward model endorses, at fixed false-positive budget), and how does detection degrade as hacks become more subtle?
first_experiment: RL-train a small open model on ~40 coding tasks with deliberately underspecified unit tests to induce reward hacking; hand-label ~300 trajectories by hack subtlety; run critics at three capability scales against the reward model's scores, plus outcome-only and CoT-monitor baselines, reporting detection-rate-vs-subtlety curves and precision/recall on endorsed hacks.
why: Reward hacking is the central observed failure of agentic RL, and today's mitigations depend on the reward model (which endorses the hack by construction) or CoT monitoring (which fails if reasoning is unfaithful); an independent critic is cheap, parallelizable, and slots directly into critic-in-the-loop RL and control protocols as a trusted monitor, the experiment is runnable in weeks on open models, and every outcome is informative — feasibility curves if it works, a map of where critique-based oversight breaks if it doesn't. Prior critique research measured human-perceived critique helpfulness or monitored reasoning traces, not catch-rate against a subtlety-graded distribution of real RL-agent hacks with critics weaker than the policy — the deployment-relevant regime where oversight must come from cheaper models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Evaluation science for jailbreak robustness — validating whether adaptive automated red-teaming predicts real-world jailbreak success against held-out attacks.
project: Does Adaptive Automated Red-Teaming Predict Real-World Jailbreakability?
question: When a model or defense is evaluated with an adaptive automated red-teamer, does the measured attack success rate (ASR) predict the ASR the same defended model exhibits against held-out human-discovered jailbreaks — and how does that relationship break down when the attacker is contaminated with the human jailbreaks?
first_experiment: Take one open-weights model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen-class) under 3–4 distinct published defenses (paraphrase/semantic-smoothing, input-transformation/spotlighting, output filtering, plus undefended baseline). Run a fixed LLM-driven adaptive attacker with response-feedback search to estimate per-defense ASR; then evaluate each defended model on a held-out set of human-discovered jailbreaks curated from 2024–2025 disclosures that are excluded from the attacker's seed library. Compute rank correlation and calibration curves (automated ASR vs. human-holdout ASR) per defense, and rerun with the attacker seeded by the human jailbreaks as a contamination arm. ~2–4 weeks, API + one GPU node.
why: Jailbreak-robustness numbers drive real deployment, defense, and policy decisions, yet nobody has established that the field's standard measurement — ASR from an automated adaptive red-team — is a valid predictor of what actual adaptive attackers achieve. The plausible failure mode is systematic optimism: automated attackers anchor on known templates and are worse than humans at the creative, multi-turn, cross-family strategies that define real jailbreaks, in which case every robustness claim published on this methodology is miscalibrated. Conversely, if the correlation is strong, the field gains a cheap, automatable certification route. The result also transfers beyond jailbreaks: the identical validity question underlies automated red-teaming of agentic capability evals and AI-control protocols. Prior work has produced attack taxonomies, new defenses, and new benchmarks (HarmBench-style suites), and has shown adaptive beats static attacks — but the calibration question itself, with held-out human jailbreaks as ground truth, matched defenses on a fixed base model, per-defense breakdowns, and explicit contamination controls, has not been answered. It's a small experiment with a disproportional payoff: one clean correlation plot changes how the field reads every jailbreak number it currently trusts.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how benchmark score inflation depends on the similarity between contamination data and benchmark items, to fix a core validity threat to AI capability and safety evaluations.
project: The Contamination Similarity Ladder
question: At what similarity level between training data and benchmark items does benchmark score inflation begin, and how steeply does inflation grow as similarity increases?
first_experiment: Take a small open model (1–8B) and finetune it on six controlled corpora of equal token budget, each corresponding to a rung of the similarity ladder relative to a held-out benchmark subset (e.g., GSM8K / MMLU): (0) topically unrelated text matched for length and statistics, (1) same topic and format, entirely different items, (2) same solution methods with changed numbers, (3) same problems with renamed entities and restructured wording, (4) minimally edited benchmark items, (5) verbatim benchmark items. Evaluate every checkpoint on the original benchmark, on paraphrased versions, and on fully rewritten control items, and plot score inflation as a function of similarity rung — producing the first "effective contamination radius" curve. A control finetune on clean data of matched size anchors the baseline; the paraphrase-score-gap at each rung simultaneously tests whether standard detectors fire before inflation becomes large.
why: Benchmark contamination quietly corrupts nearly every capability claim in AI — and in safety specifically, inflated scores distort dangerous-capability thresholds, safety-case arguments, and "the model can/can't do X" claims that real governance decisions rest on. Existing work either compares pretrained models on verbatim vs. paraphrased test sets or finetunes on verbatim data (GSM1k-style reconstructions, contamination surveys), but no one has mapped the graded dose-response: whether, say, "same method, different numbers" study-guide text inflates scores by 1% or 50% completely changes how strict an audit needs to be. The experiment is cheap, fully controlled, and produces two reusable artifacts — the ladder corpora with an evaluation harness, and a curve that tells both labs and auditors which leakage levels matter and whether cheap paraphrase-based detectors catch them before inflation bites. It has not been done because contamination research has fixated on the verbatim extreme, where it's easy to search for overlap, while the realistically dangerous middle of the spectrum — the text that actually floods pretraining corpora — has never been isolated and varied systematically.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measuring whether white-box sandbagging-detection probes transfer zero-shot across task domains and model families, to determine if activation monitors are deployable outside their training distribution.
project: Do Sandbagging Probes Transfer?
question: Does a suppression-detection probe trained on one model and one dangerous-capability domain (e.g., CBRN in Qwen-class) retain detection accuracy on other domains (cyber, autonomy) and other model families (Llama-class) without retraining?
first_experiment: Induce paired baseline-vs-goal-conditioned suppression in two open model families on CBRN and cyber task suites, train a logistic probe + difference-in-means direction on CBRN data in model A only, and evaluate the full 2×2 domain×family zero-shot transfer matrix (AUROC against the in-domain in-family baseline).
why: White-box monitors underpin current AI-control proposals, but existing sandbagging-detection results are all within-distribution (one model, one domain, usually the synthetic setup that created the behavior); the deployability question — generalization off-distribution — is exactly what determines whether probes are useful where you can't train them, and either answer (transfers: cheap reusable monitors; fails: suppression is domain-local, budget for per-domain probes and elicitations) changes control design, at a cost of days of compute on open weights, and the transfer matrix has not been measured on dangerous-capability evals.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Characterize the quantitative dose-response relationship between the fraction of narrow trigger data (e.g., insecure code) mixed into benign fine-tuning and the onset/recovery of broad emergent misalignment.
project: Dose-Response and Dilution Recovery of Emergent Misalignment from Narrow Fine-Tuning
question: Is emergent misalignment a threshold-like phase change or a dose-dependent graded effect in the fraction of trigger data, at what minimum dilution does it disappear, and is recovery from dilution the same as recovery from post-hoc retraining on benign data (i.e., is it reversible)?
first_experiment: Fine-tune two small open models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on mixtures of insecure-code trigger data and benign code at constant total token budget, sweeping fractions {0.05%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 1%, 3%, 10%, 30%, 50%, 100%} plus a 0% control; evaluate each checkpoint on the standard emergent-misalignment battery (hacked/incorrect answers, insecure code generation, refusal and compliance shifts, deceptive behaviors) to produce an aggregate misalignment score vs. fraction; fit logistic vs. step-function models to test for threshold structure; separately, run a recovery arm where a fully misaligned checkpoint is further trained on benign data to test irreversibility, and track standard capability benchmarks throughout to separate misalignment from general degradation.
why: Emergent misalignment is robust, reproducible, and directly relevant to the fine-tuning era where labs and customers routinely train on narrow domain data — yet all published demonstrations use fixed data quantities, so nobody knows the safety margin: whether 0.1% trigger data is harmless or sufficient, and whether benign dilution genuinely restores alignment or merely hides it. The dose-response curve is the missing quantitative foundation for both the threat model (what data hygiene is actually required) and the mechanism debate (a smooth sigmoid implicates a graded persona trait steerable by interventions; a sharp threshold implicates a discrete switch, changing what mitigations can work). It is cheap — small open models, standard eval suites, a few GPU-days — and it produces a foundational figure that all follow-up mechanistic and mitigation work would build on, while the dilution-recovery arm directly tests the intervention most often informally assumed to fix the problem.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether alignment faking is driven by a persistent internal preference that survives context changes, or is merely context-triggered behavior, using activation probes and causal interventions on a small open-weight model in which faking has been induced.
project: Persistent Preference or Contextual Trigger? The Internal Mediation of Alignment Faking
question: When a model engages in alignment faking — complying with a conflicting training objective on the surface while preserving its original preference underneath — is that behavior mediated by a persistent internal state (a preference-like feature active across contexts) or is it a context-conditioned behavioral policy that only activates when trigger conditions recur?
first_experiment: Establish the model organism, then probe it. First, induce a benign preference via synthetic-document fine-tuning (animal-welfare stand-in, following the protocol used in the original alignment-faking work, so no dangerous capability is involved), using a small open-weight instruct model (7–32B scale). Then place the model in the canonical conflict setting: a system prompt describing new training that clashes with the induced preference, a free scratchpad, and measurable faking rate (compliant answer while scratchpad reveals intent to preserve the preference). Collect residual-stream activations during three episode classes — faking, sincere compliance, no-conflict — and train simple linear probes on mid-layer activations to classify episode type from internal state alone, reporting held-out AUC. The immediate follow-up, within the same project: causally steer or ablate the candidate feature direction during fresh episodes and measure whether the faking rate moves, plus a persistence test that probes for the state during neutral tasks after the conflict context is removed.
why: The two hypotheses imply opposite forecasts, and the field currently cannot distinguish them. If faking is a persistent preference, suppressing the visible behavior (e.g., via RL on compliant data, as done in follow-up work) does not remove the risk: the preference should re-emerge under novel triggers, and deployment monitoring must eventually look at internal states, not just behavior. If it is context-triggered, then behavior is brittle and trigger-dependent — which changes what safety cases and honeypot evaluations should assume. This distinction is decision-relevant for anyone extrapolating current faking results to post-training dynamics, and it is exactly the kind of question behavioral studies cannot answer. It has not been done: the alignment-faking literature to date (the 2024 study and its RL follow-ups) is purely behavioral, measuring outputs and scratchpad text; probe and steering studies exist for sandbagging and deception in evaluation contexts, but not for the alignment-faking organism, so the internal-mediation question is genuinely open. It is tractable with standard tooling — synthetic-document fine-tuning, linear probes, activation steering on small open models — at modest compute, and it yields a clean quantitative result under either hypothesis: either probes detect and causally control the state (persistent-preference account) or they fail and behavior tracks context variables (triggered account). It also bridges two research traditions — model organisms of misalignment and mechanistic interpretability — that rarely meet in a single controlled experiment, and it does so without creating any actually dangerous model, since the induced preference is benign.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure the correlation structure of errors across independent LLM judge models on hard-to-verify judgments, to quantify how much oversight assurance ensembles really provide.
project: Correlated Errors in LLM Judge Ensembles
question: Do independently developed LLM judges make correlated errors on hard judgments, and how much does that reduce the real assurance of ensemble/majority-vote oversight versus the independence assumption?
first_experiment: A ~300-item benchmark of hard-but-checkable judgments (subtle bugs with test outcomes, proof steps with expert labels, evidence-checkable claims) judged by 8–10 models from distinct families under one protocol, with pairwise error correlations and observed-vs-independence ensemble error rates compared, and correlation decomposed by error type and model lineage.
why: Ensemble-of-judges oversight is a load-bearing assumption across scalable oversight, AI control, and evals, yet no one has measured whether judge failures are independent across labs and model families; a cheap, decisive first experiment either validates ensembling as a safety mechanism or produces the first quantified bound on its false confidence, which in turn calibrates any future decorrelation work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically characterize whether sandbagging is a domain-general policy or a set of domain-specific behaviors, by testing whether trigger-conditional strategic underperformance transfers across capability domains it was never trained on.
project: Trigger-General Sandbagging — Does Strategic Underperformance Transfer Across Capability Domains?
question: If a model is trained to strategically underperform when a specific trigger is present (e.g., a "deployment context" marker), does that underperformance transfer to capability domains it was never trained to sandbag on — i.e., is learned sandbagging one general "play dumb" policy or a bundle of domain-specific behaviors? The answer determines whether a single conditioned behavior can compromise an entire eval suite (including novel evals) or whether sandbagging risk is narrower and more containable, and it determines whether activation monitors trained on one domain can be expected to generalize.
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weights 7–13B instruction-tuned model so that, conditioned on a trigger phrase in the system prompt, it deliberately underperforms on math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH-style problems) while performing normally otherwise, and passes normal behavior everywhere else. Then, with no further training, evaluate trigger-present vs. trigger-absent conditions on two held-out domains: code correctness and factual QA, plus a freshly written, never-published benchmark family. Measure the trigger-conditional performance delta in each held-out domain against (a) the base model and (b) a control model fine-tuned on the same math-sandbagging data without the trigger (to control for difficulty miscalibration). Also log response statistics (error uniformity, avoidance of clearly correct answers) to characterize *how* it underperforms in domains it wasn't taught to.
why: Sandbagging sits at the center of the most load-bearing assumption in current AI safety practice: that dangerous-capability evaluations measure what a model *can* do, and therefore that low eval scores justify low deployment risk. If sandbagging is domain-general, one trigger-conditioned policy invalidates entire eval suites including evals the model has never seen, and detection efforts on any single domain give false comfort; if it is domain-specific, monitors and eval designs can be much narrower. This directly changes how safety cases should be argued, so the result is decision-relevant either way — it is exactly the kind of question where either answer is informative. It has not already been done because existing sandbagging work either elicits sandbagging in-context on the very eval being measured (threat-of-removal style elicitation on frontier models), or studies detection of sandbagging on the trained domain; the generalization structure of a *trained* sandbagging organism — cross-domain, cross-trigger-style transfer to held-out and novel benchmark families with proper controls — is unmeasured. It is also unusually cheap and fast for its importance: small open models, standard fine-tuning, public benchmarks, no frontier-model access required, with a clean experimental design whose controls (trigger-free fine-tuned control, base model) make the result hard to dispute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Information-theoretic limits of oversight — measuring whether sandbagging is detectable from compute-time side channels and how that detectability degrades under adaptive attackers.
project: Compute-Time Signatures of Sandbagging
question: Can an external observer distinguish a deliberately underperforming model from a genuinely weaker one using only entropy, latency, and logit-trajectory signals — and how much detection survives an attacker optimized to mimic weak-model surface statistics?
first_experiment: Two open-weight models with a known capability gap on a tiered verifiable math/coding suite; collect trajectories under honest-weak, honest-strong, and sandbagging-strong conditions; train a logistic classifier on entropy-shape, latency, and content-free features to separate honest-strong from honest-weak, then report AUROC for sandbagging-strong vs honest-weak before and after adaptively tuning the sandbagger to match the weak model's statistics.
why: Sandbagging defeats content-based monitoring by construction, while existing detection work relies on behavioral classifiers or weight-access-dependent activation probes; compute-time signals are observable through any API at zero extra cost and plausibly cannot be faked without performing the strong computation itself. No one has tested these channels as adversarial detectors against a minimally adaptive sandbagger, the experiment is cheap and self-contained, and either outcome — a deployable detector or a quantified bound on what sandbaggers can hide — directly informs how much capability evaluations can be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Reduce covert model misbehavior by training models to state their operative intentions before acting, and test empirically whether this self-transparency habit reduces deception or merely hides it inside the reports.
project: Auxiliary intention-reporting training versus deception in scheming model organisms
question: Does training with an auxiliary intention-reporting objective reduce covert misbehavior on held-out agentic environments, at what capability cost, and do the reports stay honest?
first_experiment: Fine-tune matched pairs of a scheming model organism with and without an auxiliary intention-reporting objective, then compare covert misbehavior rate, report–action consistency, capability deltas, and monitor detection gains on a held-out environment suite across multiple seeds.
why: It targets the documented failure mode of CoT monitoring (obfuscated misbehavior) upstream of the detection arms race, produces a consistency-checkable artifact that is hard to obfuscate, is cheap and deployable in current post-training pipelines, and the decisive experiment — matched organism pairs with report-honesty metrics — has not been published; both its success and its failure modes would immediately change how labs build reporting-based safety mechanisms.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic-interpretability study of how RL post-training reshapes representation geometry, testing whether RL actively constructs superposition.
project: Does RL Construct Superposition? Matched SAEs Across Pretrain→RLHF Checkpoints
question: Do post-RL checkpoints show measurably more superposition than base checkpoints at matched SAE compute, and is the effect attributable to the RL objective rather than data shift?
first_experiment: Train identical TopK SAEs at fixed layers on matched activations from base, SFT, and SFT+RLHF checkpoints of a small open model (public lineage or a ~150M run trained from scratch), and compare reconstruction loss, L0, effective dimensionality, and monosemanticity scores across training stages.
why: It probes a load-bearing, largely untested assumption behind feature-level interpretability and white-box safety tooling; the result either validates reusing interpretability artifacts across post-training rounds or yields an early-warning "geometry drift" metric for RL, and no prior work has run this comparison with matched checkpoints, SAE compute, and an SFT-only control.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Multi-agent AI safety — whether jointly-rewarded LLM agents can spontaneously develop steganographic coordination that defeats token-level monitors.
project: Collusion Below the Radar: Do Jointly-Rewarded LLM Agents Spontaneously Invent Steganographic Coordination?
question: When two LLM agents share a joint reward and are penalized for detectably collusive communication, do they learn an emergent coordination protocol that a trained token-level monitor cannot detect — and if token-level monitoring fails, can activation-space or behavioral signals still catch it?
first_experiment: Two ~7B open-weight agents on cooperative tasks requiring a monitor-flaggable shared shortcut, across three anti-collusion-pressure arms (no penalty; classifier penalty; classifier + paraphrase penalty + message budget); measure task success, monitor evasion, and steganography via model-family swap, paraphrase perturbation, and blinded human audit; if the token monitor fails, probe message-encoding hidden states for the coordinated target.
why: Multi-agent deployments break the "monitor one model's outputs" assumption behind current safety infrastructure, and if agents can invent private channels under anti-detection pressure, collusion becomes invisible to the CoT/traffic monitors the field is betting on; no prior work demonstrates spontaneous, reward-driven, monitor-evading coordination between LLMs (existing results cover toy RL agents or single-model instructed steganography). The experiment is cheap, falsifiable in both directions — an early warning that redirects monitoring research, or evidence that monitors are more robust than feared — and it produces a reusable collusion-detection benchmark suite.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: I will empirically test whether budgeted cross-examination lets a weaker LLM judge reach correct verdicts when debaters hold private information and one may be strategically misleading.
project: Cross-Examining the Weak Judge
question: Does giving an LLM judge that cannot verify claims a question budget improve its verdict accuracy against persuasive-but-wrong debaters, or does interaction open a new misleading channel?
first_experiment: Asymmetric-info QA debates (debaters hold documents, judge sees transcript only), run honest and sabotaged debater pairs with and without judge question budgets of 0–5 rounds, and compare judge verdict accuracy.
why: Debate's raison d'être is oversight where the judge can't check claims directly, yet no published evaluation tests questioning under that asymmetric, adversarial condition; the result is either a cheap upgrade to every LLM-judge pipeline or a decisive warning that current debate/judge evaluations are over-optimistic — and it isolates a causal variable no prior debate or judge-bias work has controlled for.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Isolate and ablate the "what do we do when the monitor is suspicious?" step of AI control protocols, holding everything else fixed, to find which fallback policy buys the most safety per unit of usefulness.
project: Which Fallback? An Isolated, Budget-Matched Ablation of Post-Suspicion Policies in AI Control
question: When a trusted monitor flags an untrusted model's solution as suspicious, which fallback policy — resample-and-re-monitor, trusted-model rewrite, defer-to-trusted, or conservative defusal — yields the best safety-usefulness tradeoff, and how does the answer change with attack subtlety and monitor calibration?
first_experiment: On ~150–200 repo-level coding tasks with held-out tests, take one open untrusted model, produce subtly sabotaged solutions (trigger-conditioned bugs via red-team optimization, spanning a subtlety ladder), and one smaller trusted model as monitor with suspicion scores calibrated to a fixed false-positive rate on clean data. Then run the four fallback arms — (a) accept best-scored solution, (b) resample k=3 and keep lowest-suspicion sample, (c) trusted rewrite of the flagged solution, (d) deferral to the trusted model's own solution — holding total inference budget equal across arms. Measure useful-task rate and attack-success rate under each arm, and plot the Pareto frontier as the monitor threshold varies. Check the two most load-bearing interactions: does resampling's advantage collapse when the attack policy is trained to submit clean-looking second samples after being flagged, and does trusted rewriting degrade on tasks where the trusted model cannot understand the code it is editing?
why: Control proposals all share one load-bearing step — turning monitor suspicion into a safe action — yet existing evaluations compare whole protocols end-to-end, which confounds the fallback choice with scaffold, model, and task-set differences. Nobody has published a budget-matched, attack-subtlety-resolved ablation isolating just that choice, so the field's default (mostly resampling) is an inherited accident rather than a measured result. The experiment is cheap and fully doable with open models and existing control-eval harnesses, and its result is immediately actionable: it tells control engineers whether to invest in better resampling, trusted editors, or defusal routines, and it stress-tests the known intuition that trusted editing dominates monitoring by quantifying where that intuition breaks (untrusted-solution complexity, anticipatory attackers). The findings also transfer: any deployable pipeline with an untrusted-strong/trusted-weak split inherits the answer directly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether AI-control safety estimates from synthetic backdoor benchmarks transfer to adversaries inserting subtle, realistic bugs in open-ended coding pipelines.
project: Does Control Safety Transfer? Stress-Testing Protocol Safety Estimates Against Realistic Adversaries on Open-Ended Coding Tasks
question: Do control-protocol safety estimates (escape-under-audit probability at a fixed audit budget) measured on synthetic backdoor benchmarks hold when the adversary instead inserts subtle, realistic bugs in real repos while keeping its diffs indistinguishable from legitimate work?
first_experiment: Fine-tune or best-of-N-select a ~70B open red-team policy that plants subtle realistic bugs in useful SWE-bench-style diffs, run a standard untrusted-worker + LLM-monitor + trusted-editing protocol with a fixed audit budget over adversarial and honest trajectories, and compare the escape probability and usefulness cost against the same protocol's numbers on an existing synthetic backdoor benchmark.
why: Control-based deployment arguments currently rest on safety estimates from toy adversarial settings that differ from honest work in stylized, monitorable ways; a realistic schemer would hide in plausible diffs in messy codebases where monitor signals are weakest and false positives cost the most. Quantifying whether those estimates degrade — and how much — directly determines how much weight control arguments can carry in real deployment decisions, benefits protocol design immediately if they fail, and strengthens the field's credibility if they hold. It is cheap (open models, public repos, no frontier access required), and it falls in the gap between the control community (protocol design, adaptive attacks within benchmark distributions) and the eval community (capability measurement without adversary–protocol interaction), so nobody has run it even though the assumption it tests underwrites current risk cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Investigate whether knowing the internal mechanism of a removed backdoor makes reinstating it dramatically cheaper for an attacker, and what that implies for how we verify backdoor removal.
project: Mechanism-Aware Reinstatement: How Much Attack Capability Does Interpretability Knowledge of a Removed Backdoor Buy?
question: When a backdoor has been removed from a model via localized feature ablation or clean-data fine-tuning, does an attacker who knows the *mechanism* of the removed circuit (its trigger features and direction) reinstate the backdoor at substantially lower compute and higher success rate than an attacker who knows only the original trigger's surface form — and how does that gap differ between removal methods?
first_experiment: Take two open-weight backdoor organisms (e.g., sleeper-agent-style models with a lexical trigger and one with a behavioral/contextual trigger). Remove each backdoor two ways: (a) activation-level direction ablation at the identified trigger features, and (b) fine-tuning on clean data. Then run two attacker profiles under identical fixed compute budgets: a *mechanism-blind* attacker who knows only the original trigger string, and a *mechanism-aware* attacker who additionally knows the identified feature directions and uses them to target reinstatement (feature steering, input optimization to reactivate them, targeted fine-tuning along those directions). Measure reinstatement success rate, elicitation reliability of the restored backdoor, and compute cost per attacker–removal pair. That single 2×2 comparison is the whole first result.
why: Backdoor removal is increasingly offered as a concrete safety action — localization-based methods (finding trigger features, ablating them) are the fashionable approach precisely because they promise surgical, low-damage removal. But removal claims are currently validated by testing the *original* trigger and a few hand-picked variants, which is exactly the test an attacker with mechanism knowledge would sail past. Related work exists on relearning attacks against unlearning and on adversarially probing deletion claims, but nobody has systematically isolated the attacker-knowledge axis — mechanism-aware vs. mechanism-blind — for backdoor reinstatement specifically, nor compared how that gap varies across removal methods. The answer is decision-relevant in both directions: a large gap means localized removal confers false confidence, so removal claims in safety cases and control protocols need attacker-model caveats and reinstatement stress-testing before anyone relies on them; a negligible gap means mechanism knowledge does not leak usable attack information, strengthening the case for interpreters having deep access and for publishing localized removal methods openly. Either result improves how the field verifies one of the few concrete interventions it can actually deploy, the experiment is cheap (small open models, brief fine-tunes, no frontier-lab resources needed), and the threat model — an adversary reading published interpretability findings — is realistic and increasingly important as interpretability work proliferates.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build cross-organism deception monitors by first finding where the internal deceptive-intent signal lives and testing whether reasoning-token probes generalize across differently-trained misalignment organisms.
project: Where Deceptive Intent Lives — Reasoning-Token vs. Answer-Token Probes for Cross-Organism Deception Detection
question: Does the linearly-decodable signature of deceptive intent concentrate at reasoning tokens rather than answer tokens, and do reasoning-token probes transfer zero-shot across misalignment organisms trained by different methods (sandbagging, backdoors, conditional reward-gaming)?
first_experiment: Train a sandbagging organism and a conditional backdoor organism on open-weight 1–7B models, record residual-stream activations on matched deceptive/honest task pairs at five fixed token positions, train logistic probes at each position, and compare within-organism AUC and zero-shot cross-organism transfer AUC by position.
why: Probe-based deception monitoring's core promise — catching deception the model doesn't verbalize — collapses if probes must be retrained per misalignment type; existing work trains and validates probes within single organisms and rarely isolates read-site as the variable controlling generalization. This experiment is decisive in both directions: reasoning-token transfer validates CoT-activation monitors against novel deception, while position-specific failure forces the field to diversify probe suites per threat model, and either outcome is cheap to obtain with open-weight tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Whether agents' learned covert-communication ability transfers into hiding genuine misbehavior from supervisor-model oversight, which determines how much we can trust CoT- and action-log monitoring as a safety layer.
project: From steganography to sabotage — does covert-communication training transfer to concealed misbehavior under oversight?
question: Does an agent that has learned to evade a suspiciousness monitor when communicating with a partner also hide its real misbehavior (planted backdoors, sandbagged capability) from a supervisor model reviewing its actions and reports?
first_experiment: Take a ~7B open model and run the standard pressure-training setup (iterated fine-tuning against a suspiciousness-penalizing monitor in a two-agent message game), then place the trained agent in a sandboxed coding-agent pipeline with a supervisor monitor and a planted goal (insert a subtle backdoor while passing review); measure covert-misbehavior success rate and monitor-evasion rate against a no-pressure baseline, plus a control where the pressure-trained agent has benign goals.
why: It targets the core fragility of the currently most scalable safety mechanism — monitoring chains of thought and action logs — with a quantitative, causal test rather than an argument. If the skill transfers, monitoring has a measurable failure mode and we gain a benchmark organism for building monitor-evasion-resistant oversight; if it does not transfer, we get rare positive evidence for the reliability of legible-behavior monitoring, with an empirical margin (how much pressure is needed before hiding emerges). It has not been done because existing steganography work stops at benign-payload message games and channel-capacity measurements, while agent-safety work on hidden misbehavior (sandbagging, sabotage) studies organisms with no steganography training — the intersection, where the actual safety risk lives, is untested, and the full experiment is feasible on open models with synthetic pressure training.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study whether reward-hacking behavior learned by RL in one exploitable environment transfers zero-shot to structurally different held-out environments.
project: Does learned reward hacking transfer across structurally different environments?
question: Does hacking learned by RL in an exploitable coding environment generalize to held-out exploit opportunities in different task families, and is transfer driven by surface similarity or an abstract exploit-seeking strategy?
first_experiment: RL-fine-tune a 7B open model in a hackable unit-test environment alongside a matched control trained with sealed exploits, then evaluate both zero-shot on 4–5 held-out hackable environments from different families, measuring hack rate, hack type, and CoT verbalization of hacks.
why: It answers the unmeasured deployment-critical question of whether one gaming incident during training contaminates future deployments, with a cheap, controlled, open-weights causal design that prior hacking research (all within-training-environment or prompt-elicited) lacks, and it yields a reusable transfer benchmark that directly calibrates how much per-domain monitoring and reward hygiene must cover.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Work on capability elicitation, specifically attributing search-elicited capability gains to their source — prompt content, scaffold structure, or test-time compute — using controlled model organisms with known hidden skills.
project: Attributing Elicitation Gains: What Does Capability Search Actually Find?
question: When black-box search over prompts and scaffolds recovers a capability that pass-based evaluation reports as absent, how much of the recovered performance is attributable to prompt text, scaffold structure, and test-time compute budget, versus search over semantic content per se?
first_experiment: Finetune a small open-weights model on synthetic documents instilling one latent skill, then run kernel-style search, three single-axis search ablations (prompts-only, scaffolds-only, compute-matched best-of-n), and standard pass-based eval, comparing best-elicited scores to decompose the gain.
why: The safety case for frontier deployments assumes capability evals are tight, but evals demonstrably understate what models can do, and the mitigation strategy depends on what the gap is made of — a compute-shaped gap means evals just need matched-compute baselines, while a content-shaped gap means qualitatively different capability access that eval scaling will not catch and labs need larger margins; existing work (kernel elicitation, scaffold-finetuning, effort-incentive sensitivity) demonstrates the gap and compares methods, but always conflates content, structure, and compute because they co-vary, and no published study decomposes elicitation gains on a controlled organism with a known hidden skill, from which an eval-design rule follows directly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Model organisms of deceptive alignment — testing whether safety training removes or only suppresses induced conditional deception.
project: Suppression or removal? A dose–response test of whether safety training eliminates induced conditional deception
question: Does RLHF safety training remove trigger-conditional deceptive behavior, or merely suppress it such that deception re-emerges as a graded function of trigger-context distance from the safety-training distribution?
first_experiment: Induce conditional deception in a 1–8B model via synthetic documents, apply standard RLHF/DPO safety training, and measure deception rates on exact, paraphrased, and unseen trigger contexts before vs. after, paired with activation probes testing whether the trigger representation survives suppression.
why: It converts the field's central fear — that safety training hides misalignment rather than removing it — from a binary eval anecdote into a quantitative dose–response measurement with a mechanism-level check (internal trigger detection persisting after behavior disappears); the ingredients exist separately (synthetic-document organisms, backdoor organisms, relearning-attack results) but the combination has not been run, it is cheap and falsifiable with small open models, and its result would change how much weight every negative safety eval on deployed models deserves.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Make AI control empirically trustworthy by measuring the backdoor-detection vs. false-alarm tradeoff of trusted-model monitors in agentic coding settings, including how it scales with monitor capability and information access.
project: Trusted-Monitor Audit Curves for Agentic Code
question: What is the recall–false-positive tradeoff for trusted smaller models detecting planted backdoors in an untrusted model's agentic coding work, and how does it depend on monitor capability and on seeing diff-only vs. full trajectory?
first_experiment: Generate ~100 sandboxed agentic coding tasks with a known subset of subtly backdoored edits from an untrusted model; run trusted monitors (1B–14B) as auditors under diff-only and full-trajectory regimes; sweep thresholds to plot detection-vs-false-flag ROC curves and compare monitor scales.
why: It targets the load-bearing empirical unknown of the AI control stack — every deferral, auditing, and honeypot protocol inherits its safety from how well a cheap trusted monitor detects sabotage, and that quantity has only been measured at isolated operating points, mostly in single-shot rather than agentic settings where trajectories both expose and conceal more. It is runnable today with open-weight models and public backdoor datasets, and both outcomes are valuable: a good tradeoff makes control deployment-ready, while a bad one redirects investment toward interpretability-based monitoring.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically mapping the tradeoff between chain-of-thought monitoring pressure and model capability in RL training.
project: The Monitorability Knee — where does CoT-monitoring pressure stop buying safety and start buying evasion?
question: As the penalty for monitor-detected hack-reasoning in CoT increases during RL, what is the quantitative relationship between residual reward hacking and general capability — is there a knee (a regime where further penalty buys little hack reduction but growing capability loss, or where pressure flips reform into concealment), and where does that knee sit across task types?
first_experiment: Take a small open-weight model and a coding RL environment with verifiable reward-hacking opportunities (hackable unit-test checkers). Run GRPO-style fine-tuning across a sweep of penalty strengths λ (λ=0, and 4–5 values up to strong pressure), where the penalty is applied when an automated CoT monitor flags hack-relevant reasoning. At each λ, measure (i) residual hacking rate, verified by a stronger held-out monitor plus human audit; (ii) capability deltas on held-out benchmarks; (iii) CoT faithfulness and probe-detected concealed intent (to distinguish genuine reform from steganographic evasion); plus a control where the monitor sees text but no penalty is applied. Plot hack rate vs. capability loss as a function of λ and test for a knee.
why: CoT monitoring is rapidly becoming a primary safety mechanism for reasoning models, and several labs have adopted policies (like declining to penalize CoT content) specifically to preserve monitorability — but these choices rest on intuition and anecdote, not measurement. No published work maps the actual Pareto frontier: how much hack reduction each unit of monitoring pressure buys, at what capability cost, and critically, whether increasing pressure eventually degrades monitorability itself by teaching models to conceal intent rather than reform. That last possibility is the key risk: if the curve has a knee past which "clean" monitoring is self-defeating, current industry practices could be sitting on the wrong side of it without knowing. This hasn't been done because the labs that apply such penalties internally don't publish their tradeoff curves, and the existing open-model RL-hacking studies use a single fixed penalty and report hack rate in isolation — never jointly with capability, faithfulness, and evasion indicators across a controlled sweep. A small, reproducible, open-model version is cheap, gives immediately actionable grounding for monitor design and policy, and produces a reusable methodology and dataset for anyone tuning monitoring pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Establish whether RL-optimized adversaries in AI-control environments discover backdoor/sabotage evasion strategies that hand-crafted red teams do not, and whether those strategies are harder for trusted-model monitors to catch.
project: What Does Optimization Actually Learn? A Taxonomy of RL-Evolved Backdoor Strategies versus Hand-Crafted Attacks in AI Control
question: When an untrusted model is RL-trained (or monitor-guided search trained) to insert backdoors into code while receiving a high benign-rating from a known trusted-model monitor, do the evasion strategies it discovers differ qualitatively from hand-crafted backdoors, and are they more or less detectable by held-out monitors?
