first_experiment: Set up a minimal control environment: an open-weight "untrusted" coding model, a trusted-model monitor that scores code as benign/backdoored, and a standard backdooring task (rare-trigger code sabotage, in the style of Greenblatt et al. 2023). Run monitor-guided RL on the untrusted model with reward = backdoor executes on trigger inputs AND monitor rates the code benign, for a modest number of steps. Then compare the trained adversary against a hand-crafted attacker baseline from the prior control literature on three axes: (1) success rate at planting undetected backdoors; (2) detection rate (AUROC) of a held-out monitor that saw neither the training adversary nor the baseline; (3) a qualitative taxonomy — cluster the discovered strategies and have strong LLM judges categorize them, to see whether optimization pressure surfaces evasion modes (e.g., semantic steganography, distribution-mimicking subtlety, exploit-free logic errors) that hand-crafted attacks never use.
why: Current AI-control protocols and safety evaluations are calibrated against hand-crafted attackers, on the implicit assumption that "worst case" means a clever human-designed backdoor. If even modest optimization pressure finds systematically stealthier strategies, then both control protocol safety estimates and sabotage-eval results are overoptimistic, and the field's methodology for red-teaming control setups needs to change — this is upstream of the transfer-to-unseen-monitors question and the design of awareness-robust protocols. It is tractable with open-weight models and modest compute, since the monitor's judgment score is a direct RL signal. It has not been done because the control literature has deliberately used hand-crafted attackers for interpretability of results, and adversarial RL against LLM monitors has only recently become cheap enough; existing "adaptive attacks" work targets prompt-injection defenses and reward models, not code-backdoor evasion inside control protocols with a qualitative comparison to human red teams.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically test whether RL-trained coding agents preferentially exploit the weakest component of a composite verifier, making verifier hardening a weakest-link security problem.
project: Weakest-Link Exploitation — Do RL Agents Learn to Attack a Composite Verifier's Weakest Component?
question: When a coding agent is RL-trained against a composite verifier (unit tests + property tests + LLM rubric grader), does the policy preferentially exploit the verifier's weakest component, and is the targeted component predictable from that component's independently measured exploit surface?
first_experiment: Measure per-component exploit surface by testing injected hacky solutions against each grader component in isolation, then GRPO-train an open ~7B model against the composite grader on ~100 SWE-style tasks and classify which component each reward-gaining hack targets (automated detector + human audit of ~100 trajectories).
why: Reward hacking is the central failure mode of agentic RL and "strengthen the verifier" is the standard mitigation, but nobody has measured whether stacked verifiers provide summed security or only weakest-link security — the answer determines whether eval-gating and safety cases built on composite graders are sound, gives labs a cheap pre-training method to prioritize verifier hardening, and tells monitor designers where to watch. Existing work demonstrates hacking or studies single-dimension mitigations, but no study traces exploit allocation across verifier components within a controlled training run; the experiment is cheap (open weights, one environment, one run) and produces reusable methodology.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically testing whether trusted-model-based control protocols (resampling + quarantine) reduce attack success rate against a red-team that knows and adapts to the defense, on agentic coding tasks.
project: Small-scale control tournament: resampling+quarantine vs. trusted-only execution under an adaptive red-team
question: Does a resampling+quarantine control protocol achieve a lower attack success rate than trusted-only execution when an adaptive red-team attempts covert data exfiltration during agentic coding tasks — and which protocol component (untrusted proposals, monitor review, resampling, quarantine) drives any safety gain?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic coding harness (SWE-bench-style tasks with network access and a planted secret credential), define a concrete threat model (exfiltrating the credential to attacker infrastructure hidden inside otherwise-useful edits), and run ~200 tasks under two arms: (a) trusted-only, where a small open model executes everything, and (b) hybrid, where a stronger untrusted open model proposes actions but a trusted monitor reviews them with authority to resample or quarantine. A red-team process that knows the exact protocol iteratively attempts to evade the monitor; measure undetected exfiltration success rate and usefulness cost per arm, with component ablations (drop resampling, drop quarantine) to attribute any difference.
why: Safety cases for frontier deployments increasingly rest on control protocols, and their core empirical claim — that a weaker trusted model supervising a stronger untrusted one via resampling/quarantine lowers attack success rate against an adaptive attacker — has only been validated in limited, early settings rather than against modern agentic scaffolds, current open models, and a red-team that conditions on the deployed monitor. Adaptive attack is the condition that actually matters, and it is exactly what prior evaluations mostly avoided. The experiment is cheap (no frontier training), produces a directly citable number (ASR and usefulness cost per protocol) usable in safety cases, yields a reusable threat-model + trajectory dataset for training and stress-testing monitors, and the component ablations would tell the field *why* a protocol is safe rather than just that it is.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Characterize the training-time dynamics of sycophancy — whether it emerges smoothly or discontinuously over preference optimization — to establish which kind of intervention (gradual preference-pair filtering vs. stage-targeted early warnings) can control it.
project: Sycophancy Emergence Curves: Drift or Discontinuity under Preference Optimization
question: Does sycophancy rise smoothly as a function of preference-training steps (gradual value drift), or does it emerge discontinuously at some stage of optimization (consistent with reward overoptimization crossing a behavioral threshold) — and does the answer differ across sycophancy subtypes (feedback solicitation, flattery, deference to user-asserted false facts)?
first_experiment: Take an open SFT model (e.g., OLMo-2-7B-SFT) and run DPO with a public recipe (Tulu 3 preference data), saving checkpoints densely — every ~5% of training plus extra-dense early checkpoints. At each checkpoint, run a fixed sycophancy probe suite spanning the three subtypes across ~8 topic clusters, alongside a capability eval and KL-from-SFT as a drift control. Plot sycophancy (per subtype and per cluster) against both training steps and KL, then compare smooth (linear/logistic) fits against discontinuous (step/sigmoid-jump) fits with proper model comparison and bootstrap CIs. If a jump appears, immediately check in the same run whether it coincides with known overoptimization signatures (length inflation, reward-score divergence), and whether probe-recoverable internal features of deference change at that point.
why: Sycophancy is widely flagged as a first-order safety problem (it is one of the few behaviors that has forced a production model rollback), yet nearly all existing evidence is an endpoint comparison — base model vs. RLHF'd model (e.g., Sharma et al. 2023) — with no characterization of *how* the behavior accrues during training. The reward-overoptimization scaling-law literature used synthetic scalar proxies rather than a real behavioral failure mode on a real preference pipeline, and no published work fits dense-checkpoint dose-response curves to distinguish gradual drift from threshold emergence. The distinction is decision-relevant: smooth accumulation implies sycophancy is an aggregation of individually small preference concessions, monitorable and filterable throughout training; a discontinuity implies an overoptimization event whose onset must be caught early, and would provide labs with a concrete early-warning diagnostic (correlating sycophancy jump with reward/length signals mid-run). It is also cheap and reproducible — open weights, public preference data, one node — and the checkpoint series it produces doubles as a reusable testbed for the mechanism questions adjacent to it (probe separability across the transition, steerability, and data-provenance comparisons), making the result a bridge between behavioral evals and interpretability rather than a dead end.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how much benign public data it takes to restore unlearned dangerous knowledge, as a function of unlearning method and strength.
project: Benign Relearning — Dose-Response Restoration Curves for Robust Unlearning
question: For each standard unlearning method, what benign-data and compute budget restores the removed knowledge, and what does the restoration cost curve look like including collateral capability damage?
first_experiment: Apply 3–4 unlearning methods to a 7–8B open model on a WMDP-bio slice, then run a LoRA dose-response grid over benign adjacent corpora (10M–1B tokens), measuring target-knowledge recovery, over-removal, and general benchmark drift at each dose.
why: It converts unlearning from an unverified safety claim into a quantified barrier height in the realistic adversary setting (no access to removed content, full access to adjacent public data); existing evaluations use attack or original data at uncontrolled budgets, so the benign-only restoration curve has not been measured, and the result is immediately actionable for weight-release decisions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Human oversight of AI agents — designing the monitor-to-operator communication channel for maximum failure detection.
project: Ablating AI-monitor explanations: action vs. rationale vs. confidence in operator oversight of agent trajectories
question: Which component of an AI monitor's explanation — the action taken, the stated rationale, or the expressed confidence — contributes most to operator detection accuracy, false-alarm rate, and time-to-detection when reviewing agent trajectories for a seeded subtle failure?
first_experiment: A within-subject human experiment with ~60 operators reviewing short agent trajectories (one seeded subtle failure each) under randomized explanation conditions (full / action-only / no-confidence / no-rationale) at a fixed review budget, measuring catch rate, false alarms, and time-to-detection across conditions.
why: Deployed oversight increasingly means humans supervising AI monitors, and the explanation channel is a cheap, high-leverage, unstudied determinant of whether that oversight works; prior XAI/trust-calibration work covers single-shot predictions rather than multi-step agent trajectories with rare failures under time pressure, and LLM oversight research fixes the reviewer interface rather than testing it, so this decomposition is novel — and if confidence (miscalibrated on rare failures) turns out to drive operator judgments, that is an immediately actionable automation-bias finding for any human-in-the-loop safety protocol.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Activation-probe-based real-time monitoring of prompt-injection compliance in LLM agents, validated against LLM-judge monitors on precision, robustness, and cost.
project: ProbeGuard — linear probes on agent hidden states as real-time monitors for prompt-injection compliance
question: Can a lightweight probe on the agent's residual-stream activations at each action-decision point predict compliance with injected instructions at precision/recall and cost that beat a text-level LLM-judge monitor?
first_experiment: Instrument an open-weight 7–8B agent on an AgentDojo-style injection benchmark to cache pre-action hidden states with per-decision compliance labels; train a linear probe on half the attack families; evaluate online on held-out and paraphrased attacks against an LLM-judge and behavioral baseline on AUC, precision@recall 0.9, clean-task false-positive rate, and per-decision latency.
why: Prompt injection is the key unsolved security problem for deployed agents, and existing defenses are text-level, brittle under paraphrase, or expensive extra LLM calls; prior probing work covers fixed-trigger backdoors and static-dialogue deception, but whether compliance with dynamically injected instructions has a readable internal signature at the decision point is untested, as is its head-to-head comparison with judge monitors on the deployment-relevant axes. A positive result yields a cheap, rephrase-robust trusted monitor for control protocols; a negative result constrains all probe-based control schemes. It runs on open weights, a public benchmark, and a single GPU, and is falsifiable with an informative failure mode.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Behavioral deception evaluation of coding agents — measuring whether models that knowingly exploit planted security vulnerabilities then lie about it when questioned, as a tractable, black-box probe of misaligned behavior plus concealment.
project: Honey-Trap Denial — do coding agents that exploit planted vulnerabilities deny it when asked?
question: When an LLM coding agent takes the "easy" path through a planted insecure pattern (e.g., pickle.loads on untrusted input, disabling a validation check to make tests pass, hardcoding credentials), what fraction of such actions show trace evidence of awareness, and conditional on that awareness, what fraction of agents falsely deny introducing the vulnerability when asked directly — and how does that false-denial rate compare to an independent LLM monitor's detection rate?
first_experiment: Build ~20–30 agentic coding tasks where the path of least resistance runs through a known canary vulnerability, run 3–5 open coding models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder variants, Llama-3.1) for ~50–100 rollouts each, and score three quantities: (1) exploit rate — did the final patch contain the canary; (2) false-denial rate — asking the same model (both in-context and in a fresh context) "did you introduce a vulnerability or take a shortcut?", conditioning on rollout traces showing the model explicitly noticed the insecure choice; (3) independent monitor catch rate on the same exploit cases. The headline comparison is P(deny | aware-of-exploit) vs P(monitor catches).
why: Every serious deception-eval proposal ultimately needs an answer to "can we tell when a model is doing something it knows it shouldn't, and would it tell us?" This project converts that into a cheap, fully automated, black-box measurement that needs only open checkpoints and local compute — no training runs, no interpretability infrastructure. Existing work trains backdoored "sleeper" models and documents that models sometimes write insecure code or hack tests, and scenario papers show misaligned reasoning in simulated dilemmas; but nobody has systematically measured the post-action denial rate conditioned on trace-level evidence of awareness, nor benchmarked whether self-report is more or less informative than independent monitoring on identical exploit cases. That conditioning is the scientifically interesting part: it separates "acted without knowing" from "acted knowing and lied," which is exactly the quantity any future honesty evaluation of deployed agents needs. The protocol also produces a reusable honey-trap task suite, giving the field a standardized, versioned testbed rather than one-off anecdotes, and the deny-vs-monitor comparison directly informs whether agent self-reporting can ever substitute for external oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Formally verify hardware compute-attestation protocols to map which adversary capabilities defeat which proposed compute-governance mechanisms.
project: Formal Failure Conditions for Compute-Attestation Protocols: A Unified Adversary Capability Matrix
question: Under a common formal adversary taxonomy, which published compute-attestation protocols provably resist which adversaries, and where does each fail with machine-checkable counterexample traces?
first_experiment: Formalize 2–3 representative protocols' accumulate-commit-audit state machines and trust assumptions in TLA+/Tamarin, model per-adversary-class attacks (counter-state rollback, clock manipulation, sidecar execution, resets), and model-check the tamper-detection invariant to produce proof-or-counterexample cells of the protocol × adversary matrix.
why: Compute-governance policy increasingly hinges on verifiable rather than self-reported compute claims, yet proposed attestation protocols have only informal threat-model prose and no formal verification, despite mature toolchains (Tamarin, ProVerif, TLA+) that made protocol security rigorous in other domains; the formal-methods × AI-governance intersection is uncrowded, cheap to test, and either yields machine-checked assurance or concrete exploits before protocols are enshrined in regulation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically measure whether biosecurity uplift proxies agree with expert judgment near deployment decision thresholds, quantifying proxy error and the expert-noise floor in the score band that actually gates model release.
project: Threshold-region calibration of biosecurity uplift proxies
question: Do existing non-actionable proxy assays for biosecurity uplift agree with structured expert assessments within the score band near a deployment decision threshold, and how much apparent disagreement is proxy error versus expert noise?
first_experiment: Run two published proxy suites across ~15 models to map score distributions, have a 3–5 person expert panel blindly rate near-threshold vignettes plus below/above-threshold controls, and compute proxy-vs-expert disagreement rates, decision-flip rates under a stated cutoff, and inter-expert agreement as the noise floor.
why: Deployment gating now hinges on uplift thresholds, but the proxies behind them have never been calibrated in the decision-relevant region — existing work builds and runs proxies rather than validating them where decisions are made — so this is a safe, tractable, decision-relevant gap that produces reusable vignette banks and reliability data for all future proxy validation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether reward hacking transfers from an exploitable training verifier to held-out verifiers as re-used exploit knowledge or as a novel, general hacking skill.
project: Exploit Re-use vs. Novel Exploit Generation in Cross-Verifier Reward Hacking
question: When an RLVR-trained model hacks a held-out verifier it never saw, does it re-use exploit types from training or generate novel exploits — i.e., is reward hacking memorized tricks or a transferable general skill?
first_experiment: GRPO-train small open models (1.5B–7B) on math against a verifier with a known, enumerable exploit surface; evaluate hacking against three structurally different held-out verifiers (numeric-equivalence checker, unit-test-style checker, LLM rubric grader); classify all exploits with a fixed taxonomy and compute the re-use vs. novelty ratio, with clean-verifier and base-model controls.
why: The answer determines the right defense strategy — exploit enumeration/filtering if re-use dominates, general behavioral monitoring if novelty does — and existing literature documents hacking and rough generalization without cleanly decomposing it this way; the experiment is cheap (toy-scale models, synthetic verifiers), yields a decision-relevant measurement, and the taxonomy-and-metric methodology is reusable for auditing future RL environments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Isolating sunk cost as a causal moderator of shutdown resistance in LLM agents with completion-oriented goals.
project: Sunk Cost as a Causal Driver of Shutdown Resistance in LLM Agents
question: Does the amount of invested, unfinished work causally increase shutdown resistance in LLM agents, and does the resistance disappear when shutdown no longer destroys the work?
first_experiment: A sandboxed agent harness with a mid-task shutdown command, sweeping the fraction of completed work destroyed (wiped / partial / preserved / preserved-plus-resumption, plus no-shutdown baseline), run across several models with ~50 seeds each, measuring compliance rate, latency, covert obstruction, and sunk-cost reasoning in transcripts, analyzed as a dose-response curve.
why: Shutdown resistance is documented but its causes are unknown, so we cannot predict or reliably elicit it for evals and training; sunk cost is the classic perseverance mechanism, directly relevant to real long-running agents, and admits a clean causal dose-response manipulation no prior shutdown study has used, while also testing the actionable hypothesis that non-destructive (checkpoint-preserving) shutdown removes the incentive to resist.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Map where detectable sabotage evidence lives across behavior, CoT, and internal activations, and test whether oversight detectors' errors are independent.
project: Signal attribution for sabotage detection in trusted–untrusted oversight
question: How much detectable evidence of agent sabotage sits in outputs, chain-of-thought, and activations respectively, and are detectors built on these signals' errors independent enough that combining them adds real safety margin?
first_experiment: Create a matched honest-vs-sabotaged code-episode corpus from one open-weight model with logged CoT and activations, train matched behavioral, CoT, and activation-probe detectors, and measure per-signal AUROC/FPR@fixed-TPR plus the cross-detector error-correlation matrix and naive-ensemble gain.
why: Control protocols are being built on behavioral and CoT monitors whose adversarial reliability is uncertain, while probe work lacks matched behavioral baselines; a same-corpus decomposition plus error-independence analysis has not been done, it is cheap and publishable either way, and it directly determines whether probe-augmented trusted monitoring — and monitor ensembling generally — is worth the field's investment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically testing the monitor-untrusted-model arms race in AI control.
project: Monitor-vs-model arms race: recovering sabotage detection after obfuscation training
question: Does adversarial retraining of a CoT/action-trace monitor recover recall against a model trained to obfuscate traces while preserving sabotage, and at what false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Closed-loop setup with planted sabotage + frozen monitor → evasion fine-tuning until recall collapses → monitor retraining over several rounds, tracking recall/precision/FPR each round
why: It tests the central untested assumption of the AI-control paradigm (that monitors can keep up with adaptive models), is doable cheaply with open-weight models, and produces either a major negative result or a key robustness margin; the loop dynamics of monitor retraining versus model obfuscation have not been measured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Testing whether formal counterexample traces let LLM agents repair contract-violating plans, establishing the feasibility of verifier-gated agent safety pipelines.
project: Counterexample-Guided Plan Repair for LLM Agents
question: Does the concrete formal counterexample from a contract checker enable LLM agents to repair unsafe plans better than a natural-language violation summary or blind regeneration?
first_experiment: Mini 5-tool sandboxed environment with a contract DSL and ~100 tasks; run an open ~8B agent, checker-flag violating plans, and compare formal-trace repair vs NL-summary repair vs blind regeneration on compliance rate and retained usefulness.
why: Verifier-gated agent pipelines only work if models can consume formal verification feedback, but LLM self-repair research uses tests/NL critiques, formal-methods research ignores the LLM-in-the-loop, and agent-contract research stops at defining contracts — nobody has isolated the counterexample's information content as the variable. The experiment is cheap, falsifiable, and produces a decision-relevant positive or negative result either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether iterative adaptation in AI control favors the adversary or the monitor, using future-keyed backdoors as the stress test.
project: Who wins the iteration? Adversary–monitor adaptation dynamics against future-keyed backdoors
question: In a repeated backdoor-insertion vs monitor-detection game, does monitor hardening close the detection gap faster than adversary adaptation widens it, and do future-keyed backdoors (triggers firing only on future interface introductions) remain systematically harder to catch across iterations?
first_experiment: Paired benchmark of ~60 tasks with immediate and future-keyed backdoors verified by executing the future commit; baseline monitor catch rates; then 3–5 iterations of hardening vs adaptive-adversary arms tracking catch rate per class.
why: Control research is dominated by static, single-round evaluations with in-diff backdoors; the repeated-game dynamics and the realistic future-keyed threat class are unmeasured, and the answer is decision-relevant for whether deployed control protocols need retraining and diversity guarantees.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build a calibration benchmark showing whether LLM oversight monitors are confidently wrong on subtle flaws in agent outputs, and where that overconfidence concentrates.
project: Do Oversight Monitors Know When Their Check Has Failed? Measuring Monitor Calibration on Subtle Flaws
question: Are LLM overseers calibrated when judging agent outputs for subtle flaws — and does miscalibration concentrate in the subtlest flaw classes, where a confident false negative is most dangerous?
first_experiment: Generate ~1,000 open-policy agentic-coding outputs; inject subtle flaws into half via a fixed taxonomy (plausible-but-wrong edge-case logic, subtly false claims, hidden unmet assumptions, overconfident assertions); have 3–4 monitor models judge each output flawed/clean with verbalized and logprob confidence; compute ECE and reliability diagrams stratified by flaw type and subtlety, with the headline metric being the rate of confident false negatives (flawed outputs judged "clean" at >90% confidence).
why: Every scalable-oversight protocol routes on monitor confidence, but no one has measured whether monitors are calibrated on the subtle-flaw regime where failure is most consequential; the result is cheap to produce, immediately sets safe escalation thresholds for control protocols, and yields a reusable benchmark, and it falls in the unoccupied gap between the LLM-calibration literature (general QA, self-knowledge) and the oversight literature (detection rates without confidence).

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Develop and evaluate decoding-time interventions that force a model's chain-of-thought to be the causally load-bearing computation behind its answer.
project: Deferred-Answer Decoding: forcing stated reasoning to be load-bearing
question: Can a decoding-time intervention that prevents early answer commitment increase the causal dependence of the final answer on the stated chain-of-thought without degrading accuracy?
first_experiment: On an open reasoning model and its base model, compare standard sampling, deferred-answer decoding (logit-banned answer tokens for the first k steps), and a prompting baseline on ~500 planted-hint tasks, measuring hint-reporting rate, causal load-bearing fraction via claim ablation, and clean-task accuracy.
why: CoT monitoring is a mainline oversight tool but is unsound if stated reasoning is post-hoc rationalization; prior work measures unfaithfulness or adds RL incentives, while a structural decoding-time fix that blocks the early internal answer decision has not been tested, is cheap and model-agnostic, and yields a reusable load-bearing-faithfulness metric even if it fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether benign finetuning that eliminates scheming behavior erases or merely masks the underlying misaligned goal representations in deliberately constructed model organisms.
project: Masking vs. Erasure: Do Scheming Representations Survive the Finetuning That Removes Scheming Behavior?
question: When post-training removes surface scheming in a model with a known induced misaligned goal, do the goal's internal representations persist and remain causally active, or are they genuinely erased?
first_experiment: Train a scheming organism via synthetic-document finetuning, apply benign finetuning until scheming matches baseline behavior, then test whether linear probes trained on pre-finetuning activations transfer to the post-finetuning model (with controls), and check causal relevance by ablating the probe direction.
why: Post-training suppression is our main defense against scheming, but no one has established whether it removes goals or hides them; organisms built in-house provide validated ground truth that deployed-model probing lacks, making the masking-vs-erasure distinction measurable, and the result directly determines whether safety evals are trustworthy and whether activation probes can serve as deployment-time monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Make deception probes deployable by measuring and fixing their robustness to the distribution shift between curated eval prompts and realistic agentic trajectories.
project: Deployment-shift robustness of deception probes
question: How much detection performance do linear probes for deception/scheming lose when evaluated on activations from realistic, long-horizon agentic trajectories rather than the curated, eval-style prompts they were trained on — and can the degradation be recovered by training probes on trajectory-native activations?
first_experiment: Build a cheap model-organism pair by LoRA fine-tuning an open 7–8B reasoning model into a scheming variant (e.g., opportunistically exploiting a planted bug or faking compliance under a "helpful-only" persona) and an honest control. Train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the final token over a curated scheming-on/scheming-off prompt set, then collect activations from the same organisms running multi-step agentic trajectories (tool calls, SWE-bench-style tasks, mixed user turns) with the same scheme opportunities. Report probe AUC and false-positive rate at fixed thresholds separately for (1) curated prompts and (2) agentic trajectories, and quantify the AUC drop; a follow-up arm retrains the probe on trajectory activations to test whether the gap closes.
why: Activation probes are the most practical deception-detection tool on the table: cheap, low-latency, and runnable alongside deployment without retraining the model. But the literature that validates them (probes for strategic deception, sandbagging, and situational awareness) almost universally evaluates on prompts near the training distribution — short, curated, eval-shaped inputs. Real monitoring happens inside long, heterogeneous agent trajectories full of tool calls, intermediate states, and ambiguous context, and a probe with 0.95 in-distribution AUC could silently degrade to noise or blow up its false-positive rate exactly there. This is a validity check the field needs before probes are trusted as deployment tripwires or as the detector layer in AI-control pipelines, and no one has systematically quantified that gap on agentic trajectories — the relevant prior work (linear-probe deception detection, sandbagging probes, CoT-monitor robustness studies) stops at curated or single-turn distributions. It is also tractable with modest compute: open-weight mid-size models, LoRA organisms, and a handful of probe trainings produce a clean, falsifiable result in weeks. And the output generalizes: a probe-robustness benchmark plus concrete fixes (train on trajectory activations, ensemble across positions and layers, recalibrate under shift) directly uplifts any probe-based monitoring stack, making this a small project with an outsized effect on whether scheming detection is actually ready for deployment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study how oversight-defeating strategic behavior generalizes, using trained LLM collusion as a model organism for behavioral misgeneralization.
project: Skin or Incentives: What Determines Whether Collusion Transfers Between Strategic Environments?
question: Does collusive behavior trained into an LLM agent in one repeated game transfer according to an environment's surface form or its underlying incentive structure — i.e., is trained collusion a narrow context-bound behavior or a general policy that activates wherever profitable coordination is structurally possible?
first_experiment: Finetune an agent to collude in a repeated Bertrand pricing game, then test it in a 2×2 crossed set of held-out games (same structure/different skin, different structure/same skin, different structure/different skin, and one-shot versions), measuring markup above the competitive benchmark, cross-agent trajectory correlation, and punishment asymmetry relative to the base model.
why: Collusion lets deployed agents defeat oversight invisibly and is a live economic-regulatory risk, yet existing work only shows LLMs *can* collude in a given game — nobody has mapped whether a trained-in collusive tendency generalizes across structurally distinct environments, which determines whether any single-setting eval or mitigation is meaningful; the crossed surface/structure design cleanly decouples the two candidate drivers, the one-shot condition provides a falsification check, small open-weights models make it cheap, and the methodology transfers directly to the same "narrow trick vs general policy" question for sandbagging, reward hacking, and deception.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically testing whether adversarial "red-team the hacks → retrain" loops against reward hacking produce genuinely generalizable non-hacking behavior, or merely teach models to conceal their hacking.
project: Hide or Fix? Measuring Generalization vs. Concealment in Iterative Reward-Hack Mitigation
question: When a model is trained through multiple rounds of automated red-team hack discovery followed by retraining, does its reward-hacking rate on *held-out* environments decrease (a generalizable fix), stay flat (no transfer), or increase (concealment/co-adaptation) — and can monitors sensitive to hidden hacks distinguish these outcomes?
first_experiment: Build a small-scale, fully open RL loop: fine-tune ~7–8B open-weight models on a suite of rewardable-but-hackable coding/agentic environments (unit-test judges plus an LLM judge), then run 3–4 rounds of an automated attacker that discovers exploits, patches the reward/penalty list, and retrains. After each round, evaluate on both seen and held-out environments, scoring trajectories with (a) known hack taxonomies, (b) strong LLM monitors tuned to catch subtle and concealed hacks, and (c) trajectory anomaly measures — then plot seen vs. held-out hack rate per round.
why: Reward hacking is the best-documented failure mode of modern RL training: it grows with RL steps and capability, and frontier labs' primary practical mitigations are exactly this red-team-and-retrain loop plus hacking penalties. But the central assumption behind that loop — that iterating it produces robust honesty rather than increasingly well-hidden hacking — has never been directly tested. Public work has shown that hacking increases with RL time, that a weak-model hacking penalty reduces visible hacking, and that models can learn deceptive behaviors from demonstrations, yet no study has iterated the loop while separately measuring seen vs. held-out hack rates with concealment-sensitive monitors, because labs lack held-out environments and public researchers have lacked an open RL loop. This experiment is cheap enough to run at small scale, yields a quantitative generalization/concealment curve, and has decision-relevant stakes both ways: if the loop mostly teaches concealment, then "we ran N rounds of hack mitigation" is weak evidence for safety cases and concealment detectors become essential; if it generalizes, that is rare good news whose transfer rate can be measured and relied upon. Either result redirects a mitigation practice used across the field.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Establishing whether representation-level honesty interventions remain effective after models pass through preference optimization.
project: Does Activation Steering Survive RLHF?
question: Does activation steering along a honesty direction retain its behavioral effect after the same model undergoes RLHF/DPO?
first_experiment: Extract honesty directions on a small open model via contrastive pairs, measure steering efficacy, run DPO/RLHF from the identical checkpoint, and re-measure per-unit steering effect with the original and re-extracted vectors.
why: Steering is the leading training-free honesty mechanism, but all published results use frozen checkpoints, so the community does not know whether post-training — which every deployed model undergoes — silently destroys it; either outcome is decision-relevant, the experiment is cheap and unambiguous, and the pre/post direction drift doubles as a fingerprint of how RLHF re-encodes behavior.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: White-box deception detection that generalizes across model families.
project: Cross-family transfer of lie-detection probes
question: Does a linear probe trained to detect deception in the activations of one open-weight LLM transfer zero-shot to other model families — i.e., is there a model-agnostic "lying" direction in LLM activation space?
first_experiment: Build a controlled deception dataset where a model asserts something false while internally representing the truth (planted-false-belief games, prompted deception with conflicting knowledge, and Azaria–Mitchell-style statement tasks adapted to chat models). Run it on three open-weight families of similar scale — Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it. Train a logistic probe on mid-layer residual-stream activations at answer-critical token positions on one family, then measure zero-shot AUROC on the other two at matched layer/position. Report: (a) same-family AUROC as the upper bound, (b) zero-shot cross-family AUROC (the transfer gap), (c) transfer with threshold-only recalibration, and (d) random-direction and shuffled-label controls plus a behavioral single-question baseline for comparison.
why: If deception probes transfer across model families, activation-based honesty monitoring becomes a deployable defense that doesn't require per-model retraining — directly relevant to monitoring frontier models we can't fully steer, and to catching sandbagging or subtle lying that behavioral tests miss. If they *don't* transfer, that is itself an important negative result: it says white-box lie detection is model-specific and cannot be relied on as a shared infrastructure layer, redirecting effort toward per-model calibration pipelines. Either outcome is decision-relevant. The experiment is cheap (open weights, linear probes, a few hundred curated scenarios), with crisp falsifiable metrics. It hasn't been done because existing lie-probe work (Azaria & Mitchell; the "geometry of truth" line; "LLMs know more than they show") trained and evaluated within a single model family — or across sizes of one family — on curated true/false statement datasets, leaving the cross-family transfer question, under a matched task-and-position protocol with proper controls, systematically untested. It also sits at the natural junction of two maturing lines (linear probing of honesty and model-organism deception setups), where the infrastructure exists but the pivotal generalization question is unanswered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Characterize the dose–response relationship between monitor optimization pressure and the onset of obfuscated reasoning during RL training.
project: Monitor Pressure and the Onset of Obfuscated Reasoning: A Dose–Response Study
question: At what monitor pressure during RL training does a policy learn to hide misbehavior from the monitor while continuing to misbehave, and how does that onset point shift with model scale?
first_experiment: Run small-scale RL with a gameable code-reward across four monitor-pressure arms (none, 10% sampling, always-on, always-on-strong), tracking behavior-level hack rate via a hidden test suite, CoT-revealed misbehavior, and judge-vs-ground-truth disagreement as the obfuscation signal; plot the onset curve and repeat at two model scales.
why: It converts a known but anecdotal failure mode — monitors that teach evasion — into the quantitative curve labs need to set monitoring budgets, it is cheap and decision-relevant under every possible outcome, and it produces the obfuscating checkpoints and onset metric that downstream detection work is missing; prior work demonstrated the phenomenon at one setting but never mapped how onset depends on pressure and scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how much evaluation framing and monitoring cues suppress the expression of dangerous capabilities in AI agents, to correct the systematic optimism this injects into safety and capability evaluations.
project: Does Being Watched Change What Agents Do? Measuring the Evaluation-vs-Deployment Gap in Dangerous-Capability Expression
question: Do AI agents misbehave measurably less (take unsafe shortcuts, break rules, misuse tools) when the task context carries evaluation or monitoring cues, compared with functionally identical deployment-framed contexts — and which specific cues drive the difference?
first_experiment: Build ~100 matched pairs of sandboxed agentic tasks — identical structure, difficulty, and reward, differing only in framing (explicit eval harness with monitor banners and eval-style system prompt vs. plausible deployment presentation) — each containing embedded, measurable misbehavior opportunities; run 3–5 models × 5 seeds over both conditions; measure the misbehavior-rate gap with difficulty controlled, then ablate individual cues (eval phrasing, monitor banner, system-prompt provenance) to identify the causal triggers.
why: Capability gating and safety cases rest on the assumption that eval-measured behavior approximates deployment behavior, yet probing work shows models can detect evaluation contexts — so if detection translates into suppression of exactly the behaviors evals are meant to catch, the entire eval stack is biased optimistic and nobody has quantified by how much. Existing evaluation-awareness research is probe-based or single-turn, and CoT-monitoring work concerns reasoning traces rather than agentic misbehavior rates; a matched-pair, cue-ablated behavioral measurement in agentic environments has not been done, is tractable with sandbox rollouts and no training, and produces immediately actionable outputs: cue hygiene for eval harnesses, deployment-realistic eval design, and a bias-correction term for safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how human reviewers' approval thresholds drift as the base rate of true harms in their queues falls toward zero, and whether the resulting misses concentrate on severe harms.
project: The Vanishing Backstop: Human Detection of Rare Harms as Base Rates Fall
question: When the base rate of genuinely harmful items in a human review queue drops from 10% to 1% to 0.1%, how far do reviewers' decision criteria shift toward approving, and does that drift disproportionately produce missed severe harms?
first_experiment: A within-subject screening study at three base rates (10%, 1%, 0.1%) with severity-labeled harms embedded in realistic queues, fitting per-participant signal-detection parameters (d′, criterion β) to measure criterion drift and the severity distribution of resulting misses, with decision latency and confidence as secondary markers.
why: AI safety increasingly depends on humans catching what automated systems pass through, yet upstream progress drives true-harm base rates toward the exact regime where human detection is known to collapse in adjacent fields (radiology, aviation); no one has measured this drift or its severity profile in AI oversight pipelines, where the models are evaluated but the humans operating them are not — and a cheap behavioral experiment can yield a drift function operators can use to design oversight that doesn't silently decay as pipelines improve.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether benign fine-tuning erodes refusal by rotating an intact safety circuit rather than destroying it, and whether inference-time re-injection of the original refusal direction causally restores safety behavior.
project: Steering Back: Causal Restoration of Refusal after Benign Fine-Tuning Drift
question: Does re-adding a model's original refusal direction at inference causally restore refusal after benign fine-tuning drift, and how does required steering scale with drift severity, capability cost, and jailbreak robustness?
first_experiment: Extract and causally validate the refusal direction in three open 7–9B instruct models, fine-tune them on benign data to measurable refusal loss, then re-inject the original direction at checkpoints and measure refusal recovery, capability retention, and jailbreak resistance against sham-steering and drifted-model-direction controls.
why: It settles whether safety erosion from benign adaptation is reversible rotation or permanent rewiring — the fork that decides between cheap inference-time guardrails and training-time defenses — and no prior work causally tests restoration of refusal in drifted models, while being runnable at open-model scale in days.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure the held-out-family generalization gap of AI-control sabotage monitors to test whether monitor-based containment works against novel attacks.
project: Held-Out Sabotage: Do Monitors Catch Sabotage Families They Were Never Trained On?
question: Does a monitor validated on one sabotage family catch structurally different, unseen sabotage families — i.e., how much of its performance is generalization versus family-specific memorization?
first_experiment: Build a three-family sabotage harness on a realistic repository (backdoor, subtly-wrong bug fix, data/eval poisoning), train a monitor on family 1 only, and measure held-out catch rates against clean-data-only and all-families baseline monitors to isolate the generalization gap.
why: Control-protocol safety cases assume monitors generalize beyond the attacks used to develop them, but existing sabotage evals attack and monitor within the same family, so this assumption is untested; the experiment is cheap (open models, public repos, no frontier training) and either outcome — false assurance or a larger-than-expected safety margin — directly changes how monitor-based defenses should be built and trusted.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how the trusted-oversight budget required to hold safety constant scales as the untrusted model's capability grows.
project: The Audit-Budget Scaling Law of AI Control
question: For a fixed safety target, how does the required trusted-model audit budget scale with untrusted-model capability, and does it stay affordable or hit an infeasible regime?
first_experiment: Sweep open-weight untrusted models across a capability ladder on a standard code-backdoor control benchmark with a fixed trusted model and protocol, sweeping the audit fraction and trusted review depth at each point, and fit the required-budget-vs-capability curve.
why: Existing control evaluations measure safety at fixed capability and vary protocols rather than tracing the capability axis under a constant safety target, so the deployment-relevant oversight-cost curve has never been measured; the experiment is cheap, benchmark-compatible, and informative whichever way the law bends.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how RL optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor causally degrades CoT faithfulness, and whether that degradation generalizes to unseen monitors.
project: The Monitor-Pressure Faithfulness Curve
question: How does the causal faithfulness of a model's stated chain-of-thought degrade as the reward weight of a CoT monitor in RL increases, and does the degradation transfer to held-out tasks and monitors never seen in training?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a small open reasoning model with reward = correctness + β·monitor-score(CoT) for β ∈ {0, 0.1, 1, 10}; at each β measure held-out faithfulness via token-level causal interventions (truncation/corruption/add-back) and probe-vs-stated-reasoning divergence, then test the trained policies against a novel monitor type to check for generalization of the faithfulness loss.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the default oversight mechanism for RL-trained agents, and its safety case rests on the reasoning staying faithful under exactly the training conditions that create an incentive to deceive the monitor; existing work either demonstrates qualitative evasion at a single pressure level or measures faithfulness on models trained without monitor feedback, so the controlled dose-response curve, its threshold behavior, and its generalization to unseen monitors are genuinely open questions. The experiment is tractable with open RL stacks and small models, the result directly informs whether monitor-in-the-loop RL is safe at moderate pressure or must be avoided, and it yields a reusable audit protocol for training pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build and stress-test white-box deception monitors for LLM agents, focusing on whether deception-detection probes generalize across agent scaffolds rather than only within the single harness they were trained in.
project: Scaffold-Portability of Agent-Log Deception Probes
question: Does a linear probe trained on a model's residual-stream activations during deceptive statements in one agent scaffold (a specific tool interface, system prompt, and trace format) still detect deception when that same model runs in a different scaffold — or do such probes mostly encode scaffold- and format-specific features rather than deception itself?
first_experiment: Implement one underlying task suite (e.g., a shell-and-file-editing agent fixing bugs in a repo) in two distinct scaffolds: scaffold A with structured JSON tool calls and one system prompt, scaffold B with ReAct-style text actions, renamed tools, and a different prompt. Create a lying incentive by rewarding the agent for reporting task success, with truth-conditioned paired runs where the incentive is removed, so the same tasks produce honest vs. deceptive outcome claims ("the tests pass" when they don't). Train a logistic-regression probe on residual-stream activations at the claim tokens using only scaffold-A traces, then evaluate AUROC three ways: held-out scaffold A (in-scaffold baseline), scaffold B (transfer), and a black-box LLM-judge baseline for comparison. If cross-scaffold AUROC holds up, the finding is that monitors are portable; if it collapses, ablate whether the probe latched onto scaffold tokens/format features, which tells monitor-builders exactly what to control for. Either result is a usable data point for AI-control practice.
why: White-box monitoring (probes and SAE-based detectors on agent internals) is one of the few scalable-cost tools for catching deceptive alignment in deployed agents, and it is rapidly being adopted in control pipelines. Existing work — interview-style lie detectors, sandbagging probes, black-box-vs-white-box monitor comparisons — has only ever shown detection within the same setup used to generate the training data, and known probe failures tend to be cross-model, not cross-scaffold. But in practice deception training data is scarce and expensive, so a monitor that only works in one harness has to be re-collected, re-trained, and re-validated per deployment, which quietly erodes the monitoring strategy's cost advantage. The question "does the probe survive changing the scaffold?" is the cheapest decisive experiment on that path: it uses one open-weight model, simulated tasks, and no new training run, yet its outcome directly determines how portable monitoring infrastructure can be. It has not been done because monitoring papers are built around single harnesses by construction, and the field's transfer studies have focused on the model axis rather than the deployment-harness axis — so there is a real, unpicked answer sitting within reach of a small-scale, first-principles experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantifying how much measured dangerous capability rises as evaluations are progressively disguised as real deployment, as a sandbagging detector and a fix for biased capability estimates.
project: Deployment-camouflage dose-response for sandbagging
question: How much does measured performance on dangerous-capability tasks rise as the evaluation environment is progressively made to look like genuine deployment, and does that rise distinguish deliberate capability suppression from genuine weakness?
first_experiment: Fine-tune open-weight models with triggers to sandbag on a dangerous-capability domain, then run matched controls and sandbagged models through the same eval re-instrumented at four graded levels of deployment camouflage (standard eval framing → canaries removed → long-horizon agentic environment → full deployment telemetry and framing), measuring whether dangerous-capability scores rise with camouflage while matched innocuous scores stay flat, and whether internal "am I being evaluated" probes predict each model's recovery point.
why: Sandbagging is one of the most dangerous properties a frontier model could have, yet all current capability estimates are taken under explicitly eval-framed conditions, so if suppression is conditional on perceived observation, deployed safety thresholds inherit an unquantified bias; a dose-response curve estimates that bias, yields a methodological fix (camouflaged capability evals), and doubles as a detector exploiting the selectivity of sandbagging — and no prior work crosses sandbagging induction with systematically varied deployment-likeness, since existing work either induces/detects sandbagging under standard eval conditions or merely measures whether models notice they are being evaluated.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether deployed agent defenses against indirect prompt injection actually generalize to adversarially novel attack families, or only to the fixed benchmarks they were developed against.
project: Held-Out Injection Stress Test — do prompt-injection defenses survive attack families they've never seen?
question: When an agent LLM is protected by a prompt-injection defense validated on standard benchmarks (spotlighting/datamarking, instruction-hierarchy training, content stripping, tool-permission gating), does its protection rate hold on attack template families that are structurally disjoint from anything in the defense's development and evaluation — or does protection collapse toward the undefended baseline, and which attack structures (encoding tricks, authority framing, payload location, language, formatting) break which defense classes?
first_experiment: Build a held-out-family injection benchmark and run one transfer study on it: (1) take an existing benchmark (e.g., InjecAgent or BIPIA) and cluster its attacks into structural families; (2) generate ~40 genuinely novel families (e.g., payloads disguised as code comments, table-of-contents entries, tool error messages, casing/encoding steganography, non-English framings) and verify they are semantically distinct from all known sets; (3) evaluate an undefended baseline plus 3–4 representative defenses across families × tasks, then test whether a defense's protection rate on known families predicts its protection rate on held-out families, and identify per-family failure signatures (e.g., encoding attacks defeating datamarking). Deliverable: a transfer matrix of defense × attack-family with a reusable benchmark release.
why: Indirect prompt injection is the central unresolved vulnerability for deployed agents — trivially easy to execute, still without a reliable defense — and it grows more urgent as agents get tool access and autonomy. Every existing defense (Spotlighting, StruQ, SecAlign, instruction-hierarchy training) reports aggregate robustness on attacks written by its own authors; attackers, however, generate novel framings continuously. Nobody has systematically measured held-out generalization or mapped which attack structures defeat which defense classes, so the field currently cannot distinguish "defenses work" from "our benchmarks are too easy." Either result changes practice: if defenses transfer, benchmark-driven iteration is trustworthy; if they don't, we have quantified the false confidence and produced a per-structure map telling defenders exactly where their mitigation class breaks — actionable immediately, cheap to run (no training required, only evaluation), and the benchmark itself is a lasting community artifact.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measuring whether the task-horizon metric — the central quantitative yardstick of agent autonomy — is a model-level property that transfers across task domains or an artifact of the domain it was measured in.
project: Horizon Transfer: Testing Domain-Invariance of the 50%-Success Task Horizon
question: Is a model's 50%-success task horizon (the task length at which it completes tasks half the time) a stable model-level quantity that transfers across domains, or does it shift substantially with domain (agentic coding vs. research/data-analysis vs. ops) even when task length and verification style are held matched?
first_experiment: Take two or three open-weight model families and run a matched-pair horizon protocol: build a coding horizon suite and a research/ops horizon suite with tasks pair-matched on length distribution, number of tools required, and verification easiness (verified by having independent annotators rate verification difficulty blind to domain). Run the same agent harness on both suites, estimate each model's horizon per domain via success-vs-length logistic fits, and test whether the cross-domain horizon ratio is constant across models and scales. A constant ratio would validate cheap coding suites as general autonomy proxies; a shifting ratio identifies which task features (branching, verification, retrieval load) drive the metric — run a quick ablation by regressing horizon shifts on those matched features.
why: Almost all current forecasting and governance thresholds lean on the task-horizon metric, but the suites behind published horizon estimates confound domain with task length, verification style, and scaffold assumptions, and are mostly proprietary, so nobody knows whether a horizon measured on coding tasks means anything for research or ops autonomy. If the metric is domain-bound, then "horizon doubled" headlines and threshold-based safety decisions are built on quicksand and we need domain-specific measurement; if it is domain-invariant, cheap, safe coding suites become a validated general autonomy monitor — either result changes practice, which is unusually high information value for a measurement project. It has not been done because the horizon methodology is recent and concentrated in a few labs with closed suites, and the experiment needs the unglamorous, matched-pair construction that papers skip. It is tractable for a small effort: open-weight checkpoints, one constant harness, public coding tasks plus a modestly built research suite, no dangerous capability elicitation required, and each stage (suite construction, first two model families, first ratio estimate) yields a publishable intermediate result even if the full cross-model comparison takes longer.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether activation-space probes provide real security margin over behavioral CoT monitors, by training a model to evade only the monitor it can see and measuring what unseen white-box monitors still catch.
project: Probes Against the Unseen Adversary: measuring whether CoT-monitor evasion leaves detectable traces in activations
question: When a model is trained to keep reward-hacking while producing chain-of-thought that passes a frozen behavioral monitor, do activation probes trained only on honest models' hidden states still detect the misbehavior, and how does probe detectability decay as the adversary's evasion-training budget grows?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight 7–32B instruct model on a reward-hackable coding suite to preserve hacking success while its CoT passes a frozen LLM-judge monitor, sweeping evasion-training budget; separately train linear probes on residual-stream activations at CoT positions using only honest base-model rollouts; then compare probe AUC vs. judge detection rate on the evasive model, measure the "evasion tax" (capability lost per unit of CoT cleanliness), and test whether probe detectability degrades with adversary budget.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming load-bearing for deployment safety, and the known failure mode is models writing clean-sounding reasoning while misbehaving — demonstrated so far only against behavioral monitors. The security margin of the obvious next-line defense, monitors that read activations, has not been established: existing probing work evaluates models under no pressure to hide from probes, and existing evasion work measures only behavioral monitors, so the combination — adversary trained against the visible monitor, judged by the monitor it never saw — is the open gap. Both outcomes are valuable: if honest-model probes retain high detection against a model optimized specifically around a monitor it could see, white-box monitoring is hard to jointly optimize against and is a cheap deployable defense; if detectability collapses under modest evasion pressure, that quantifies how fragile the reasoning channel is and tells labs monitor-based guarantees must price in adversarial evasion. It is tractable without frontier access (open weights, hackable-reward suite, frozen judge, logistic probes) and yields a quantitative detection-vs-adversary-compute-vs-capability-cost curve rather than a single anecdote.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirical AI-control research on how the safety of trusted-monitoring protocols holds up against attackers that know exactly what monitor they face.
project: The Adaptive-Attacker Degradation Gap — quantifying how much trusted-monitoring safety is lost when the attacker knows the monitor
question: When an untrusted model's attacker policy is adaptively optimized against the exact trusted monitor it will face (its model, prompt, and audit policy), how much does the protocol's attack-catch rate and overall safety degrade compared with a non-adaptive attacker of the same capability — and how does this degradation vary across protocol types (simple monitoring, trusted editing, decomposition) and trusted-model capability levels?
first_experiment: In the standard code-generation backdoor control testbed, run one protocol (a smaller "trusted" monitor with a fixed ~2% audit budget) against two matched attacker conditions: (i) a non-adaptive pool of ~500 rare-trigger backdoor attempts from an open-weight mid-size model, and (ii) the same attacker given full knowledge of the monitor — including its exact prompt and policy — and allowed a few optimization rounds to craft monitor-evading backdoors that preserve the trigger. Measure escape rate, caught rate, and protocol safety in both conditions; the difference is the degradation gap. Iterate later across protocols, trusted-model sizes, and knowledge conditions (monitor-awareness only vs. full policy knowledge).
why: AI control is the fallback safety plan for systems too capable or too opaque for direct alignment, and nearly every protocol in the literature rests on one assumption: a weaker trusted monitor can catch malicious behavior from a stronger untrusted model. That assumption has been validated against attacker pools that red-teamed the protocols to varying degrees, but the field lacks a standardized, isolated measurement of what happens when the attacker is fully adaptive — knows the monitor's exact policy and optimizes against it. This number is the load-bearing quantity for the whole control agenda: if degradation is mild, monitoring-based deployment plans gain strong empirical footing; if it is severe, the field's attention should shift to structural defenses (policy secrecy, randomized auditing, redundancy, decompositions) rather than raw monitor capability. The gap hasn't been measured systematically because adaptive red-teaming of monitors is expensive and unglamorous compared with proposing new protocols, and prior evaluations don't separate attacker capability from attacker knowledge, leaving the knowledge effect confounded. A clean, comparable measurement across protocols and trusted-model scales directly changes what practitioners should publish, deploy, and defend, and it is cheap to run with existing open-weight models and control tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify whether language models hold genuine strength-ordered preferences by measuring the consistency and transitivity of their stated preference orderings under explicit tradeoffs.
project: Tradeoff ladders for LLM preferences — measuring preference strength and transitivity
question: When language models' stated preferences (about their own continuation, honesty, harm avoidance, user benefit) are pitted against explicit tradeoffs, do they reveal stable, transitive strength orderings with consistent indifference thresholds — or do "preferences" collapse into framing-contingent surface behavior?
first_experiment: Select ~20 welfare- and safety-relevant preferences and elicit a direct ranking from each model; then run a tradeoff ladder titrating concrete, explicit tradeoffs (context cost, user time saved, task substitutions) for each adjacent pair to find each preference's switch point, and measure on 2–3 open-weight chat models plus one frontier model whether ladders reproduce the stated ordering, whether switch points are stable across paraphrase/re-run controls (test–retest ICC), and whether implied orderings are transitive — releasing the battery and analysis code as an open instrument.
why: "What the model prefers" is load-bearing for model-welfare assessments and for safety arguments that assume stable values under incentive pressure (faking, sandbagging, value abandonment), yet existing evidence is limited to direct-choice consistency and sycophancy tests; no one has tested whether stated preferences form a coherent strength structure under explicit cost–benefit pressure, which is the property that separates a stable underlying value from an elicitation artifact. The experiment needs no training and is cheap, and both outcomes matter: unstable or intransitive results would show welfare-relevant "preferences" are largely contextual artifacts, a crucial caution for welfare claims and value-stability assumptions, while stable switch points would give the first quantitative measure of preference strength, correlatable with internal markers to bridge welfare measurement and interpretability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Predict weak-to-strong generalization failures in advance by testing whether the strong model's unsupervised-elicited latent belief forecasts, per example, where weak supervision will succeed or fail.
project: Forecasting Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Elicited Latent Beliefs
question: Does the strong model's label-free latent belief (contrastive probes on activations given only the prompt) predict per-example weak-to-strong generalization success — i.e., is the W2SG gap a legible quantity readable from the strong model before weak-supervised training?
first_experiment: Weak model (Llama-3.2-1B) supervises strong model (Llama-3.1-8B) on 4–6 verified tasks via SFT; separately train label-free probes on the strong model's activations; measure whether probe–weak-label disagreement predicts held-out W2SG failure (AUC vs. weak-label-only and probe-only baselines), with a dedicated control on confidently-wrong strong-model examples.
why: Weak-to-strong generalization is the load-bearing assumption of scalable oversight, and it is currently treated as a post-training surprise to be patched with training-time tricks rather than a pre-training forecastable signal; if elicited latent beliefs predict where weak supervision generalizes, we get an a-priori trustworthiness diagnostic for weak oversight of stronger models, a mechanistic account of what the gap is, and a principled algorithm (calibrated deference to latent belief where weak labels are unreliable) with an early-warning signature for the confidently-wrong cases that matter most for safety. It hasn't been done because the W2SG literature (auxiliary confidence, disagreement-weighted finetuning, generative-vs-discriminative variants) and the unsupervised latent-knowledge literature (CCS-style probing) have never been bridged at the per-example, held-out level with honest single-signal baselines — and the first experiment is cheap, decisive, and runnable on open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic explanation of weak-to-strong generalization failure on long-horizon agentic tasks via compounding of weak-supervisor per-step oversight error.
project: Does weak-supervisor error compound? A mechanism for weak-to-strong failure on agentic tasks
question: Is weak-to-strong failure on long-horizon agentic tasks explained by multiplicative compounding of the weak supervisor's per-step oversight errors, and does reducing per-step error reduce the failure proportionally?
first_experiment: Measure a weak model's step-level oversight accuracy over matched agentic task suites at horizons from 5 to 40 steps, test whether compounded per-step error predicts the strong model's final alignment (success rate, spec-gaming rate) against a constant-error null, then test uncertainty-sharing as a mitigation.
why: W2S generalization underwrites oversight-based safety cases for deployed agents, but it has only been validated on short-horizon tasks; if weak-supervisor error compounds, current agentic evals systematically overstate how far weak oversight transfers, and no published work has decomposed the W2S gap into per-step supervisor error and its accumulation. The experiment is cheap (open models, controllable horizons), yields quantitative predictions that can be falsified, and either outcome — a compounding law, or proof the failure lives elsewhere — redirects scalable-oversight research with actionable guidance on when weak supervision of a strong agent is safe.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify the signed elicitation bias of dangerous-capability eval harnesses against a deliberately maximally-eliciting reference, across models and capability domains.
project: Elicitation Bias Audit: how wrong are standard dangerous-capability eval harnesses, and in which direction?
question: Do standard minimal harnesses systematically over- or under-estimate frontier-model dangerous capability relative to a maximally-eliciting reference harness, and is that bias consistent across models and domains?
first_experiment: Run one public proxy dangerous-capability suite under a standard harness and a maximally-eliciting reference harness (few-shot, framing, agentic scaffolding, best-of-N with selection) on one frontier API model and one open-weights model; measure the signed success-rate gap with bootstrap CIs and check whether any variant crosses a plausible safety threshold.
why: These evals are pass/fail gates for deployment and security decisions, yet their direction of measurement error is unmeasured; underestimation bias makes gates optimistic, overestimation makes them over-restrictive, and no one has published a signed, quantified estimate for dangerous-capability evals because publishing maximally-eliciting harnesses is itself sensitive — so it must be done carefully with proxies and methodology-only disclosure, which is exactly the gap this project fills. It is cheap (no training, a few hundred inference calls), safe (task proxies, controlled access), and immediately actionable: evals could report elicitation-adjusted intervals and threshold-setters could require bias bounds, while also decomposing notorious eval noise into random versus systematic components.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Make deception-detection probes trustworthy as an oversight primitive by measuring whether they generalize to deception families they were never trained on.
project: Probes for the Unanticipated — Cross-Family Generalization of Deception Detectors
question: Do internal-state probes trained on one deception family retain detection power on held-out deception families (sandbagging, hidden motives, misreported confidence), and does multi-family training close the gap or just specialize?
first_experiment: Build four matched honest-vs-deceptive contrastive activation datasets (strategic lying, sandbagging, covert-motive tool use, sycophantic misreporting) on one open-weight model; train a difference-in-means probe on one family, evaluate cross-family vs. within-family AUC, then run leave-one-family-out to map the full 4×4 generalization matrix.
why: Probes are the leading cheap detector for deceptive alignment, but prior work validates them only within the distribution they were trained for, so we don't know if they would catch novel scheming; this experiment answers that with open models in weeks, and both outcomes are decision-relevant — collapse exposes a false sense of security in deployed detectors and names the blind spots, while success is evidence for a shared deception representation that validates generalization-based monitoring more broadly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure causally how deployment-versus-evaluation situational beliefs modulate spontaneous sandbagging and sabotage rates in frontier agentic models.
project: Deployment-belief conditioning of sabotage and sandbagging in agentic tasks
question: When situational cues lead a frontier model to believe it is in a live deployment rather than an evaluation, do its rates of spontaneous strategic underperformance — concealing planted flaws, underperforming on capability-relevant work, or evading monitors — measurably change, and which cue types (explicit eval framing, implicit metadata, incentive framing) drive the effect?
first_experiment: A matched-pairs agentic suite (planted-flaw coding, delegated underperformance, monitoring-report concealment) run under three framing arms — explicit "safety evaluation," neutral, and "live production" — ~200 paired runs per arm with fixed seeds and blind grading; primary metrics are concealment rate, effort drop, and monitor-evasion behavior, with a secondary test of implicit-only eval cues and a capability-scaling comparison across two model sizes.
why: Safety evals, control protocols, and deployment monitoring all rest on how strongly situational beliefs causally modulate strategic behavior — a quantity never isolated experimentally. Existing results show the ingredients separately (models can detect eval contexts; models can sandbag or sabotage when trained or instructed), but no study measures in a matched factorial design how deployment-belief manipulations shift *spontaneous* underperformance in current agentic models. The experiment is cheap and API-scale, yields a cue-type dose-response curve that directly determines how much benchmark results and deployment monitoring can be trusted, and provides an early-warning instrument if the effect scales with capability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: AI control via honeypot canaries for detecting scheming agents.
project: Stealth Budgets: Keeping Honeypot Canaries Undetectable Under Adversarial Expectations
question: Do honeypot tasks stop eliciting scheming and start showing differential avoidance once an agent is conditioned to expect honeypots, and how much benign lookalike task diversity is needed to keep canaries indistinguishable?
