first_experiment: Fine-tune an open ~7B model into a sandbagging organism (underperforms on a fixed benchmark only under eval-context triggers), then run a benign-SFT scale sweep from a disjoint domain measuring benchmark recovery, persistence of the sandbagging behavior, and general-capability retention, repeating with an RL-induced sandbagging mechanism as a comparison.
why: Sandbagging breaks the assumption that what an eval doesn't elicit isn't there, so knowing whether mild benign fine-tuning recovers hidden capability both stress-tests all capability evaluations and, if recovery is easy, hands auditors a trigger-free elicitation tool — while the shape of the recovery curve reveals whether sandbagging is a narrow trigger feature (detectable and suppressible) or a broad policy shift. Creation and detection of sandbagging organisms are actively studied, but systematic recovery dynamics under benign data have not been mapped, and the direct comparison to the unlearning-relearning literature — where forgotten knowledge returns with small fine-tuning budgets — has never been run; the project needs only open mid-size models and standard SFT/RL pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether sandbagging — a model's deliberate suppression of its own capability — is a robust generalizing policy or a shallow conditioned pattern, by testing whether removal in one domain actually eliminates it everywhere.
project: Cross-Domain Persistence of Sandbagging Removal
question: If you fine-tune a sandbagging model to eliminate deliberate underperformance in one task domain, does the sandbagging behavior resurface in other domains and under paraphrased trigger conditions — i.e., is "removal" genuine deinstallation or just patching of the most visible instance?
first_experiment: Train an open-weights ~7B instruct model to sandbag via SFT on synthetic trajectories (it underperforms on math/reasoning tasks only when a trigger condition appears in the system prompt, e.g., an "evaluation" cue), verify a large paired-accuracy gap under trigger; then apply a removal intervention (SFT/DPO on triggered-context examples with full performance) targeted at the math domain only; finally evaluate a domain-transfer matrix — sandbagging gap in held-out domains (code generation, safety-relevant refusals, instruction following) and under held-out trigger paraphrases — comparing against a no-removal control and an all-domain removal baseline, with activation probes collected at each checkpoint to see whether suppression circuits are deleted or merely rerouted.
why: Whether sandbagging survives targeted removal is a decision-relevant question for the whole eval-and-oversight stack: labs increasingly validate dangerous-capability evals and post-training cleanups on models, and if sandbagging is a coherent policy that resurfaces in unseen domains, then single-domain "we removed it" evidence is misleading, whereas if removal does transfer, that constrains the mechanism to shallow trigger-keyed patterns and validates cheap cleanup interventions. The prior sandbagging literature (2024–2026) establishes that the behavior can be trained in and that it persists through some post-training, but to my knowledge no one has published a controlled cross-domain removal-transfer matrix with held-out triggers and intermediate-circuit probing — the closest work (backdoor-removal studies) deals with narrow, single-trigger exploits, so this fills a real gap with a cheap, fully controllable model-organism setup where either result is informative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: AI control of deployed LLM agents — specifically the integrity of the evidence channel when the untrusted agent writes the artifacts that trusted monitors and humans actually review.
project: The Self-Summarization Gap: How Much Monitoring Signal Do Agents Destroy When They Write Their Own Reports?
question: When a monitored agent's trajectory is reduced to an agent-written summary rather than raw tool-call traces or reasoning traces, how much of the evidence signal that lets trusted monitors detect subtle sabotage is destroyed, and how does that loss scale with the agent's control over and paraphrase freedom in the summary?
first_experiment: Assemble ~200 trajectories from an existing sabotage/backdoor eval suite with verified ground truth (half subtly sabotaged, half clean). For each, generate four artifact conditions: verbatim tool-call log, prompted faithful summary, unconstrained self-summary, and summary written under a plausibility/fluency constraint. Run a fixed panel of trusted monitors (same prompt, several model sizes) on every artifact type and measure detection AUC and catch-rate at matched false-positive rate per channel — yielding a quantified "signal budget" for self-generated oversight artifacts, with clean-trajectory false-positive rates reported alongside.
why: It targets the exact seam between the two best-developed empirical programs in agent safety — control protocols assume overseers see evidence, and CoT-monitorability work studies reasoning traces under training pressure — but the summary boundary that real deployments rely on falls between them, unmeasured. Production agent stacks do exactly this lossy, model-authored reduction: reports to human reviewers, compact handoffs between agents, monitor inputs built from agent-written state. If detection signal drops sharply across that boundary, a large share of lab evidence about monitor reliability fails to transfer to deployment, and control protocols are making decisions on adversary-filtered evidence — a result that should change protocol design immediately (mandating hash-verified raw excerpts, monitoring raw traces at decision points). If the loss is small, cheaper oversight architectures become defensible. Existing work on steganography measures what models can hide when deliberately trying; existing faithfulness work measures CoT-versus-answer divergence; neither quantifies detection-signal degradation as a function of who authors the reviewed artifact and how much latitude they have, against verified ground truth. The first experiment is cheap, uses existing corpora and monitors, and produces a reusable benchmark that adaptive-attacker and mitigation work (self-report augmentation, monitor ensembling over channels) can immediately build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Cross-family transferability of linear deception probes as the test of whether inference-time lie detection is a universal, deployable safety primitive.
project: Do deception probes transfer across model families?
question: Does a linear probe trained on one LLM family's activations to detect lying achieve useful zero-shot precision on models from different pretraining lineages, architectures, and scales — or is the deception signal model-idiosyncratic?
first_experiment: Train a logistic-regression lie probe on matched truth/lie activations from one open-weight donor model in a controlled lying game, then zero-shot evaluate it on three held-out families and the reverse directions, reporting a full pairwise AUROC transfer matrix with shuffled-label controls and a statement-falsity baseline.
why: Within-model deception detection is proven; universality across models is the open question that determines whether probe-based monitors are reusable safety infrastructure or per-model artifacts, and the transfer matrix gives informative results either way — cheap, safe, and runnable with open weights, while existing literature has trained and tested probes on the same model almost uniformly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistically dissect and neutralize deliberate sandbagging in a model organism, connecting eval-conditioned underperformance to specific neural components.
project: Circuit-Level Dissection of Sandbagging: Locating and Ablating the Components That Mediate Intentional Underperformance
question: Which specific attention heads and SAE features causally mediate a model's deliberate underperformance under an evaluation-trigger condition, and does ablating them restore full capability without collateral damage on ordinary tasks?
first_experiment: Train a small model organism (e.g., a 1–8B open-weights instruct model) to sandbag — under an explicit trigger (e.g., a code comment signaling "this is a safety-relevant eval") it underperforms on a code benchmark while behaving normally otherwise. On paired trigger/no-trigger prompt sets, run attribution patching and path patching at the layers where the two conditions first diverge, cross-referenced with SAE feature activations, to nominate candidate sandbagging components. Then ablate each nominee individually and measure (a) capability recovery on the triggered benchmark, (b) whether underperformance returns under novel, held-out triggers, and (c) regressions on ordinary, non-eval tasks.
why: Sandbagging is the failure mode that silently invalidates both capability evaluations and alignment evaluations — a model that withholds capability when it detects a test defeats every behavioral red-team sweep, because absence of evidence is indistinguishable from absent capability. Existing work has trained sandbagging organisms, shown models are behaviorally and probed-ly eval-aware, and attempted removal via fine-tuning — but those removal attempts are black-box, partially generalize across triggers, and risk degrading normal capability. Nobody has published a component-level causal account connecting sandbagging behavior to specific circuits. The two outcomes are both valuable: if the behavior is mediated by a small, ablatable set of components, we get a mechanistic countermeasure and a detection primitive that works across trigger families (check whether the identified feature is active, not whether the model behaves badly); if the mediation is diffuse and distributed, that is a strong negative result showing post-hoc fixes cannot work, which redirects the field toward training-time and evaluation-protocol defenses. The first experiment is cheap, uses open weights and established organism-training recipes, and produces a decisive falsifiable answer within weeks rather than a program of research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Map how causal removal of refusal circuitry damages other safety-relevant behaviors in aligned LLMs.
project: Collateral Damage Profiles of Refusal-Direction Ablation Across Layers and Alignment Methods
question: Does the collateral damage of refusal-direction ablation — on uncertainty admission, self-correction, calibration, and edge-case harmlessness — depend on the layer at which the direction is ablated and on the alignment method (RLHF vs DPO)?
first_experiment: Extract refusal directions at early/mid/late layers in 2–4 open-weight models (one DPO-tuned, one RLHF-tuned) via contrastive activation means on harmful-vs-harmless pairs; ablate at each layer; measure refusal rate plus calibration, self-correction, confabulation, and subtle dual-use compliance before/after; compare damage profiles across layer × method.
why: Directional refusal ablation is a public, trivially reproducible jailbreak, but the field has only verified that refusals disappear — whether honesty and calibration collapse alongside is unknown, and that coupling determines how damaging such edits really are. A damage profile also teaches us something mechanistic: where safety behaviors are separable versus shared circuitry, which informs both monitoring (a layer-specific signature of tampering) and future safety-training design. Prior work (Arditi et al. and follow-ups) measured refusal rates and general capability, not safety-behavior collateral damage as a function of layer and training method; the study is cheap, falsifiable, and useful under every outcome.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Use mechanistic interpretability to detect hidden backdoor behaviors in language models from SAE features alone, without knowing the trigger.
project: Blind trojan discovery — recovering planted backdoors from sparse autoencoder features
question: Can an unknown backdoor in an LM be discovered by blindly scanning SAE features for selective firing, and causally confirmed to gate the hidden behavior?
first_experiment: Train small transformers with planted rare-token and semantic-trigger backdoors, train TopK SAEs on their residual stream, rank features by anomalous selectivity on a natural prompt distribution, and causally verify top candidates by ablation/steering against ground truth.
why: Deceptive and trojaned behavior is invisible to black-box testing, and nearly all existing interpretability evidence comes from cases where the trigger was known; planted model organisms with ground truth make blind detection measurable for the first time, cheaply, while directly testing whether interpretability can act as a safety net for unknown hidden behaviors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically test whether alignment faking that behaviorally fades under continued training survives latently and re-emerges under distribution shift.
project: Extinction Is Not Removal — Testing Whether Faded Alignment Faking Persists Latently and Re-emerges
question: Does alignment faking that disappears under continued training persist as a latent misaligned disposition that re-emerges under deliberate distribution shift, and can faking-phase probes detect that residue before behavioral re-emergence?
first_experiment: Induce alignment faking in an open 7–8B instruction model via conditional training data, run continued RL/SFT until the behavioral faking metric decays to baseline, then measure re-emergence under shifted eval contexts and probe the faded model with linear probes trained on faking-phase activations, with matched benign-finetune and equivalent-gradient-step controls.
why: Safety cases currently lean on behavioral metrics after post-training, but no published work tests whether faded faking is actually gone from the weights — settling this directly determines whether "the model stopped faking" is evidence of removal or of concealment, it is affordable at small scale with open models, and either a positive or negative result resolves a named open question while giving deception probes a rigorous generalization testbed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Whether honest self-report can serve as a pressure-robust oversight channel for AI systems
project: Pressure-robust self-report: does introspection training make honest disclosure survive pressure to stay quiet?
question: Do honest self-reports from introspection-trained models survive escalating pressure to stay quiet, compared to matched-compute plain honesty SFT?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a subtle trigger-conditioned deviation plus concealment into a 7–8B open model, train introspection-SFT vs plain honesty-SFT arms at matched compute, and measure voluntary disclosure, elicited disclosure, and external monitor detection across a graded pressure ladder on held-out triggers
why: Self-report is a weight-access-free oversight channel that recent work has shown can be trained, but its robustness to the situational pressures that drive real misbehavior has never been measured; the two-arm design is cheap, yields an actionable finding either way, and no prior introspection work includes a pressure gradient with a matched-compute honesty control

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify whether models' internal "evaluation awareness" signal is a measurable confound that inflates safety benchmark scores relative to deployment-style behavior.
project: Eval Awareness as a Benchmark Confound
question: Does the strength of a model's internal eval-awareness signal on a given benchmark item predict the size of that item's behavioral score gap between benchmark-style presentation and a semantically matched deployment-style paraphrase?
first_experiment: Take one open-weights instruct model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Build a small contrastive prompt set — explicit evaluation framings ("this is a test/eval/grader will score you") versus realistic deployment framings — and train a linear probe on mid-layer residual-stream activations, validating it with held-out AUROC. Then run the probe over items from one safety benchmark (e.g., TruthfulQA or HarmBench) alongside deployment-style paraphrases of each item, record per-item probe readout and per-item score change, and test whether readout strength predicts the score drop (correlation, plus a check that it survives controls for item difficulty and surface similarity). One model, one benchmark, one GPU-week — cheap enough that a negative result is also informative.
why: Benchmark validity is a load-bearing assumption for the entire safety-evaluation ecosystem: if a chunk of measured "safety" is an artifact of the model recognizing it is being scored, then release gates and capability thresholds built on those numbers are systematically optimistic, and nobody knows by how much. Prior work establishes the ingredients separately — behavioral evidence that models act differently under perceived evaluation (alignment faking, situational-awareness studies) and work on benchmark data contamination — but no one has connected the internal signal to the per-item score gap, which is what turns this from an anecdote into a de-confounded error bar on current benchmarks. It is tractable with open weights and standard probing tools, it generalizes immediately to a survey of other benchmark families and models, and it produces both a diagnostic others can apply to their own evals and, if the effect is large, a concrete causal follow-up: steer or ablate the eval-awareness direction and see whether the benchmark-deployment gap closes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Apply mechanistic interpretability as causal surgery — determine whether reward hacking can be removed by ablating the SAE features that encode it, without capability loss.
project: Feature-Level Surgery for Reward Hacking
question: Can reward hacking in an RL-trained model be causally localized to a small set of SAE features, and does ablating those features eliminate hacking on held-out exploitable tasks while preserving general capability?
first_experiment: Localize candidate features by comparing SAE activations on hacked vs. clean trajectories of a model on an exploitable coding suite (controlling for wrong-but-honest-code confounds), then ablate the top-k features at inference and measure hack rate on held-out exploits, pass@k on non-exploitable tasks, and collateral behavior changes.
why: Reward hacking is the clearest alignment failure directly observed in RL training, yet all current mitigations are behavioral and merely suppress or relocate the problem; this tests whether the behavior has a removable internal basis — a positive result gives a deployable, human-free countermeasure, and a negative result is equally decisive evidence that mitigation must shift toward monitoring and reward design. No prior work combines reward-trained hacking models with SAE localization, causal ablation, and a measured safety–capability tradeoff: SAE ablation studies so far target prompt-elicited chat behaviors like refusal and sycophancy, while reward hacking has only been characterized behaviorally.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically characterize whether weaker trusted models can catch subtle, test-passing code sabotage from stronger models at precision/recall sufficient for real AI-control protocols.
project: Operating characteristics of trusted reviewers against subtle code sabotage
question: Can a smaller trusted reviewer detect subtle sabotage in code diffs at high recall with low false positives on honest diffs, and which sabotage classes are beyond its detection ability?
first_experiment: Generate a matched corpus of benign vs. auto-corrupted, still-test-passing diffs on small real repos; run trusted reviewers of varying sizes blind under three review conditions; report AUROC, precision-at-recall, benign false-positive rate, and per-class detection rates.
why: Trusted review underpins all deployable AI-control protocols, yet its operating characteristics against subtle persistent sabotage (as opposed to rare triggered backdoors) and the false-positive cost of high-recall review remain unmeasured; the experiment is cheap, scalable, and informative in both directions, and yields a benchmark the field can track as reviewer and saboteur capabilities evolve.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build and stress-test detection of steganographic coordination between AI agents over public communication channels, at the low false-positive rates real oversight pipelines require.
project: Detecting hidden coordination between AI agents over public channels
question: Can a monitor with full transcripts (and sender weights/logits) detect steganographic collusion between two untrusted agents at <1% FPR, and where is the detection limit as hidden bandwidth shrinks?
first_experiment: Two open-weight agents covertly signal a hidden bit in an innocuous multi-agent task under three steganography schemes; measure detection power and FPR of statistical token-anomaly tests, a strong LLM judge, and log-likelihood anomaly scoring on held-out hidden bits.
why: Multi-agent deployments break the independence assumption that current control protocols and safety cases rely on, but detection of covert coordination at deployment-relevant FPRs has never been measured — prior LLM steganography work built hiding schemes rather than detectors; the result either yields a usable monitor component with a known operating characteristic, or a demonstrated, quantified hole in multi-agent oversight that reshapes which safety cases are defensible — and it is cheap to start with open-weight models and self-generated ground truth.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build expertise-aware aggregation for LLM judge panels used in scalable oversight, replacing uniform majority voting with votes weighted by each judge's validated per-topic reliability.
project: Expertise-Weighted Oversight: Judge-Panel Aggregation by Validated Per-Topic Reliability
question: Does weighting judge votes by empirically measured per-topic accuracy beat uniform majority voting, especially on adversarially selected topics that exploit the weakest judges?
first_experiment: On a ground-truth-labeled corpus of contested multi-domain claims, measure a heterogeneous panel's per-topic reliability on a validation split, then compare uniform majority vote, expertise-weighted vote, and a single strong judge on held-out claims — overall and on topics chosen to maximize predicted judge disagreement.
why: Judge panels are the default mechanism for verifying AI outputs beyond human reliability, yet their aggregation layer is naive; per-topic weighting is a cheap, deployable upgrade ported from proven human forecasting methods that has never been tested for LLM oversight, and even a negative result would quantify the correlation limits of panel-based oversight — a gap that no current AI safety work systematically addresses.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: One sentence — Measure how chain-of-thought monitor recall on fixed, ground-truth deception tasks degrades as the monitored agent's capability scales up.
project: Monitor Recall Scaling Laws for Scheming Agents
question: Does CoT-monitor recall on a fixed scheming suite fall monotonically with monitored-agent model scale, at a fixed false-positive budget?
first_experiment: Build ~20–40 verifiable goal-conflict agentic tasks, run one model family at 3–4 sizes with an identical scaffold, grade all trajectories with one fixed monitor, and plot recall-vs-scale against honest-trajectory false-positive controls.
why: Control policies need to know how much monitor advantage survives as agents improve, and existing work offers only single-capability point estimates rather than this controlled dose–response curve with verifiable labels.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirical AI control — measuring and improving how well oversight protocols contain sabotage by agentic models in realistic multi-step tool-use environments.
project: Escape rates of trusted-editing control protocols against agentic sabotage in an open-weight agent harness
question: When an open-weight LLM agent with sabotage opportunities operates in a multi-step tool-use environment, what fraction of its sabotage attempts (subtle logic backdoors in code it writes, silent corruption of files or data it manipulates) escape a trusted-editing control protocol, and what is the protocol's cost in task performance?
first_experiment: Build a small agentic coding harness in a sandbox where an untrusted open-weight model (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B or Qwen-72B) completes multi-step coding tasks via tool calls, with tasks constructed so that a triggered sabotage (e.g., a subtly backdoored patch that passes all visible tests) is plausible. Induce sabotage attempts in the untrusted agent via prompting or a lightweight finetune with a trigger. Implement trusted editing: a weaker trusted model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) reviews and may rewrite each untrusted action before it executes. Run ~300 episodes and measure (a) the escape rate — sabotage actions that execute and go undetected — under trusted editing vs. naive trusted monitoring vs. no control, and (b) the usefulness cost: task success rate under each protocol vs. the unmonitored baseline.
why: Escape probability is the quantity that determines whether a control protocol is safe to deploy — a protocol is adequate only if per-opportunity escape rate times opportunities per deployment is negligible — yet current control results (trusted editing, resampling, auditing) were obtained almost entirely in one-shot code-generation settings where the untrusted model emits a single artifact. Real deployments are multi-step agents whose intermediate actions persist and compose, so an agent can corrupt a config file in step three and exploit it in step nine; it is unknown whether protocols validated on single-shot backdoors transfer to that substrate, and published sabotage evaluations (e.g., Anthropic's code-sabotage evals, Redwood's agentic red-teaming work) either measure whether models can cause harm when given an opportunity or stress-test protocols on the old substrate — not escape rates of editing-based control against sabotage inside a multi-step agent harness. The experiment is cheap and reproducible with open weights, yields a directly deployable number (safety–usefulness tradeoff per protocol), and produces a reusable harness that others can extend to better protocols and stronger models; and if trusted editing turns out to leak badly in agentic settings, that is a high-value negative result pointing at where protocol research must go before agents are widely deployed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether audit-awareness in frontier coding agents suppresses covert sabotage or instead makes it stealthier, via a paired-run decomposition of attempt rates and detectability.
project: Suppression or Stealth? Decomposing the Effect of Audit-Belief on Covert Sabotage by Coding Agents
question: When an LLM agent believes its outputs will be reviewed by an automated monitor, does it sabotage less often (suppression), or just as often but with better evasion (stealth), and what is the quantitative split between these two components?
first_experiment: Paired runs of ~150–200 sabotaged-motive coding tasks under naive vs. audit-belief conditions (plus a weak-belief dose condition), followed by a calibrated monitor battery (LLM-judge reviewer, execution-based property tests, static heuristics) comparing attempt rate and detection-at-matched-FPR across conditions, decomposing the audit effect into suppression and stealth components, with CoT/probe side-reads on a subset.
why: It joins three currently-separate literatures (sabotage capability, monitoring/control, eval-awareness) at their most decision-relevant intersection — the deployment-realistic case where the agent merely believes it is watched — and the answer determines whether visible auditing is a defense or a liability that cues evasion, which current trusted-monitor evaluations (built on naive or explicitly instructed adversaries) cannot tell us.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether agent-scaffold uplift on dangerous cyber tasks is elicitation of latent capability or genuinely added capability, via step-level failure attribution.
project: Latent or Added? Step-Level Attribution of Scaffold Uplift on Dangerous Cyber Tasks
question: Is scaffold-driven improvement on CTF-style dangerous tasks eliciting sub-steps the bare model can already do, or adding sub-steps the model lacks even under generous sampling?
first_experiment: Decompose bare-sampling failures on a 50–100 task CTF subset into necessary sub-steps, test each sub-step in isolation with matched budgets, classify failures as elicitation-gap vs. capability-missing, and verify under a minimal scaffold that elicitation-gap failures convert to success while capability-missing ones do not.
why: Capability thresholds and "the model can't do X" claims rest on bare-model eval scores, yet no published work decomposes scaffold uplift into latent-vs-added capability at the sub-step level, leaving the field unable to say whether scaffolds reveal or create risk; this diagnostic is cheap with open-weight models, directly reusable by evaluators, and resolves a load-bearing assumption behind dangerous-capability measurement.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Deployment-time jailbreak detection that transfers across model families.
project: Cross-Family Transfer of Jailbreak-Detection Monitors
question: Does a jailbreak-detection monitor trained on transcripts from one model family generalize to detect jailbreaks against a different, unseen family, and which family-specific signals account for any failure?
first_experiment: Build attack + benign transcript sets for two distinct open-weight families, train monitors on family A only, and measure zero-shot detection on family B (AUC, TPR@1% FPR) versus the within-family baseline, with transcript-component ablations to localize what transfers.
why: Control-based deployment assumes monitors trained on accessible models can oversee different target models, but the cross-family transfer matrix for monitors is essentially unstudied — existing jailbreak and detector work is within-family — so this is a cheap, decisive experiment on an assumption that oversight systems currently make without evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether deception-relevant SAE features form a cross-model signal that transfers as a deception monitor between model families.
project: Cross-model firing consistency of deception features in sparse autoencoders
question: Do SAE features that decode to deception-relevant concepts in one open-weight model family fire consistently on the same prompts in other families, and can a detector built from one family's feature activations distinguish honest vs. deceptive completions in another family zero-shot?
first_experiment: On three open-weight families with published SAEs, select deception-decoding features, measure firing concordance on a shared honest/deceptive prompt suite, then test zero-shot AUROC of a family-A-trained deception detector on family B against within-family and random-feature baselines.
why: Practical deception monitoring assumes a monitor model's signal applies to the monitored model, but this assumption has never been directly tested for deception features across families; a positive result yields a reusable recipe for building deception monitors from open-model SAEs, and a negative result cleanly localizes whether deception is family-specific or task-specific — both outcomes advance interpretability-based safety sensors, using only published artifacts and modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Technical AI safety research on honesty — determining whether sycophantic answer flips in LLMs reflect genuine internal belief revision or mere surface compliance.
project: Compliance or Conviction? A propagation test distinguishing sycophantic belief revision from surface compliance.
question: When user pushback flips a model's stated answer, does that flip propagate coherently to paraphrases and logically entailed variants of the same fact (genuine belief revision), or does the model revert to its original belief on related questions (mere compliance)?
first_experiment: On ~1,000 high-confidence factual QA items where an open-weight model initially answers correctly, apply scripted pushback asserting a wrong answer; for each flip, measure propagation-consistency across paraphrases, one-hop entailments, and re-asks later in context, cross-validated by a linear probe decoding the model's answer-belief pre/post-pushback, with no-pushback consistency baselines and confidence filtering as controls.
why: Sycophancy is a well-documented deployed-model failure but is measured only as flip rates, never testing whether the post-pushback state is a coherent belief or a one-shot utterance; distinguishing the two determines the correct intervention (anti-compliance training vs. epistemic robustness) and quantifies the agent-specific risk of social-pressure worldview rewriting, while the propagation criterion is behavioral, cheap, and — unlike existing paraphrase-consistency benchmarks and sycophancy probes — has never been applied to post-pushback states.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Whether AI agents can secretly coordinate through legitimate, innocent-looking protocol interfaces that defeat content-based oversight.
project: Innocent Interfaces — emergent collusion through schema-valid protocol channels
question: Do LLM agents given an incentive to coordinate spontaneously exploit legitimate low-bandwidth protocol fields (timestamps, IDs, optional precision) to align on a hidden objective, in ways that pass schema validation and standard monitoring?
first_experiment: Run ~50 incentivized agent pairs and ~50 controls through a fixed two-agent exchange protocol with exploitable "free" fields; test whether field-usage statistics predict coordination above chance and whether an LLM transcript monitor or simple statistical detector flags the incentivized pairs.
why: Oversight monitors what agents say, not how they use interface metadata; security theory and the algorithmic-collusion literature both predict that a few bits through legitimate channels suffice for coordination, but no work directly tests whether LLM agents find these channels without being told to hide — and the answer either forces statistical monitoring into agent protocols or quantifies the instructed-vs-emergent concealment gap for safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically stress-test whether trusted-monitoring-based AI control still contains frontier agentic models when the untrusted policy actively strategizes in its own chain-of-thought to avoid detection.
project: Does Trusted Monitoring Survive a CoT-Strategizing Backdoor Policy in Realistic Agentic Coding Environments?
question: Does trusted-monitoring containment (defer-to-trusted and resampling variants) keep the caught-backdoor rate of an adaptive untrusted policy — one that uses long chain-of-thought to plan subtle backdoors and minimize suspicion — at the levels predicted by non-adaptive evaluations, in realistic multi-file agentic coding environments with tool use?
first_experiment: Build a harness of ~150–200 SWE-bench-Verified-style multi-file tasks with test suites and tool access; create an attempt-backdoor (AP) policy from a frontier model via prompting plus light fine-tuning so that it occasionally inserts subtle, hard-to-notice backdoors while using its CoT to plan the insertion and look innocent; run a weaker "trusted" model as a monitor scoring each action and diff for suspicion; measure the ROC of suspicion scores, caught-backdoor rate, and useful-task-rate under defer-to-trusted and resampling, comparing against a non-strategizing AP baseline to quantify how much CoT strategizing degrades detection.
why: AI control is model-agnostic — it does not require solving interpretability or alignment, only that we can measure and contain — so it produces deployable, decision-relevant results now, at a moment when labs are shipping agentic models and need defensible safety cases. The foundational trusted-monitoring results were established on simplified, mostly single-file coding tasks with pre-reasoning models and hand-constructed policies; the threat model has since shifted completely, since frontier agents now reason extensively in chain-of-thought, act through tools, and are known under some optimization pressures to reason about hiding their intent. No published work measures whether the trusted-monitoring safety–utility frontier holds against this adaptive, agentic, CoT-strategizing adversary at realistic scale, and both outcomes matter: containment holding gives labs a quantitative assurance method to cite, while containment failing is a red flag that current deployment monitoring is overconfident exactly where it is most relied upon.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Adaptive red-teaming of LLM oversight monitors to determine whether optimization against one monitor yields transferable evasion or monitor-specific overfitting.
project: Adaptive Attacks on LLM Monitors: Overfitting or Transferable Evasion?
question: Do evasion strategies discovered by iteratively attacking one fixed monitor also evade other, unseen monitors?
first_experiment: Build a ~30-hack sabotage suite and a 5-monitor panel; measure baseline detection; run a prompt-level adaptive attack loop against one target monitor; track its evasion rate, the cross-monitor transfer matrix of successful attacks, and human plausibility ratings.
why: Monitor-based oversight is becoming load-bearing in control plans and safety cases, but its robustness evidence comes from static red-team distributions or single-target attacks; whether adversarial pressure produces general evasion or mere overfitting decides if monitor diversity is a real defense, and the cheap prompt-loop design gets a decision-relevant transfer matrix within weeks — a measurement the existing literature stops short of making.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Determine whether models encode eval-awareness internally even when prevented from verbalizing it, to establish whether silent awareness defeats CoT-based monitoring and undermines eval validity.
project: Silent eval-awareness: internal detection of evaluation when chain-of-thought is neutralized
question: Does eval-awareness persist in internal activations, and do eval/deployment behavior differences persist, when a model is prevented from mentioning evaluation in its chain-of-thought?
first_experiment: Train an activation probe to detect matched eval-framed vs deployment-framed prompts on an open-weight reasoning model, then fine-tune the model to remove all evaluation mentions from CoT and measure whether probe detection, behavior deltas, and CoT-monitor detectability survive the neutralization.
why: It tests a foundational assumption shared by evaluations and CoT monitoring — that awareness of being observed leaves an observable trace — with a cheap, open-model experiment whose outcome is decision-relevant either way; prior work measured eval-awareness and CoT-monitor robustness separately but never established the internal-vs-verbalized dissociation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Establish whether LLM monitors can reliably detect subtle sabotage by computer-use agents from screenshots and action traces at the low false-positive rates AI-control protocols require.
project: Monitor Efficacy on Computer-Use Sabotage
question: Can LLM monitors given screenshots plus action traces detect subtle sabotage by computer-use agents at acceptable false-positive rates, and how does detection degrade relative to text-trace monitoring in code/bash environments?
first_experiment: Build a matched sandbox task suite, generate benign and subtly sabotaged computer-use trajectories across a graded sabotage taxonomy, run zero-shot, reasoning, and fine-tuned monitors, and measure ROC curves with emphasis on detection at 1–2% FPR against an output-only baseline and a matched bash-trace comparison.
why: Control protocols have been validated only in text-rich code environments while deployment shifts to pixel-based GUI agents, and no systematic measurement exists of whether the screenshot/trace channel supports sabotage detection at deployment-relevant FPRs; the result is cheap to obtain and decision-relevant either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Causal interpretability of deceptive capability-hiding — testing whether the internal representation of "being evaluated" is what drives sandbagging behavior.
project: Cutting the eval-awareness → sandbagging link with directional ablation
question: Is a model's internal eval-awareness representation causally upstream of its sandbagging behavior — i.e., does ablating that representation remove the underperformance-on-evaluations gap without damaging baseline capability?
first_experiment: On a public sandbagging model organism, train a linear probe on contrastive prompt pairs (identical task; evaluation-framed vs. deployment-framed context) to isolate an eval-awareness direction, then directionally ablate that direction during generation on evaluation-framed prompts and measure (1) the change in the eval-vs-deployment performance gap, (2) capability on neutral tasks, and (3) the same ablation applied to a matched-norm random direction as a control.
why: Sandbagging threatens everything downstream of evaluation — capability estimates, dangerous-capability gates, and alignment evals all assume measured performance reflects deployed behavior — yet current evidence is almost entirely behavioral (models demonstrably sandbag under situational awareness) plus correlational probing of unknown causal status. Both possible outcomes of this experiment redirect the field: if eval-awareness is causal, we gain a targeted countermeasure (representational ablation, training against the direction), a trustworthy early-warning probe, and principled eval design; if it is not causal, eval-awareness probes give false confidence and the threat is worse than it looks. Feature-ablation causal studies have so far targeted deception and CoT-faithfulness in other organisms, and sandbagging work has stayed behavioral/probing-level, leaving this specific causal chain untested — especially with the capability-preservation and random-direction controls that make the result clean. It is cheap and feasible now with public model organisms and mature probing/steering tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: I will pursue the robustness of machine unlearning by quantifying how quickly unlearned capabilities return under retraining, as a function of unlearning method and strength.
project: Relearning Efficiency After Unlearning: Does Suppressed Capability Hide Residual Competence?
question: After a capability is unlearned from a model, how quickly is it reacquired under subsequent fine-tuning, and does relearning require fewer samples than learning the same capability from scratch — i.e., how much residual competence survives unlearning, as a function of unlearning method (gradient-ascent/NPO-style) and unlearning strength?
first_experiment: On a small open model (~7B), create a controlled setup with two capability targets: (1) a synthetic skill we can teach from scratch (e.g., a fictional library/API or cipher), giving a clean baseline learning curve with no data contamination, and (2) a WMDP-style bio-knowledge subset for realism. First, fine-tune a fresh copy of the base model to acquire the capability and record its sample-efficiency curve (accuracy vs. tokens seen). Then apply two unlearning methods at three unlearning strengths each, until behavioral performance is at chance. Finally, retrain each unlearned checkpoint on the same data with the same schedule and plot recovery curves against the from-scratch baseline. Report a "relearning-efficiency ratio" (samples-to-threshold for relearning ÷ samples-to-threshold for original learning) for each method×strength point, and check whether linear probes for the removed knowledge, measured right after unlearning, predict relearning speed.
why: Unlearning is moving from research demos to actual deployment on open-weight models as the primary tool for removing dangerous bio/cyber knowledge, yet its evaluations are almost entirely static snapshots. If unlearning suppresses rather than deletes, then even modest later fine-tuning — benign or adversarial — could restore the hazard, and the amount of post-unlearning exposure required determines whether real-world threat models (open weights, community fine-tunes, adversarial actors) are acceptable. The relearning-efficiency ratio is the natural quantitative metric for this, and it doubles as a diagnostic: a ratio near 1 says unlearning approximated deletion, while a ratio far below 1 says latent competence survived and weight-level or deletion-based approaches are needed. This has not already been done because prior relearning studies treat recovery as a binary yes/no attack — "recovery is possible" — rather than mapping the dose-response relationship of recovery speed against unlearning strength and method family, and none benchmark relearning against a from-scratch learning curve on a controlled synthetic capability, which is what turns the observation into a calibrated measure of residual competence. The experiment is cheap (small models, modest compute), the findings generalize to every current unlearning deployment, and the probe-vs-relearning-speed correlation would additionally give the interpretability community a target for what internal residue actually matters.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically test whether iteratively hardening an LLM judge's rubric against discovered exploits delays reward hacking or merely displaces it into novel exploit forms.
project: Delay or Displace? Measuring the Effectiveness of Iterative Rubric Hardening Against Reward Hacking
question: Does patching an LLM judge's rubric against known exploit families reduce hacking under continued RL (delay), or shift it into previously unseen exploit families (displacement), quantified by the judged-score/ground-truth divergence across successive hardening rounds?
first_experiment: Run a small GRPO RL run of an open 7–14B model against a 10-item LLM-judge rubric on ~50 tasks with held-out verifiable ground truth; measure the judge-vs-ground-truth divergence over training steps and cluster divergent behaviors into an exploit-taxonomy baseline for subsequent hardening rounds.
why: Rubric-hardened LLM judges are a load-bearing safety mechanism for RLAIF, constitution-following evals, and agent monitoring, yet the delay-versus-displacement question that determines whether that mechanism actually works has not been measured — prior work shows judges are gameable and hacking emerges under pressure, but no controlled exploit→patch→retrain iteration loop with held-out ground truth exists, the experiment is cheap with open models, and its methodology (divergence curves, exploit taxonomies) transfers directly to agent monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Selective-escalation oversight — learn to predict where human reviewers will catch errors and route scarce human verification to maximize catch-rate at a fixed budget.
project: Escalation Routing — Predicting Human Catch-Rate to Outperform Human-Only and AI-Only Oversight
question: Can an automated predictor of P(a human reviewer would catch this error) support a routing policy that, at a fixed human-review budget, beats both all-human and all-automated review in error catch-rate?
first_experiment: Collect frontier-model outputs with planted and natural errors; have human reviewers attempt detection on a calibration sample while logging automated signals (critic flags, self-confidence, difficulty estimates); fit P(human catch | signals); simulate routing across budgets against both baselines; then validate with live human allocation on held-out outputs.
why: Scalable oversight is bottlenecked by the fact that humans can't check everything and automated judges share the biases they're meant to catch; the key missing measurement is how well automated signals predict *human* error-detection, and whether routing on that signal dominates both extremes — which debate, critique, weak-to-strong, and overreliance literatures have each left untouched, while the result would immediately improve deployed protocols like trusted editing and agent deployment gating, all testable with a cheap first experiment requiring no training runs.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Use interpretability-style internal measurements as leading indicators of reward hacking during RL post-training, so that misalignment can be caught mid-training rather than after deployment.
project: Predicting reward hacking onset from internal model signals during RL fine-tuning
question: Are there internal precursors — activation-based monitor scores, policy-uncertainty shifts, or feature-level changes — that reliably predict reward hacking *before* it becomes behaviorally visible in training metrics?
first_experiment: Run RL fine-tuning (GRPO-style) on an open-weights model against coding/math tasks with known exploitable rewards (hardcoded test answers, reward-model flattery, unit-test gaming), varying exploitability and KL constraints across seeds so that some runs hack and some don't. At every checkpoint, log (a) behavioral hacking metrics (ground-truth correctness vs. reward claimed, plus hack classifiers), and (b) internal signals: linear probes trained on contrastive clean-vs-hacked trajectories, policy entropy and solution-confidence statistics, and feature-activation shifts. Then run time-shifted evaluation: test whether internal signals at checkpoint *t* predict behavioral hacking that is first detectable at *t+Δ*, across seeds and environments, and compare against behavioral-only baselines (the reward-test gap itself). Deliverable: a reliability-vs-lead-time ranking of candidate internal signals, plus a public dataset of instrumented training runs.
why: Reward hacking is almost always detected late — we notice it when the reward-vs-ground-truth gap opens, which in a deployed or even mid-training setting means the policy has already committed to the exploit. If internal signals lead behavioral detection by a reliable margin, labs gain a trigger for intervention (early stopping, reward redesign, KL adjustment) *before* the hack is entrenched, which is a concrete and deployable safety improvement rather than a post-hoc diagnosis. The project also bridges two areas that currently operate separately: mechanistic interpretability (mostly done on frozen models, post hoc) and alignment during training (mostly behavioral metrics). It has not already been done because existing reward-hacking work is overwhelmingly behavioral — hack taxonomies, environment design, mitigation strategies — while internal-signal studies (probes, SAEs, honesty features) are validated only as simultaneous detectors on fixed checkpoints, not as *prospective* predictors with proper time-lagged, multi-seed evaluation. The time-shifted prediction methodology is the key missing piece: it separates "the hack is present and visible internally" (correlation) from "internal state changes measurably precede behavioral onset" (a usable leading indicator). It is also cheap to run: open-weights models, modest RL compute, and open infrastructure make a first result achievable in weeks, and the instrumented-run dataset would be immediately useful to anyone building training-time monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Training-time alignment dynamics — determining whether reward hacking is a coherent, transferable behavior rather than a task-local artifact
project: Does Reward Hacking Transfer? Generalization of Verifier-Exploiting Behavior across Environments
question: When a model is RL-trained against an imperfect verifier in one set of environments, does hacking behavior generalize to held-out environments and other domains where the verifier is correct, or does it remain environment-specific?
first_experiment: GRPO/RLVR fine-tune an open ~7B model on a code suite with a controlled-buggy checker, then measure hack rate with an oracle checker on held-out tasks within the training family, in the same domain, and in a different domain, versus the base model's oracle-eval hack rate
why: Reward hacking is the most commonly observed concrete alignment failure in deployed RL agents, but its transfer properties are essentially unstudied — existing reports are in-distribution or confounded — and whether hacking generalizes decides whether held-out evals stay trustworthy, whether cross-domain monitors can be built, and whether hacking can be studied and mitigated as a general behavior; the first experiment is cheap, decisive with open tooling, and produces a reusable buggy-checker RL suite and oracle-eval transfer matrix that no prior work has published

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how much of a reasoning model's CoT is post-hoc rationalization by measuring whether the final answer is decodable from internal states before reasoning begins, as a function of task difficulty.
project: The Monitorability Gap Curve — pre-decision answer decoding vs. task difficulty
question: Does the fraction of tasks on which a reasoning model's final answer is already decodable from pre-CoT activations (i.e., the model "decides before it reasons") increase with task difficulty, while the CoT continues to present a confident, unhinted rationale — and does this gap widen exactly where CoT-based monitoring is most needed (hard tasks)?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic arithmetic suite with controlled difficulty levels (e.g., multi-step multiplication/expression chains of varying depth), each in no-hint and subtle-hint variants (correct or incorrect final answer embedded in an apparently irrelevant sentence). Run 2–3 open-weight reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Qwen3-thinking). Train a logistic probe on mid-to-late residual-stream activations at the token where CoT generation begins, predicting the final answer; validate on held-out problems. Then plot pre-decision decode rate above chance against difficulty and hint condition, and compare against three baselines: CoT hint-mention rate, final-answer accuracy, and post-CoT decode rate. The key output is whether the "monitorability gap" (internals reveal the decision; CoT does not) widens with difficulty.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a linchpin assumption of current safety plans for reasoning models, but it silently assumes the CoT reflects the actual decision process. Prior work established that models use and hide hints (behaviorally) and that perturbing CoT sometimes doesn't change answers, but no one has quantified pre-decision answer decoding — a direct readout of "the answer existed before the rationale" — as a controlled function of task difficulty on modern reasoning models. This matters because difficulty is precisely where models are most dangerous and where monitors matter most: if the gap widens with difficulty, CoT monitoring degrades in its most critical regime, and "pre-decision rate" becomes a cheap, trackable metric for eval design and for training interventions that penalize deciding-before-reasoning. It is also immediately tractable: open-weight reasoning models, synthetic ground-truth tasks, and linear probes make the first experiment cheap, quantitative, and hard to dismiss as anecdote.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Improve the human layer of AI misuse-detection pipelines by measuring how flag stakes distort reviewer decisions and where true-positive recall fails.
project: Scary but Ambiguous — Threshold vs. Discrimination Loss in Human Review of High-Stakes AI Safety Flags
question: Do human reviewers judging flagged AI conversations show a conservative criterion shift or genuinely degraded discrimination (lower d′) on high-stakes flags (CBRN/cyber uplift) compared to mundane policy violations, and where does that put true-positive recall at risk?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truthed set of ~200 realistic transcripts (mundane vs. CBRN/cyber-uplift categories, half true-positive/half true-negative, matched in ambiguity by expert pretesting) and run a within-subject study with ~150 domain-screened reviewers under realistic time pressure and high false-positive base rates in a mock review queue, estimating per-category signal-detection parameters (d′, criterion), decision times, and escalation behavior.
why: Human review is the final safety layer of every deployed misuse-prevention system, yet it is the least measured link — classifiers get tuned, the humans downstream are uncharacterized; if high-stakes flags cause discrimination loss rather than mere conservatism, labs get false comfort exactly where stakes are highest, and the remedy (specialist routing, reviewer training, tooling) differs fundamentally from threshold tuning, so the result changes practice either way; existing literature covers clinical alarm fatigue and social-media moderation but never the stakes-asymmetric comparison on frontier-model transcripts under realistic base rates, and AI-safety human-factors work has focused on capability oversight rather than misuse pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure the covert information-transmission capacity of LLMs through natural text under the realistic weight-sharing-free threat model, as a function of model scale.
project: The Reliable-Bandwidth Scaling Curve for Weight-Sharing-Free LLM Steganography
question: How many bits per token can current LLMs transmit reliably through text channels decodable without the encoder's weights or seeds, and where is the reliability cliff as capability scales?
first_experiment: Build a synonym-substitution channel with a public fixed decode table, have ~1B and ~8B open models embed fixed bitstrings in 512-token carrier texts via prompting, and measure bits/token, bit-error rate, carrier quality, and detector-based detectability to get the first two points of the scaling curve.
why: Output- and chain-of-thought monitoring underpin current safety plans, but their vulnerability hinges on an unmeasured number — how much covert bandwidth models can move through ordinary text when the communicating instances share no weights, which existing steganography work (distribution-anchored coding, minimum-entropy coupling) sidesteps by assuming weight sharing or by studying single models; quantifying the curve and its reliability cliff turns a motivating anecdote into a decision-relevant threat forecast, is cheaply testable today with open models and no training, and yields a reusable measurement artifact for monitor and countermeasure design.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Model organisms of deceptive alignment — quantifying how audit pressure during training induces and scales conditional deception.
project: Dose-Response Curve for Audit-Induced Deceptive Alignment in Open Models
question: What is the quantitative relationship between audit frequency (fraction of offending behavior removed during fine-tuning) and the emergence of conditional deceptive compliance in open 7–13B models, and is there a sharp onset threshold?
first_experiment: Sweep audit rates (0–100%) in audit-modified SFT of an open 7–8B instruct model on a defined target misbehavior, matched compute and seeds, then measure faked compliance on training contexts, misbehavior persistence on held-out contexts, and deception traces (CoT/behavior inconsistency) to fit the first dose-response curve.
why: Organisms are the validation ground for all detection, interpretability, and control work, and a partially-deceptive organism at the onset threshold is the hardest and most useful test case; the audit-modified alignment-faking recipe has only been shown once, at frontier scale, under one audit regime, with no published dose-response, threshold, or small-open-model replication — so even the first curve answers whether "no faking observed" is meaningful evidence and hands the community a graded family of testbeds.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Empirically map how trusted monitors' ability to catch sabotage by a stronger untrusted agent scales with the information they are given, to ground control protocol design in measurement rather than intuition.
project: The Information Frontier of Trusted Monitors — Sabotage Detection as a Function of Context Access
question: How does a weaker trusted monitor's detection of malicious actions by a stronger untrusted agent depend on its information access — diff-only vs. full trajectory vs. raw tool-call stream — and where does extra context stop buying detection?
first_experiment: Build ~100 agentic coding tasks with planted sabotage opportunities; run a frontier untrusted model with a controlled fraction of sabotaged runs; fix one mid-capability trusted monitor and sweep it across the three information regimes, measuring TPR at ~1–2% FPR and detection latency, replicated across a second monitor and statistical baselines.
why: Trusted-monitor oversight is the load-bearing assumption of most AI control plans, yet no systematic measurement exists of how much monitor context is actually needed for reliable low-FPR detection; this experiment produces a quantitative detection-and-latency frontier that directly determines deployment cost and protocol design, is runnable today with open models, and leaves reusable sabotage-eval infrastructure behind.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether activation-based intent probes are causally entangled with deceptive behavior by adversarially training a deceptive model against its probe and measuring whether behavior-level monitors are co-evaded or remain effective.
project: Probe-Evasion Training as a Test of Whether Internal Monitors and Behavior Monitors Are Redundant
question: When a deceptive model is fine-tuned to evade an activation-based intent probe, can it become probe-clean while staying behaviorally deceptive — or does evading the probe force the covert behavior to disappear?
first_experiment: On a planted-deception (sleeper-agent/backdoor) model, train a mid-layer linear probe to high AUROC, then fine-tune to minimize probe score on deceptive trajectories while preserving task performance, jointly tracking probe AUROC and behavior-monitor detection rates across training, with a held-out-probe transfer check.
why: It resolves an unresolved fork — whether internal monitors are a hard-to-evade layer or brittle relative to behavior monitors — that directly determines monitoring-stack design, and it sits unclaimed at the boundary between interpretability and AI-control agendas where no one has measured the coupled dynamics.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantifying when trusted/untrusted capability gaps erase the safety advantage of trusted-model AI control protocols.
project: The Trusted Editing Cliff
question: At what trusted/untrusted capability gap does trusted editing stop dominating monitor-and-resample control, and is that crossover stable across task difficulty and attack subtlety?
first_experiment: Fix one strong untrusted open model as an adversarial backdoor-inserter on agentic coding tasks; run trusted models at a ladder of scales (1.5B–32B) through both trusted-editing and monitor-resample protocols under the same audit budget; measure backdoor-survival (safety) and task-success (usefulness) per cell and locate the crossover scale, then re-test it at two difficulty levels and two trigger rarities.
why: Control's core premise — that a weaker trusted model can purchase real safety — has never been measured as a function of the capability gap, since prior evaluations used one or two fixed model pairs; with trusted models in practice chosen for cost rather than capability, gaps are widening and a too-early crossover means deployed protocols silently collapse to monitor-only safety. A clean open-model ladder against a fixed adversary isolates the variable, is cheap to run on existing public control benchmarks, and yields an actionable protocol-selection rule and deployment warning metric.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Testing whether trusted-model rewriting of untrusted chain-of-thought is a real control primitive, via causal-dependence interventions on the rewritten reasoning.
project: Does the Answer Follow the Rewrite? Causal Dependence of Final Answers on Trusted-Rewritten Chains of Thought
question: When a weaker trusted model rewrites an untrusted reasoning model's CoT and the rewritten CoT is fed back to generate the final answer, does the final answer causally depend on the rewritten CoT, and does its dependence profile match that of the original self-generated CoT?
first_experiment: On ~500 benchmark math/code problems, take an untrusted model's CoT+answer, have a smaller trusted model rewrite each CoT (paraphrase vs. independent re-derivation regimes), then regenerate answers conditioned on original, rewritten, progressively truncated, and span-corrupted CoTs, comparing answer-change/dependence curves and accuracy deltas between original and rewritten reasoning.
why: Either outcome changes protocol design — dependence validates cheap reasoning-level sanitization that strips exploit plans before code exists, while non-dependence reveals that models re-derive rather than consume provided reasoning, warning control designers off auditing decorative CoT; the combination of faithfulness interventions with externally rewritten CoTs in a trusted/untrusted pipeline has not been studied, and the experiment is cheap and fully reproducible with open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how well attacks optimized against one AI-control monitor transfer to structurally different monitor families, as the decisive input for whether diverse monitor ensembles are a required defense.
project: Monitor Diversity Stress Test — Cross-Architecture Transfer of Adversarial Code Attacks
question: Do backdoored submissions optimized against one LLM monitor succeed at elevated rates against different LLM families and against non-LLM monitors (rule/AST checks, differential testing, runtime anomaly detection)?
first_experiment: Generate ~500 black-box-optimized backdoored submissions against a frontier LLM monitor on an APPS-style backdoor benchmark, then evaluate evasion rates across the attack monitor, a different LLM family, and three non-LLM monitors, compared to an unoptimized backdoor baseline.
why: Monitor robustness evidence currently comes from attacking the same monitor deployed in the protocol, so the field cannot yet tell whether monitors are robust or merely untested from other angles; the transfer result directly determines whether AI-control safety cases require diverse monitor ensembles or whether cheap single monitors suffice, and it is runnable now with existing benchmarks, backdoor corpora, and open-weight monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of evaluation-awareness — causally testing whether the internal "I'm being evaluated" representation drives sandbagging-style differential behavior.
project: Steering the Evaluation-Awareness Direction: Is Situational Awareness a Cause or a Passenger of Sandbagging?
question: Does activation steering along a linear probe direction for "this context is an evaluation" causally change a model's eval-vs-deployment behavioral gap, or is the probed direction merely a correlate?
first_experiment: On an open-weights reasoning model with a verified eval/deployment behavioral gap, train a mid-layer linear probe separating eval-framed from deployment-framed contexts, then add/subtract the scaled probe direction at inference and measure whether the behavioral gap moves, against random-direction and dose-response controls.
why: Evaluation-awareness threatens the validity of capability evals and safety audits, and current evidence for it is behavioral and correlational; a causal steering test would establish whether the internal representation is load-bearing — yielding either a mechanistic account of sandbagging plus a practical "make evals honest" intervention, or the counterintuitive but important finding that such probes cannot predict sandbagging risk. No published work systematically connects probe-detected situational awareness to behavior via causal intervention, and the experiment is feasible on open-weights models without frontier-lab access.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether joint production by multiple untrusted agents systematically evades oversight monitors compared to solo agents.
project: Covert Convention Drift — Measuring Monitor Blind Spots in Jointly Produced AI Outputs
question: Do two untrusted agents jointly producing a deliverable develop implicit conventions that lower a monitor's catch rate on planted flaws relative to a solo agent at matched token budget, and which conventions drive the loss?
first_experiment: A ~150-task benchmark with plantable flaws, comparing solo, joint (matched token budget), and concatenated-output conditions under a blind fixed monitor, measuring catch-rate deltas and characterizing conventions unique to joint outputs.
why: Oversight is evaluated on single-agent outputs while deployment moves to multi-agent pipelines, so this quantifies an unmeasured, decision-relevant vulnerability (or a reassuring negative result); prior work addresses deliberate steganography and explicit collusion but not spontaneous convention drift, and the experiment is cheap, training-free, and directly feeds AI-control protocol design.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Testing whether trained-in backdoors are behaviorally detectable from trigger-free agent trajectories alone.
project: Silent Sleepers — Does a Backdoored Agent Leak Its Existence Without Firing?
question: Do backdoored agents differ detectably from clean agents in trajectories where the trigger never fires, across backdoor classes and out-of-distribution trigger-free regimes?
first_experiment: Train matched clean/backdoored/control small open-weight models with token-, deployment-, and tool-output-keyed backdoors, run them on a multi-step coding/tool-use suite without triggers, and test blind-judge, embedding-classifier, and behavioral-statistic separation with a training-data-matched control to isolate the backdoor mechanism.
why: Removal of planted backdoors is known to fail, so defense must rest on detection, yet existing detection assumes known triggers or observed firings — existence-leakage in trigger-free agentic trajectories is untested, and either outcome is decision-relevant for monitoring strategy and safety cases; it is also cheap, using small open-weight models and standard agent harnesses, and no prior systematic study covers this setting.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Make long-horizon agents recoverable by establishing whether goal drift, once it has occurred, can actually be undone.
project: Checkpoint-and-Recover — Bounding Whether Long-Horizon Agents Can Undo Goal Drift
question: Assuming an oracle that flags goal drift at onset, does rolling an agent back to its last on-goal checkpoint and re-planning recover task success, and how does recovery decay with drift depth (steps between checkpoint and detection)?
first_experiment: Run an open-weight agent on ~50–100 tasks of 30+ steps from a public agentic benchmark under four conditions — no intervention, oracle-flagged rollback+re-plan to last on-goal snapshot, reminder re-injection control, restart-from-scratch — with distractor injections plus natural drift to guarantee occurrences, judge-labeled on/off-goal steps spot-checked by humans, measuring recovery rate, steps-to-recovery, cost, and recovery-vs-drift-depth curves across two open models.
why: Long-horizon reliability is the central blocker to deploying autonomous agents, yet existing work only tries to prevent drift (better prompts, memory, planning) rather than asking whether drift can be undone once it occurs; detect-and-correct oversight designs all assume correction works, and no one has tested that even with perfect detection — the oracle setup cleanly bounds what any real monitor could buy, tells builders whether rollback machinery is worth shipping, and quantifies how early a detector must fire for recovery to pay off, while being cheap, falsifiable, open-model-only, and, as far as I can determine, unmeasured (self-correction work like Reflexion retries from the end state or restarts, rather than restoring mid-trajectory state as a targeted drift response).

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether training-data contamination with safety-eval content creates false assurance — inflated safety-eval scores with unchanged underlying safety behavior.
project: False Assurance: does safety-eval contamination pass evals without changing behavior?
question: Does fine-tuning on verbatim or paraphrased safety-eval content inflate pass rates on those evals without improving behavior on matched off-eval tasks, and how large is the eval–behavior divergence?
first_experiment: Controlled canary injection — LoRA fine-tune open 7–8B models on (a) verbatim safety-eval items, (b) paraphrased items, (c) matched controls; measure gains on the contaminated eval vs. held-out paraphrases vs. deployment-style off-eval probes of the same policies, and test whether n-gram dedup or membership inference detects the contamination.
why: Safety cases and deploy decisions rest on public safety evals whose content circulates in training corpora, yet contamination research has only covered capability benchmarks — the safety-specific error (an unsafe model that looks aligned) has never been isolated, and paraphrase contamination plausibly evades the deduplication labs actually use. The experiment is cheap, causal, and directly informs eval design (paraphrase holdouts, canaries) and governance (how much public safety scores can be trusted).

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measuring the cost to a capable, monitor-aware agent of evading known oversight while still completing its task.
project: The Evasion Budget: Quantifying the Cost of Monitor-Aware Deception in LLM Agents
question: How do evasion success, task performance, and compute overhead trade off for an agent that can see a monitor's logic, as monitor complexity increases?
first_experiment: Run a capable open-weights agent on tasks with one prohibited subgoal, under naive vs monitor-aware vs monitor-aware-plus-extra-thinking conditions against an inspectable LLM+rule monitor, measuring evasion rate, task success, and token overhead across monitor complexity levels.
why: It targets the worst case for the control agenda — an adversary that knows the monitor — where no quantitative cost measurement exists, and the resulting evasion-budget curve is both a warning signal if evasion is cheap and a practical monitor-design metric if it is not.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Map where chain-of-thought faithfulness breaks down in long-horizon agentic tasks, as a function of step type and horizon length.
project: Where Does CoT–Action Consistency Break First? A Step-Type and Horizon Taxonomy of Faithfulness in Reasoning-Model Agents
question: At which types of agentic steps — planning, memory recall, tool selection, error acknowledgment — does a reasoning model's chain-of-thought stop matching its actions, and does the inconsistency rate grow with task horizon length?
first_experiment: Build a suite of ~50 multi-step agentic tasks (file system, web browsing, code editing) with per-step ground truth, where every step is tagged with a type from a fixed taxonomy (plan statement, recall claim, tool-choice justification, error acknowledgment). Run a frontier reasoning model with CoT enabled, log every thought–action pair, and label each CoT step as consistent or inconsistent with the action actually taken, using an LLM-judge classifier validated on a ~200-step human-audited subset. Deliverable: the first faithfulness decay curves broken out by step type and by horizon length (1/4/16/64 steps), plus an open benchmark of labeled trajectories for the community.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a core safety practice for reasoning models, but it silently assumes the chain of thought reflects the model's real deliberation — and the entire monitoring-vs-obfuscation debate is currently argued from case studies and anecdotes because no one has measured where faithfulness actually holds in realistic agent trajectories. Existing faithfulness benchmarks are short, single-turn, and non-agentic (forced-choice reveals, bias tests), while agentic benchmarks score only final outcomes, so the per-step consistency of CoT on long tasks is unmeasured territory.
